questions.strategy: Three options accept that all three findings matter. They differ in what the nurse does next: label the wound, wait for a fever, or assess more closely now.

steps.detail: Age 81, daily immunosuppressant, poor intake for 3 weeks.

steps.action: Drop the option that discounts one
steps.detail: Nutrition affects immune protection too.
Labeling infection overreaches, and waiting for fever delays.

elimination.verdict: All three raise concern, so closer assessment against baseline starts on admission.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: An 81 year old client is admitted with a wound on the left lower leg. The nurse reviews the history to identify factors that may affect the client's immune protection. Which information does the nurse review for this purpose? Select all that apply.

options.text: Current medications, including any that suppress the immune system
options.rationale: Immunosuppressants can affect immune function.

options.text: Recent food intake and any change in weight
options.rationale: Malnutrition impairs immune cell function. Protein, vitamins, and minerals support immune responses and wound healing.

options.text: Chronic health conditions
options.rationale: Chronic disease impacts immune competence and disease susceptibility.

options.text: Pain rating at the wound today
options.rationale: This is an assessment finding to compare with baseline. It is not a factor that affects immune protection.

options.text: Recent environmental exposures
options.rationale: Environmental exposures are one of the factors that affect immunity.

options.text: Size of the redness around the wound on admission
options.rationale: This is the baseline for the wound. It is not a factor that affects immune protection.

questions.takeaway: The factors that affect immunity are age and developmental stage, nutritional status, disease and overall health, medications, and environmental exposures.
questions.strategy: Every option is something the nurse collects. Separate the factors that affect immune protection from the findings that describe the wound.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Age, nutrition, disease, medications, environmental exposures.
Medications, intake and weight, chronic conditions, and exposures all match.

steps.action: Leave out what does not match
steps.detail: A pain rating and the size of the redness are findings, not factors.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.scenario: An 82 year old client was admitted 2 days ago after a fall and has a scrape on the left lower leg from the fall. The client takes a daily immunosuppressant and has eaten about one quarter of each meal since admission. On admission and again today the redness extends 1 cm around the scrape, the area is warm with mild swelling, pain is 2 of 10, and the client walks to the bathroom without help. Oral temperature today is 36.6 °C. The client says, "I have no fever, so there is no infection in my leg."
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Report the scrape to the provider today as infected because of the immunosuppressant
options.rationale: Immunosuppressants can affect immune function, but the scrape findings are unchanged from admission. Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection.

options.text: Compare the scrape findings with the admission baseline at each assessment
options.rationale: Findings are compared with the patient's baseline and changes are documented over time.

options.text: Arrange a review of the client's intake of protein, vitamins, and minerals
options.rationale: Malnutrition impairs immune cell function; adequate protein, vitamins, and minerals support immune responses and wound healing. The client eats one quarter of each meal.

options.text: Use the oral temperature as the trigger for closer checks of the scrape
options.rationale: This client's medication and age reduce immune protection, so the nurse watches the scrape findings and their trend, not the temperature alone.

options.text: Inflammation in a client with reduced immune protection
options.rationale: The scrape shows cardinal signs that match admission. Older age, an immunosuppressant, and poor intake all reduce immune protection, so close assessment is needed.

options.text: Infection masked by the immunosuppressant
options.rationale: The medication raises concern, but every scrape finding is the same as on admission. Nothing is worsening that would point to infection.

options.text: Expected healing with no added risk
options.rationale: Age, the immunosuppressant, and poor intake are all factors that affect immunity, so the risk is not ordinary.

options.text: Failure of the tissue repair stage
options.rationale: The findings are unchanged after 2 days, which does not by itself show failed repair.

options.text: Size of the redness and swelling around the scrape, compared with admission
options.rationale: A change in size from baseline is a key sign of worsening.

options.text: Size of the redness alone, measured once a day
options.rationale: Redness alone leaves out swelling, pain, and function, and once a day may miss change.

options.text: Oral temperature as the main sign of infection
options.rationale: Temperature is one finding. With reduced immune protection, the scrape findings and function are trended alongside it.

options.text: Pain rating and ability to walk on the left leg
options.rationale: Pain and decreased function are cardinal signs to trend over time.

questions.takeaway: Age, immunosuppressants, and poor nutrition reduce immune protection. The nurse responds by comparing every cardinal sign with baseline over time and supporting nutrition, not by labeling unchanged findings as infection or waiting for a fever.
questions.strategy: The condition pool has a tempting choice: infection masked by the immunosuppressant. The cue that decides is that every scrape finding is the same as on admission; risk calls for closer comparison, not a diagnosis.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Age 82, daily immunosuppressant, one quarter of meals.
Redness, warmth, swelling, pain, and walking are unchanged.
Inflammation in a client with reduced immune protection.
Compare with baseline, review nutrition, trend size, pain, and function.

elimination.verdict: Actions: compare with the admission baseline and review nutrition. Condition: inflammation with reduced immune protection. Parameters: redness and swelling size against admission, and pain with walking.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: An 81 year old client was admitted 3 days ago with a wound on the left lower leg and takes a daily immunosuppressant. On admission the client was alert, talkative, and ate about one quarter of each meal. Today the redness is 1 cm around the wound and pain is 2 of 10, both the same as on admission. Oral temperature is 36.5 °C. The client has slept through two meals, is slow to answer questions, and ate a few bites at breakfast. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Report the change in alertness and intake now, even though the wound and temperature are unchanged
options.rationale: The client has changed from baseline in behavior and function. In a client with reduced immune protection, the nurse does not rely on the wound or on fever alone, and worsening is reported.

options.text: Wake the client for lunch, encourage fluids, and report if alertness is no better this afternoon
options.rationale: Supporting intake is reasonable care, but it delays the report of a change from baseline in a client with reduced immune protection.

options.text: Report the wound as infected now, because the client is at risk and is sleeping more than before
options.rationale: Reporting is right, but the wound findings have not changed. The report should state what changed, not name a cause.

options.text: Document the change in alertness, and report it if the temperature rises above the admission reading
options.rationale: This client takes an immunosuppressant and is 81 years old. The nurse does not wait for a fever before acting on a change in behavior.

questions.takeaway: Compare the whole client with baseline, not only the wound. A change in behavior or function is reported, and fever is not required, especially when immune protection is reduced.
questions.strategy: The wound and the temperature both say nothing has changed, which makes waiting look reasonable. The deciding cue is the client: alert and talkative on admission, now slow to answer and sleeping through meals.

steps.detail: Unchanged.
Alertness and intake are both worse than on admission.
Age 81 and an immunosuppressant: do not wait for fever.

steps.action: Choose the report that states findings
steps.detail: One report names infection, which the wound does not support.

elimination.verdict: Report the change in alertness and intake now.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: During the 0800 assessment, the nurse finds a warm, red, swollen area 4 cm across on a client's left lower leg. The admission assessment at 2000 yesterday describes both legs with no redness or swelling. The client is alert and oriented and has not mentioned the area. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Ask when the area appeared and about any recent bump or fall, then assess warmth, pain, and use of the leg
options.rationale: Assessment comes first: ask about symptom onset and recent injury, then assess warmth, color, swelling, pain, and functional ability. The client is alert and oriented and can give this history now.

options.text: Report the new area to the provider now, since it was not present on the admission assessment 12 hours ago
options.rationale: The area is new, which makes reporting tempting, but the report would have no onset, injury history, or full assessment. The nurse gathers these first.

options.text: Mark and measure the area, document it as the new baseline, and recheck it at the next scheduled assessment
options.rationale: Measuring helps, but this skips the history and the full assessment of pain and function, and treats a new finding as routine.

options.text: Report the area as an infection that began after admission, then ask about any recent bump or fall
options.rationale: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection, and the history should come before any report.

questions.takeaway: A new finding is assessed before it is reported: ask about onset and recent injury, then assess the cardinal signs and function, then decide.
questions.strategy: A and B both respond to a new finding, and B feels urgent because the area was not there 12 hours ago. The cue that decides is "alert and oriented": the client can give the onset and injury history right now, so assessment comes first.

steps.detail: Both legs had no redness or swelling at 2000.
The client is alert and oriented.
Onset, recent injury, then warmth, pain, and use of the leg.
Reporting without data or calling it infection skips assessment.

elimination.verdict: Ask about onset and recent injury, then assess warmth, pain, and use of the leg.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A client bumped the left lower leg on a bed frame 2 days ago. The skin over the area is intact. Yesterday the red area was 3 cm across, warm, and swollen, and pain was 5 of 10. Today the red area is 3 cm across, warm, and swollen, and pain is 5 of 10. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C. A family member says, "It is still red and swollen after 2 days, so it must be infected." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Redness that lasts 2 days can mean an infection is starting, so I will report it to the provider now to be safe."
options.rationale: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection. The area has not changed since yesterday, so there is no worsening to report.

options.text: "These signs can come from the bump. They match yesterday's, so I will keep comparing and report any worsening."
options.rationale: Inflammation can occur without infection after an injury. The findings match yesterday's baseline, so the nurse keeps comparing over time and reports worsening symptoms.

options.text: "These signs come from the bump itself, so the leg needs no more checks from me unless a fever develops."
options.rationale: Fever is not the trigger the nurse waits for. Findings are compared with baseline and changes are documented over time.

options.text: "These signs can come from the bump itself, but I will report them now because redness and swelling are both present."
options.rationale: This option names the injury as a cause but then treats redness and swelling as enough to report. Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection, and nothing has changed.

questions.takeaway: Inflammation after an injury can last for days without infection. When the findings match the earlier baseline, the nurse keeps comparing and reports worsening, rather than acting on redness and swelling alone.
questions.strategy: A and D both feel cautious, and caution pulls students toward reporting. The cue that decides is that every finding today matches yesterday: 3 cm, warm, swollen, 5 of 10, intact skin.

steps.detail: A bump on a bed frame with intact skin.
Size, warmth, swelling, and pain are unchanged.
Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection.
The nurse compares over time, not only when a fever appears.

elimination.verdict: These signs can come from the bump; keep comparing and report any worsening.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.nursesNote:
Yesterday 0800, day 3 after a bump to the left lower leg: red area 2 cm across, warmth limited to the red area, pain 3 of 10 at rest and 3 of 10 when standing, walks to bathroom without help, skin intact, oral temperature 36.6 °C.

Today 0800: Red area on left lower leg is 2 cm across. Warmth extends from the red area to the left ankle. Pain is 3 of 10 at rest and 6 of 10 when standing. Walks to bathroom without help. Skin over the area is intact. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: Red area on left lower leg is 2 cm across
segments.rationale: The red area is the same size as yesterday.

segments.text: Warmth extends from the red area to the left ankle
segments.rationale: Yesterday the warmth was limited to the red area. Warmth spreading to the ankle is a worsening cardinal sign, even though the redness has not grown.

segments.text: Pain is 3 of 10 at rest and 6 of 10 when standing
segments.rationale: Pain at rest is unchanged, but pain when standing rose from 3 to 6 of 10. A rise in pain is a worsening symptom to report.

segments.text: Walks to bathroom without help
segments.rationale: Function is the same as yesterday.

segments.text: Skin over the area is intact
segments.rationale: The skin is intact, as yesterday.

segments.text: Oral temperature is 36.8 °C
segments.rationale: A difference of 0.2 °C from yesterday is not a meaningful change.

questions.takeaway: Compare each cardinal sign with yesterday, one by one. A sign can worsen while another stays the same, as when warmth spreads while the red area keeps its size.
questions.strategy: The traps hide inside unchanged findings. The red area is the same, so warmth looks the same too, but it now reaches the ankle. Pain at rest is the same, but pain when standing doubled.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 2 cm both days.
Limited to the red area yesterday; reaches the ankle today.
At rest 3 of 10 both days; standing 3 then 6 of 10.
Unchanged or a 0.2 °C difference.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A client bumped the left lower leg 5 days ago and the skin is intact. Yesterday at 0800 the note read: red area 2 cm across, pain 5 of 10, walks to the bathroom with one person helping. Today at 0800 the red area is still 2 cm across, the client rates pain 7 of 10, and the client is unable to stand on the left leg. The client slept in a chair overnight with the left leg bent and says, "I just slept on it wrong. Please do not bother anyone about it." Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Respect the client's request, document today's findings, and recheck the left leg in 4 hours
options.rationale: Listening to the client matters, but pain and function are clearly worse than baseline. A request not to bother anyone does not remove the duty to report worsening.

options.text: Give the ordered pain relief, reassess the pain in 1 hour, and report then if the client still cannot stand
options.rationale: Treating the pain is reasonable care, but it delays the report of two findings that are already clearly worse than baseline.

options.text: Report the rise in pain and the loss of standing now, and explain to the client why it needs to be reported
options.rationale: Pain has risen from 5 to 7 of 10 and the client can no longer stand on the left leg. Worsening is reported whatever the suspected cause, and the nurse tells the client why.

options.text: Ask the client to stand once more with help, and report only if the client is still unable to stand
options.rationale: The assessment already shows the change. Repeating it delays the report and adds nothing.

questions.takeaway: Changes from baseline that show worsening are reported. A client's explanation is heard and documented, and the report is still made.
questions.strategy: Three things pull toward waiting: the redness has not changed, the client offers another cause, and the client has asked the nurse not to report. The deciding cue is that pain and function are both worse than yesterday, and the nurse reports findings without having to settle the cause.

steps.detail: Redness same. Pain 5 to 7 of 10. Walking with help to unable to stand.
It is heard, but it does not change the findings.
Pain relief does not replace reporting a loss of function.

steps.action: Do not repeat what is known
steps.detail: Standing again only delays the report.

elimination.verdict: Report the rise in pain and the loss of standing now, and explain why.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A nurse is orienting a new nurse to the care of a client with a red, swollen area around a wound on the right heel. The client has eaten poorly for a month. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C. Which statement by the new nurse requires correction?

options.text: "I will compare what I find today with the earlier notes before I decide anything."
options.rationale: This is correct. Findings are compared with the client's baseline.

options.text: "A temperature inside the range does not tell me this wound is free of infection."
options.rationale: This sounds wrong but is correct. The nurse does not rely on fever alone; findings at the site and changes from baseline are assessed as well.

options.text: "The redness is the same size as yesterday, so the wound is the same as yesterday."
options.rationale: Redness is one finding. Swelling, pain, and functional ability are assessed and compared with baseline before the nurse can say nothing has changed.

options.text: "Poor intake of protein and vitamins for a month can slow the healing of this wound."
options.rationale: This is correct. Adequate protein, vitamins, and minerals support immune responses and wound healing.

questions.takeaway: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection, and one unchanged finding does not establish that nothing changed. The nurse assesses every sign, including pain and function, compares with baseline, and does not rely on temperature alone.
questions.strategy: The question asks for the wrong statement. The one that sounds wrong, about temperature, is true; the one that sounds careful judges the whole wound by a single finding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Look for the statement that is not accurate.

steps.action: Test the statement that sounds wrong
steps.detail: A temperature inside the range does not rule out infection, so B is accurate.
C judges the whole wound by redness alone and skips swelling, pain, and function.
Comparing with earlier notes and linking nutrition to healing are accurate.

elimination.verdict: C. One unchanged finding does not show that the wound has not changed.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: A client has a wound on the right heel and has eaten poorly for a month. Yesterday at 0800 the note read: redness 1 cm around the wound, mild swelling, no drainage, pain 2 of 10. Today at 0800 the redness extends 3 cm around the wound, the swelling has increased, the dressing holds thick yellow drainage (pus), and the client rates pain 6 of 10. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C. A new nurse says, "Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection, so I will chart this as inflammation." Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Agree, document the findings as expected inflammation, and compare the heel again at 2000
options.rationale: The rule is quoted correctly, but it no longer fits. There is more than redness and swelling here: the drainage is new, and the redness, swelling, and pain are all worse.

options.text: Report the wider redness, new thick yellow drainage, and higher pain now as findings that suggest infection
options.rationale: Redness has spread from 1 cm to 3 cm, pain has risen from 2 to 6 of 10, and thick yellow drainage is new. Pus is a sign of local infection, and worsening findings are reported.

options.text: Clean away the drainage, apply a fresh dressing, and report if drainage appears again by 2000
options.rationale: Wound care is appropriate, but waiting for the drainage to return delays the report of findings that are already worse.

options.text: Report the findings once the oral temperature rises above the 36.8 °C measured this morning
options.rationale: The nurse does not wait for a fever. The local findings have already changed.

questions.takeaway: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection. Spreading redness, rising pain, and new pus are more than that: they are worsening findings that suggest infection and are reported.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The new nurse's rule is true and it is the trap. Ask what the stem adds beyond redness and swelling, and whether the findings match yesterday.

steps.detail: Redness 1 cm to 3 cm. Pain 2 to 6 of 10. Drainage: none to thick yellow.

steps.action: Test the rule against the stem
steps.detail: "Alone" no longer applies. Drainage is new.
For more drainage, or for a fever.
It states the findings and what they suggest.

elimination.verdict: Report the wider redness, new drainage, and higher pain as findings that suggest infection.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client fell on the sidewalk 1 day ago. The skin over the right wrist is intact. The right wrist is warm, red, and swollen; pain is 5 of 10, was 6 of 10 yesterday, and the swelling is the same size as yesterday. A scrape on the left palm from the same fall now has redness 3 cm around it, was 1 cm yesterday, and pain at the palm is 4 of 10, was 2 of 10 yesterday. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C.

The findings at the right wrist are best explained by [[1]].

The finding that most requires follow up is [[2]].

The nurse does not document the right wrist as infected because [[3]].

options.text: inflammation caused by microorganisms that entered through the skin
options.rationale: Inflammation is the right idea, but the skin over the right wrist is intact, so nothing shows microorganisms entering there.

options.text: inflammation without infection, a protective response to the injury
options.rationale: Inflammation can occur after injury without infection. The skin over the wrist is intact, and the pain is less than yesterday.

options.text: infection, because warmth, redness, and swelling are all present
options.rationale: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection. Inflammation can occur without infection.

options.text: an adaptive immune response directed at a specific antigen
options.rationale: Inflammation is part of innate immunity, a rapid, broad response to the injury.

options.text: the oral temperature of 36.8 °C
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem shows a change in temperature. The palm findings are the ones that changed.

options.text: the pain of 5 of 10 at the right wrist
options.rationale: Pain at the wrist is lower than yesterday's 6 of 10, so it is not worsening.

options.text: the warmth and swelling at the right wrist
options.rationale: Warmth and swelling are cardinal signs of inflammation, and the swelling is the same size as yesterday.

options.text: the redness and pain at the left palm scrape
options.rationale: The palm redness spread from 1 cm to 3 cm and the pain rose from 2 to 4 of 10 since yesterday. Worsening findings over time are documented and reported, and this site has broken skin.

options.text: redness and swelling alone do not establish infection
options.rationale: This is the principle the lecture states. Inflammation can occur without infection, and the wrist findings are not worsening.

options.text: the pain at the right wrist is below 6 of 10
options.rationale: No single pain number rules out infection. What matters is the trend compared with baseline.

options.text: the injury happened only 1 day ago
options.rationale: Time since injury does not rule out infection. The palm scrape from the same fall is worsening within the same day.

options.text: the oral temperature is 36.8 °C
options.rationale: A temperature without fever does not rule out infection, and the nurse does not use it as the reason. Infection is judged on the findings and their change over time.

questions.takeaway: Injury can cause inflammation without infection, and redness and swelling alone do not establish infection. The finding that needs follow up is the one getting worse over time, here the scrape with spreading redness and rising pain.
questions.strategy: Blank 3 holds the trap: a temperature without fever feels like a reason, but it does not rule out infection. Blank 2 needs a comparison with yesterday at both sites, not a judgment from today's numbers alone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Wrist pain lower and swelling the same; palm redness and pain rising.
Inflammation without infection, skin intact.
The palm scrape.
Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection.

elimination.verdict: Inflammation without infection; the redness and pain at the left palm scrape; redness and swelling alone do not establish infection.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: A nurse educator reviews findings from six clients with a new nurse. None of the clients has an abnormal temperature. Which findings suggest infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: A warm, swollen bruise on the left thigh 2 days after a fall, the same size as yesterday, skin intact
options.rationale: Warmth and swelling after a fall with intact skin and no change fit inflammation without infection.

options.text: Redness around a stitched cut on the right forearm that has spread past the line marked yesterday
options.rationale: Redness that extends beyond the marked edge is spreading. Extended redness around a wound points to infection.

options.text: Redness around a stitched cut on the left shin that reaches the line marked yesterday, pain 2 of 10 as yesterday
options.rationale: Reaching the line is not passing it. The redness and pain are unchanged, so this fits inflammation.

options.text: A cut on the right index finger that is red and swollen and now drains thick yellow fluid
options.rationale: Thick yellow drainage is pus, a sign of local infection, along with redness and swelling.

options.text: A blister on the right heel from new shoes, filled with clear fluid, the covering skin unbroken
options.rationale: Clear fluid under intact skin after friction is inflammation from injury. Fluid alone is not pus.

options.text: Red, itchy skin on both hands after cleaning with a new chemical product without gloves, skin intact
options.rationale: An irritant can trigger inflammation without infection. The skin is intact and nothing shows pus or spread.

questions.takeaway: Infection is suggested by pus and by redness that spreads beyond a marked baseline. Unchanged redness, clear blister fluid, and irritant reactions fit inflammation without infection.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The item pairs near twins. Compare the two stitched cuts (past the line versus on the line) and the two fluids (thick yellow drainage versus clear fluid under intact skin).

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Past the line is spread; on the line is unchanged.
Thick yellow drainage is pus; clear blister fluid under intact skin is not.

steps.action: Reject the injury and irritant findings
steps.detail: Bruise and chemical reaction with intact skin and no change.

elimination.verdict: B, D.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: A client admitted 2 days ago takes an immunosuppressant. The admission note describes a 4 cm bruise with mild swelling on the right forearm at the site of a blood draw. Today the client reports a sore, swollen area on the right forearm. The nurse has asked when it began and has assessed warmth, color, swelling, pain, and use of the right hand and forearm. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Report the area to the provider now, since an immunosuppressant can hide the usual signs of infection
options.rationale: Immunosuppressants affect immune function and raise concern, but the nurse first needs to know whether this is the same bruise recorded on admission or a change.

options.text: Recheck the right forearm tomorrow morning to see whether the swollen area has spread further
options.rationale: Waiting a day skips the comparison that can be made right now with the admission note.

options.text: Document today's findings as the new baseline for the right forearm and continue routine care
options.rationale: Replacing the baseline erases the comparison. A change from admission would be missed.

options.text: Compare today's findings with the bruise described in the admission note before deciding what to report
options.rationale: Findings are compared with the patient's baseline. The admission note records a 4 cm bruise with swelling at this site, so the comparison shows whether the area is unchanged or worsening.

questions.takeaway: After assessing a finding, compare it with the recorded baseline. The comparison decides whether the finding is a change to report.
questions.strategy: A and D are both defensible, and the immunosuppressant pulls toward A. The cue that decides is the admission note's 4 cm bruise with swelling at the same site: without comparing, the nurse cannot tell new from old.

steps.detail: History and assessment of the forearm.
Admission note: 4 cm bruise with mild swelling at a blood draw site.
Same as admission, or larger and more painful?
Rechecking tomorrow or resetting the baseline loses the comparison.

elimination.verdict: Compare today's findings with the bruise in the admission note.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A nurse is planning closer assessment for clients on a medical unit whose immune protection may be reduced. Which clients does the nurse identify? Select all that apply.

options.text: A 3 week old infant admitted with a feeding problem
options.rationale: Infants have immature immune systems.

options.text: A 34 year old with a sprained left ankle that is warm, red, and swollen
options.rationale: These are cardinal signs of inflammation after an injury. They do not show reduced immune protection.

options.text: A 79 year old admitted after a fall who lives alone and is independent at home
options.rationale: Older adults face immunosenescence, which reduces the ability to fight infection, even when they live independently.

options.text: A 38 year old who takes a daily antirejection drug after a kidney transplant
options.rationale: Antirejection drugs suppress the immune system and raise infection risk.

options.text: A 38 year old who donated a kidney to a sibling 1 year ago and takes no daily medicines
options.rationale: The donor takes no antirejection drug, has no chronic disease described, and has no other factor in the stem that reduces immune protection.

options.text: A 52 year old with diabetes mellitus
options.rationale: Chronic disease such as diabetes mellitus affects immune competence and raises infection risk.

questions.takeaway: Age at either extreme, chronic disease, and immunosuppressing drugs all reduce immune protection. A healthy kidney donor is not on the drug that a transplant recipient takes.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two pairs carry the item. The 79 year old looks independent, but age alone counts. The two 38 year olds both relate to a kidney transplant; only the recipient takes the antirejection drug.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 3 week old and 79 year old.
The transplant recipient takes an antirejection drug; the donor takes none.
Diabetes mellitus.
A sprain shows inflammation, not reduced protection.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, F.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A nurse receives report on four clients. Which client does the nurse assess first?

options.text: A 34 year old with a sprained left ankle; redness is 8 cm across and pain is 6 of 10, both the same as yesterday
options.rationale: The redness is large, but it and the pain match yesterday. Unchanged cardinal signs after an injury fit inflammation without infection.

options.text: A 58 year old with a right shin wound; redness grew from 2 to 3 cm and pain from 3 to 5 of 10 since yesterday
options.rationale: Redness and pain have both worsened since yesterday. A temperature is not needed before acting on a change at the site.

options.text: A 78 year old with a right hand wound and dementia; oral temperature 37.4 °C and confusion, both unchanged since admission yesterday
options.rationale: The reading is above the reference range and the client is confused, which pulls hard. The deciding cue is that both findings are unchanged since admission.

options.text: A 45 year old with a rash on both forearms after using a cleaning product; the rash is smaller than yesterday
options.rationale: Inflammation can follow an irritant, and a rash that is smaller than at baseline is not a worsening finding.

questions.takeaway: Priority goes to the client who has changed from baseline. A finding outside a range that has not changed is less urgent than a worsening one, and the nurse does not wait for fever.
questions.strategy: Two options pull hard: the only temperature above the range belongs to an older, confused client, while the other client has a modest change. The deciding cue is "unchanged since admission yesterday" against "since yesterday": unchanged findings wait, worsening findings come first.

steps.detail: Ankle unchanged, temperature and confusion unchanged, rash smaller, shin wound worse.

steps.action: Do not let one number decide
steps.detail: A temperature above range that has not changed is not new.
Assess the client whose findings have worsened.

elimination.verdict: Assess the client whose shin wound redness and pain have worsened since yesterday.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A nurse reviews findings for four clients on a medical unit. Which finding is best described as colonization?

options.text: A sore throat with swollen, tender lymph nodes in the neck; oral temperature 38.6 °C
options.rationale: Pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy often accompany infection, and a temperature above the reference range adds a sign of systemic involvement. This is infection.

options.text: A leg wound grows methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA); redness spread 2 to 6 cm, pus; oral temperature 37.0 °C
options.rationale: An organism is present, as in colonization, but spreading redness and pus are signs of local infection. A temperature inside the range does not change that.

options.text: A urine culture from a long term catheter grows bacteria; urine clear, no pain, temperature 36.9 °C
options.rationale: Colonization means microorganisms are present in tissues without causing symptomatic disease. Bacteria were found, but nothing shows symptomatic disease.

options.text: Sneezing, clear nasal drainage, and swollen nasal tissue each spring; oral temperature 36.7 °C
options.rationale: Inflammation can follow exposure to an irritant. Allergic rhinitis is inflammation that occurs without infection and without an organism.

questions.takeaway: Finding an organism is not the same as infection. Colonization has an organism and no symptomatic disease; infection has an organism that multiplies and causes signs; inflammation can occur with no organism at all.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options name an organism on a culture. The catheter pulls toward infection, but decide by whether the site shows signs of disease.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the options with an organism
steps.detail: The leg wound and the urine culture both grew an organism.
The wound has spreading redness and pus: infection. The urine is clear with no pain: colonization.
The sore throat with a temperature above range is infection; the seasonal sneezing is inflammation without an organism.

elimination.verdict: C. Bacteria are present without symptomatic disease.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: A client was admitted yesterday with acute pancreatitis. Current findings: oral temperature 38.4 °C, heart rate 112 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, and white blood cell (WBC) count 13,500 per mm3. No source of infection has been found. Blood cultures drawn on admission show no growth so far. The client is alert and oriented, as on admission, oxygen saturation is 97%, and urine output is 60 mL/hr. A new nurse says, "This meets SIRS criteria, so the client has sepsis." Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "SIRS criteria are met here, so sepsis is present and the antimicrobial is given within 1 hour."
options.rationale: SIRS describes a widespread inflammatory response and can occur with noninfectious causes such as pancreatitis. SIRS alone does not establish sepsis.

options.text: "This is widespread inflammation. Sepsis also needs infection with organ dysfunction, not shown here."
options.rationale: Sepsis requires infection plus organ dysfunction. Mentation matches admission, oxygen saturation and urine output are inside their ranges, and no infection source has been found.

options.text: "Sepsis can be ruled out, because no organism has been found in the client's blood cultures at this point."
options.rationale: An organism does not need to be found in the bloodstream for sepsis to be present. The diagnosis is clinical, based on signs of organ dysfunction.

options.text: "These findings point to early sepsis, because the respiratory rate of 22 breaths/min is now above 20 breaths/min."
options.rationale: A respiratory rate above 20 breaths/min is concerning and is trended. Alone it does not show organ dysfunction when mentation, oxygen saturation, and urine output are inside their ranges.

questions.takeaway: SIRS is inflammation spread through the body, and pancreatitis can cause it without infection. Sepsis needs infection plus organ dysfunction, so look for new confusion, poor oxygenation, or falling urine output.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Option D is the pull: a respiratory rate above 20 breaths/min is a sepsis cue on the slides. The deciding cue is that every marker of organ function in the stem, mentation, oxygen saturation, and urine output, is at baseline or inside its range.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pancreatitis is a noninfectious cause of SIRS.
"Ruled out" ignores that sepsis is a clinical diagnosis.
Mentation at baseline, oxygen saturation 97%, urine output 60 mL/hr: none shown.
It is concerning and is trended, but one number does not establish sepsis.

elimination.verdict: SIRS alone is not sepsis; sepsis needs infection with organ dysfunction, and none is shown.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: A client has a draining wound on the right foot that was cultured 3 days ago. Today the white blood cell (WBC) count is 16,800 per mm3 and band neutrophils are 12%. Oral temperature is 37.0 °C. Which statement by the nurse interprets these results accurately?

options.text: "The marrow is releasing immature neutrophils that cannot engulf the organism. I will read this with the wound findings and baseline now."
options.rationale: A left shift means more immature band neutrophils are circulating because the marrow cannot keep up with a continuing infection, and immature neutrophils cannot phagocytose. Results are interpreted with the assessment and baseline.

options.text: "The marrow is releasing immature neutrophils that cannot engulf the organism. I will act on this once the temperature is above 37.2 °C."
options.rationale: The interpretation is right, but infection can be present without fever, and the nurse does not rely on fever alone.

options.text: "Memory cells are forming that target the organism in the wound. I will read this with the wound findings and baseline now."
options.rationale: Memory cells come from lymphocytes, part of adaptive immunity. Band cells are immature neutrophils, part of innate defense.

options.text: "Memory cells are forming that target the organism in the wound. I will act on this once the temperature is above 37.2 °C."
options.rationale: This has two errors. Memory cells come from lymphocytes, part of adaptive immunity, while band cells are immature neutrophils. The nurse also does not wait for fever, because infection can be present without it.

questions.takeaway: A left shift means the marrow is sending out immature neutrophils that cannot phagocytose, a sign the body is losing ground to a continuing infection. Read the results now with the wound and the baseline, not alone and not by temperature.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each option has an interpretation and an action. Judge each half on its own: two options name the right cell, two take the right action, and only one gets both.

steps.detail: Bands are immature neutrophils, which cannot phagocytose.
Memory belongs to lymphocytes, which removes C and D.
Waiting for fever removes B and D; reading the result with the wound and baseline now fits A.

elimination.verdict: A. Immature neutrophils signal a marrow that cannot keep up, and the result is read now with the wound and baseline.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A client was admitted 2 days ago with an infected wound on the left lower leg. At 0800 the client was alert and oriented, respiratory rate was 18 breaths/min, and heart rate was 88 beats/min. At 1400 the client is restless and asks where they are. Respiratory rate is 28 breaths/min, heart rate is 118 beats/min, and urine output is 40 mL over the past 2 hours. Oral temperature is 37.1 °C. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Recheck the oral temperature in 1 hour and notify the provider if it rises above 37.2 °C
options.rationale: Notifying the provider is the right idea, but tying it to fever is the error. New confusion, a rising respiratory rate, and falling urine output are already present, and the nurse does not wait for fever.

options.text: Mark the edge of the wound redness now and compare it at the next dressing change
options.rationale: Comparing the site with baseline is right in general, but the changes now are in breathing, mentation, and urine output, and they cannot wait.

options.text: Explain the unit routine to ease anxiety, then reassess the restlessness in 1 hour
options.rationale: Anxiety does not explain urine output below its reference range. New confusion is compared with the 0800 baseline and treated as a sepsis cue.

options.text: Notify the provider or activate rapid response now for possible sepsis from the wound
options.rationale: An infected wound plus new confusion, a respiratory rate above 20 breaths/min, and urine output below range are early cues of sepsis. When sepsis is suspected, the nurse escalates immediately.

questions.takeaway: Sepsis is an immune response to infection that has become uncontrolled and disrupts organ function. New confusion, faster breathing, and falling urine output are the early cues, and a temperature inside the range does not delay escalation.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The temperature inside the range is the trap. Name the problem from the changes since 0800: mentation, respiratory rate, heart rate, and urine output.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Alert to restless and disoriented; respiratory rate 18 to 28; heart rate 88 to 118; urine output 20 mL/hr.
An infected wound with organ dysfunction cues points to possible sepsis.
Waiting for fever, for the next dressing change, or for an hour of reassurance all postpone escalation.
Escalate now to the provider or the rapid response process.

elimination.verdict: D. Possible sepsis calls for immediate escalation, without waiting for fever.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A client reports pain in both knees for 2 weeks. Both knees are warm and swollen, and the client rates the pain 5 of 10. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is 42 mm/hr. The white blood cell (WBC) count is 7600 per mm3, and oral temperature is 36.9 °C. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "The raised ESR shows infection in both knees, so I will report it before I assess further."
options.rationale: The ESR rises with inflammation and with infection. It does not name a cause or a location, and the knees have not yet been assessed.

options.text: "The WBC count and temperature are in range, so the ESR shows inflammation without infection."
options.rationale: Infection can be present without fever, and a WBC count inside the range does not rule it out. The ESR cannot separate the two.

options.text: "The ESR shows inflammation or infection somewhere, so I will ask about onset, then assess each knee."
options.rationale: An ESR above 20 mm/hr indicates inflammation or infection somewhere in the body. Assessment begins with onset, recent injury, and illness history, then the findings at each site.

options.text: "The ESR shows inflammation or infection somewhere, so I will apply ice and recheck pain in 1 hour."
options.rationale: The interpretation is right, but comfort measures come after the history and the assessment of each knee. Assessment comes before intervention.

questions.takeaway: An ESR above 20 mm/hr says inflammation or infection is present somewhere in the body. It cannot say which, so the nurse reads it together with the history and the assessment of the site.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A and B each turn a lab value into a conclusion about cause. Ask what the ESR can tell you: that something is inflamed, not why. Then choose the option that gathers more data before acting.

steps.action: Read the value against its range
steps.detail: 42 mm/hr is above 0 to 20 mm/hr.

steps.action: Reject the leap to a cause
steps.detail: The ESR rises with both inflammation and infection, so it cannot confirm infection (A) or rule it out (B).
C and D read the ESR correctly; D intervenes before the knees are assessed.
History, then a focused assessment of each knee.

elimination.verdict: C. The ESR shows inflammation or infection without naming which, so the nurse takes the history and assesses each knee.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy has a central venous catheter in the right upper chest. Today the absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is 400 per mm3; the provider reviewed it at 0800 and neutropenic precautions are in place. At the catheter site the skin is pink 0.5 cm around the insertion point, there is no drainage, and pain at the site is 4 of 10, up from 1 of 10 yesterday. Oral temperature is 37.0 °C. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document the site as free of infection, since there is no drainage and the pink area is only 0.5 cm
options.rationale: Little redness and no drainage would be reassuring with an ANC in range. With an ANC of 400 per mm3, few neutrophils reach the site, so these signs cannot be relied on.

options.text: Report the new site pain now, since a low neutrophil count mutes the redness and pus of infection
options.rationale: Pus forms from dead WBCs, and the ANC of 400 per mm3 is far below range. Local signs are blunted, so the rise in pain from 1 to 4 of 10 is reported as a change from baseline.

options.text: Report the ANC of 400 per mm3 now, since a count this low places the client at high risk for infection
options.rationale: The ANC is low, but the provider reviewed it at 0800 and neutropenic precautions are in place. The change that has not been reported is the rise in site pain.

options.text: Recheck the site and temperature in 4 hours, since a fever would show whether the site is infected
options.rationale: Infection can be present without fever when immunity is low, so waiting for fever delays the report of pain that has already risen from 1 to 4 of 10.

questions.takeaway: Pus and much of the redness of infection come from neutrophils at the site. When the ANC is very low, those signs are muted, so a smaller change such as new pain is reported.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is partly covered in Reading (Iggy) and completed by standard NCLEX teaching.
questions.strategy: B and C both escalate. The deciding cue is that the provider reviewed the ANC at 0800 and precautions are in place, so the unreported change is the pain rising from 1 to 4 of 10.

steps.action: Read the ANC against its range
steps.detail: 400 per mm3 against 1500 to 8000 per mm3.
Few neutrophils means little pus and muted redness.
Pain 1 to 4 of 10 since yesterday.
The ANC has already been reviewed and acted on.
Infection can be present without fever when immunity is low (Iggy), so waiting for fever delays the report.

elimination.verdict: Report the new site pain now; a low ANC blunts redness and pus.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the admission note for a client. Which findings increase the client's risk for infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Peripheral intravenous catheter in the left forearm, inserted in the emergency department
options.rationale: Invasive devices such as IV catheters raise the risk for infection.

options.text: Healed surgical incision on the right knee from 2 years ago, skin intact
options.rationale: Intact skin is the best barrier. A healed incision does not raise the current risk.

options.text: Drinks 6 cans of beer every day
options.rationale: Alcohol use is a host factor that raises infection risk.

options.text: Stopped smoking 20 years ago
options.rationale: Nicotine use is a host factor, but this client has not smoked for 20 years.

options.text: Burn on the left forearm with open blisters from 3 days ago
options.rationale: Burns break the skin, removing the best barrier against infection.

options.text: Received an influenza vaccine 1 month ago
options.rationale: A recent vaccine does not raise infection risk.

questions.takeaway: Host factors that raise infection risk include current alcohol or nicotine use, invasive devices, and broken skin from surgery, trauma, or burns. Intact, healed skin and past habits do not.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each risk has a near twin: an IV catheter now versus a healed incision, drinking now versus smoking that stopped 20 years ago. Ask whether the factor is present today.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The IV catheter is an invasive device.
The burn has open blisters; the knee incision is healed.
Daily beer counts; smoking that stopped 20 years ago does not.
A vaccine does not raise infection risk.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A client with sepsis from an infected wound on the left lower leg has received the prescribed antimicrobial and intravenous fluids for 12 hours. The nurse compares findings at 0600 with the findings recorded when sepsis was suspected at 1800. Which findings at 0600 require further escalation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Alert and oriented, as on admission; at 1800 the client was confused
options.rationale: Mental status moving back toward baseline is a sign of response to treatment.

options.text: Urine output 45 mL/hr; at 1800 it was 15 mL/hr
options.rationale: Urine output is a key marker of perfusion, and it is now inside the range.

options.text: Capillary refill 4 seconds in the fingers of both hands; at 1800 it was 4 seconds
options.rationale: Capillary refill is unchanged and outside the range. Persistent signs of poor perfusion require further escalation.

options.text: Oral temperature 37.0 °C; at 1800 it was 38.6 °C
options.rationale: The temperature has returned inside the range. It is one number and is judged with the rest of the trend.

options.text: Skin on both legs cool and mottled; at 1800 the skin was cool and mottled
options.rationale: Skin findings are part of the perfusion assessment. Unchanged cool, mottled skin is a persistent sign of poor perfusion.

questions.takeaway: Judge the whole trend, not one number. Mentation, urine output, and temperature moving toward baseline count as response, and persistent signs of poor perfusion still call for escalation.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The temperature drop is the eye catcher, and it pulls toward calling the whole picture a success. Judge each finding on its own trend: two perfusion signs have not moved.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Mentation, urine output, and temperature have moved toward baseline.
Capillary refill and skin findings are unchanged.
Persistent signs of poor perfusion require further escalation.

elimination.verdict: C, E.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A client was admitted 1 day ago with an infected wound on the left lower leg. The nurse compares findings at 1400 with findings at 0800. Which finding at 1400 indicates that the infection has become systemic?

options.text: Thick yellow drainage on the dressing, was clear at 0800, with redness 2 cm around the wound, as at 0800
options.rationale: New pus shows the wound infection is worsening and is reported, but pus is a local sign. The redness has not spread since 0800.

options.text: Warmth and swelling at the wound edges, as at 0800, with pain at the wound 6 of 10, was 4 of 10
options.rationale: Warmth, swelling, and pain at the site are local signs. Rising pain is a change from baseline, but it does not show spread to the whole body.

options.text: Tired after walking to the bathroom, as at 0800, with an oral temperature of 37.0 °C, was 36.9 °C
options.rationale: Both findings are essentially unchanged from 0800. Nothing here shows a new systemic response.

options.text: Chills and malaise that began at 1200, with an oral temperature of 38.5 °C, was 37.0 °C at 0800
options.rationale: Fever, chills, and malaise are primary indicators of systemic infection. All three are new since 0800. Spreading redness from the wound would also suggest systemic spread; here the redness is unchanged.

questions.takeaway: Pain, swelling, heat, redness, and pus at the site describe local infection. Fever with chills and malaise means the infection now involves the whole body.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A is the tempting answer because the wound now drains pus. The stem asks about systemic spread, so look for the option whose findings are outside the wound.

steps.detail: Systemic, not simply worse.
Pus, warmth, swelling, and pain at the site are local; redness that has not spread stays local.
Fatigue and temperature are the same as at 0800.
New fever, chills, and malaise.

elimination.verdict: Chills and malaise with an oral temperature of 38.5 °C.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: A client has an infected wound on the right foot with thick yellow drainage. Oral temperature is 38.6 °C and heart rate is 108 beats per minute. The client is alert and oriented, as on admission. At 1000 the provider prescribed a wound culture, two sets of blood cultures, and an intravenous antimicrobial to start as soon as possible. Laboratory staff drew both sets of blood cultures at 1015. The wound culture has not been obtained. At 1030 the antimicrobial arrives on the unit. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Obtain the wound culture now, then start the antimicrobial as soon as the specimen is collected
options.rationale: Antimicrobial therapy should not begin until after the culture specimen is obtained. The wound culture is still outstanding, and collecting it takes minutes, so it comes first and the antimicrobial follows without delay.

options.text: Start the antimicrobial now, since both sets of blood cultures were drawn before the first dose
options.rationale: Drawing the blood cultures first is correct, but the wound culture has not been obtained. Giving the antimicrobial now can keep the wound organism from growing and leave it unidentified.

options.text: Start the antimicrobial now, and obtain the wound culture at the next scheduled dressing change
options.rationale: This delays the wound culture until after the antimicrobial is running, so the specimen may not grow the organism.

options.text: Hold the antimicrobial until the culture results identify the organism causing the wound infection
options.rationale: Culture results take time. The specimen must be collected first, but the antimicrobial is started once it is obtained, not after results return.

questions.takeaway: Culture is the best way to identify the organism, and every prescribed specimen is collected before the first antimicrobial dose. Collecting it promptly lets the dose start without delay.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A and B both protect the cultures and both start treatment quickly. The cue that decides is "the wound culture has not been obtained": blood cultures drawn first do not cover the wound specimen.

steps.detail: Wound culture and two sets of blood cultures.
Blood cultures drawn at 1015; wound culture not obtained.

steps.action: Apply the rule to each specimen
steps.detail: Antimicrobial therapy begins after the culture specimen is obtained.
Waiting for a dressing change or for results postpones treatment or loses the specimen.

elimination.verdict: Obtain the wound culture now, then start the antimicrobial.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A client has a wound on the right shin and walks with a limp because of pain in the right leg. At 0800 the nurse assesses the right leg for the signs of inflammation. Which entry by the nurse best supports comparing the client's findings over time?

options.text: "Right shin, 0800: redness 2 cm from wound edge, edge marked. Pain 4 of 10. Walks 10 m in the hallway with a limp."
options.rationale: The entry names the side and time, measures and marks the redness, rates pain, and measures function. Each cardinal sign that is affected can be compared at the next assessment.

options.text: "Right shin, 0800: redness 2 cm from wound edge, edge marked. Pain 4 of 10. Dressing clean, dry, and intact."
options.rationale: This entry is well built, but the client's walking is limited and the entry leaves out function, a cardinal sign the next nurse needs to compare. A dressing note is not a sign of inflammation to trend.

options.text: "Right shin, 0800: redness past the wound edge, edge marked. Pain 4 of 10. Walks 10 m in the hallway with a limp."
options.rationale: Function is included, but the redness is not measured and the time is missing, so change cannot be measured.

options.text: "Right shin, 0800: redness 2 cm, wound appears infected. Provider made aware. Walks with a limp."
options.rationale: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection. The entry labels a cause and leaves out pain and a measured distance.

questions.takeaway: A baseline entry names the side and time and measures each affected cardinal sign, including function, so later findings can be compared.
questions.strategy: A and B are both well built. The cue that decides is "walks with a limp because of pain in the right leg": function is affected, so the entry must measure it.

steps.action: Read what the stem says is affected
steps.detail: Redness, pain, and walking.

steps.action: Check each entry for all three
steps.detail: Only A and C include walking.
C lacks a measured redness and a time.
Redness alone does not establish infection.

elimination.verdict: The entry with time, measured and marked redness, pain rating, and walking distance.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.scenario: An 87 year old client with dementia who lives in a group home was admitted at 0900 today with an indwelling urinary catheter. Group home staff report that the client is usually confused about the day and year. The nurse compares findings at 1400 with findings at 1000.
questions.stem: For each finding at 1400, indicate whether it requires follow up or no follow up is needed.

rows.text: Oral temperature 37.3 °C, was 36.1 °C at 1000
rows.rationale: Older adults often have a lower baseline temperature and may have a fever at about 37.2 °C. A rise of 1.2 °C from this client's baseline can be a fever.

rows.text: Hard of hearing in both ears, as at 1000
rows.rationale: This finding is unchanged from 1000 and does not point to infection or dehydration.

rows.text: Heart rate 104 beats per minute, was 76 beats per minute at 1000
rows.rationale: A new rise in heart rate can accompany systemic infection and is a sign of dehydration in an older adult.

rows.text: Confused about the day and year, as at 1000
rows.rationale: Group home staff report this confusion as the client's usual baseline, and it is unchanged since 1000.

rows.text: Pulling at the catheter and trying to climb out of bed, was resting quietly at 1000
rows.rationale: Restlessness is a sign to assess for in an older adult with possible infection or dehydration, and it is new since 1000.

rows.text: Dark amber urine in the catheter bag, was pale yellow at 1000
rows.rationale: Darker urine is new and points to dehydration, which the nurse assesses for in an older adult with possible infection.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, compare each finding with the client's own baseline. A small temperature rise from a low baseline, a faster heart rate, new restlessness, and darker urine need follow up; long standing confusion that matches the reported baseline does not.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two rows are traps. 37.3 °C looks close to normal, but the client's baseline was 36.1 °C. Confusion looks alarming, but group home staff describe it as usual and it has not changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Anchor each row to its baseline
steps.detail: 1000 readings and the group home report.
Fever may appear near 37.2 °C; tachycardia, restlessness, and dark urine can signal infection or dehydration.
Hearing and the usual confusion.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1, 3, 5, and 6 require follow up. Rows 2 and 4 need no follow up.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A client has an oral temperature of 38.6 °C, chills, and loose stools 6 times in the past 24 hours. The loose stools began yesterday. The nurse takes an exposure history. Which findings help the nurse identify a possible source of the infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Returned from travel abroad 3 days before the loose stools began
options.rationale: Recent travel is part of the infection history because it can expose the client to organisms.

options.text: Returned from travel abroad 8 months ago, with no illness since then
options.rationale: Travel 8 months before an illness that began yesterday, with no illness in between, is too distant to point to this source.

options.text: A household member has had loose stools for 4 days
options.rationale: Exposure to ill contacts is a possible source, and the household member's illness began before the client's.

options.text: Ate grilled chicken at a picnic 2 days ago, cooked through and eaten right after grilling
options.rationale: Food is part of the exposure history, but food that was cooked through and eaten right away is not described as contaminated.

options.text: Drank untreated water from a stream while camping 4 days ago
options.rationale: Contaminated water is a possible source of infection, and the timing fits.

options.text: Cleans a pet turtle's tank each week without gloves
options.rationale: Animal contact is part of the exposure history.

questions.takeaway: The exposure history looks for where an organism came from: travel, ill contacts, contaminated food or water, and animal contact. The timing and the details decide whether a given exposure fits this illness.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each category appears with a twin that fails on one detail: travel 8 months ago, and food that was cooked through and eaten right away. Ask of each whether it could have brought an organism to the client in the days before the illness began.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Loose stools began yesterday.
Travel 3 days before onset, ill household member, stream water, turtle tank.
8 months ago with no illness since.
Cooked through and eaten right away.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, F.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A client, 81 years old, is admitted with vomiting for 2 days. Blood pressure is 78/42 mm Hg, and heart rate is 112 beats per minute. The nurse calculates the mean arterial pressure and compares it with the 60 to 70 mm Hg needed to maintain perfusion of the major body organs. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: 54 mm Hg, which is below the level needed to perfuse the major organs
options.rationale: Mean arterial pressure is the systolic pressure plus twice the diastolic pressure, divided by 3: (78 + 84) divided by 3 is 54 mm Hg, which is under 60 mm Hg, so perfusion of the major organs is at risk.

options.text: 60 mm Hg, which is at the lower edge of the level needed for organ perfusion
options.rationale: This is the simple average of 78 and 42. The diastolic pressure is counted twice because the cycle spends more time in diastole, so the true value is lower.

options.text: 66 mm Hg, which is within the level needed to perfuse the major organs
options.rationale: This doubles the systolic pressure instead of the diastolic pressure: (156 + 42) divided by 3. The heart rate of 112 beats per minute is not part of the formula and does not raise the value.

options.text: 36 mm Hg, which is far below the level needed to perfuse the major organs
options.rationale: The interpretation that perfusion is at risk is right, but 36 mm Hg is the systolic pressure minus the diastolic pressure, which is the pulse pressure, not the mean arterial pressure.

questions.takeaway: Mean arterial pressure equals the systolic pressure plus twice the diastolic pressure, divided by 3. A value of 60 to 70 mm Hg is necessary to maintain perfusion of the major body organs, so anything under 60 mm Hg puts them at risk.
questions.strategy: Write the formula before you look at the choices. The wrong numbers come from the common slips: averaging the two pressures, doubling the wrong one, or subtracting them. Then check the interpretation against 60 to 70 mm Hg.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 42 times 2 is 84.

steps.action: Add the systolic and divide by 3
steps.detail: 78 plus 84 is 162; 162 divided by 3 is 54 mm Hg.
54 mm Hg is below 60 to 70 mm Hg, so perfusion is at risk.
60 is the simple average, 66 doubles the systolic, and 36 is the pulse pressure.

elimination.verdict: A. 54 mm Hg, below the level needed to perfuse the major organs.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.scenario: A nurse completes admission assessments for several clients aged 76 to 88 years. None of these clients has a known heart disease.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate the age related change in the cardiovascular system that best explains it.

rows.text: A soft murmur at the apex in a client who reports no shortness of breath
rows.rationale: With age the mitral and aortic valves calcify. A murmur may be detected before any other symptom appears.

rows.text: Resting heart rate 56 beats per minute, with occasional premature ventricular contractions on the monitor
rows.rationale: Pacemaker cells decrease in number and conduction time increases. A rate below 60 beats per minute and premature ventricular contractions are common in older adults.

rows.text: Heart rate rises only to 96 beats per minute during a walk in the hallway, and the client stops to rest after 20 meters
rows.rationale: A larger, stiffer left ventricle lowers stroke volume and cardiac output during exercise, and the maximum heart rate with exercise is lower. The result is activity intolerance.

rows.text: Dizziness each time the client moves from lying to standing
rows.rationale: Less sensitive baroreceptors do not adjust the pressure quickly when position changes, which causes orthostatic dizziness.

rows.text: Lightheadedness 30 minutes after lunch, with a seated blood pressure of 98/60 mm Hg compared with 132/78 mm Hg before lunch
rows.rationale: A drop in pressure after eating is a postprandial change. It comes from the same less sensitive baroreceptors as the orthostatic change, not from the valves or the ventricle.

rows.text: During an exercise test, ejection fraction falls to 48%, although it was 62% at rest
rows.rationale: A larger, stiffer left ventricle lowers stroke volume, ejection fraction, and cardiac output during exercise, so the heart is less able to meet increased oxygen demands.

questions.takeaway: Five areas change with age: the valves calcify, pacemaker cells decrease, the left ventricle grows larger and stiffer, the large arteries stiffen, and the baroreceptors lose sensitivity. Each change has its own finding to assess.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Link each finding to the structure that produces it. Pressure drops with position or meals belong to the baroreceptors; a limited response to activity belongs to the left ventricle; rate and premature beats belong to the conduction system.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A murmur with no symptoms points to calcified valves.
Below 60 with premature beats points to fewer pacemaker cells.
A limited rise in rate with early fatigue points to the left ventricle.
Both the positional and the after meal drops come from the baroreceptors.
A fall in ejection fraction with activity points to the stiff, enlarged left ventricle.

elimination.verdict: Cardiac valves; conduction system; left ventricle; baroreceptors; baroreceptors; left ventricle.

questions.objective: Identify important cardiovascular changes associated with aging.

questions.stem: A client, 79 years old, has been on bed rest for 3 days and takes a diuretic. Before the first walk to the bathroom, the nurse checks orthostatic vital signs. After 3 minutes supine: blood pressure 134/82 mm Hg, heart rate 70 beats per minute. After 1 minute standing: blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg, heart rate 80 beats per minute. Normal blood pressure is below 120/80 mm Hg, and the reference range for heart rate is 60 to 100 beats per minute. The client reports no dizziness. How does the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: No orthostatic change, because the systolic pressure fell by less than 20 mm Hg
options.rationale: The systolic fall of 16 mm Hg is under 20 mm Hg, but the definition is met by either pressure. The diastolic pressure fell 12 mm Hg.

options.text: No orthostatic change, because the client reports no dizziness on standing
options.rationale: Dizziness is observed and recorded, but the definition rests on the measured changes. The absence of symptoms does not cancel a diastolic fall of 12 mm Hg.

options.text: Orthostatic hypotension, because the standing systolic pressure is below 120 mm Hg
options.rationale: A standing systolic value below 120 mm Hg is not the test. Orthostatic hypotension is judged by the size of the fall from supine to standing.

options.text: Orthostatic hypotension, because the diastolic fell 12 mm Hg as the rate rose
options.rationale: The diastolic pressure fell from 82 to 70 mm Hg, a fall of 12 mm Hg, and the heart rate rose from 70 to 80, about 14%. This meets the definition.

questions.takeaway: Orthostatic hypotension is a fall of more than 20 mm Hg systolic or more than 10 mm Hg diastolic, with a 10% to 20% rise in heart rate. Either pressure can meet it, and the client does not have to feel dizzy.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Option A is the defensible trap: the systolic fall is under 20 mm Hg. The cue that decides is the diastolic fall of 12 mm Hg. Calculate both pressures and the heart rate change before you choose.

steps.detail: Systolic 134 to 118 is 16 mm Hg; diastolic 82 to 70 is 12 mm Hg; heart rate 70 to 80 is about 14%.
More than 10 mm Hg diastolic with a 10% to 20% rise in heart rate is met.
A and B say no change; C and D say orthostatic hypotension. The measurements place the answer in the second pair.
C reaches the right label for the wrong reason; D names the fall that meets the definition.

elimination.verdict: D. The diastolic fall of 12 mm Hg with a 14% rise in heart rate meets the definition.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A client, 58 years old, comes to the clinic for a cardiovascular risk assessment. Which findings are modifiable risk factors for cardiovascular disease? Select all that apply.

options.text: Has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes per day for 30 years
options.rationale: Cigarette smoking is a modifiable risk factor and a major risk factor for coronary artery disease. This history is recorded as 30 pack years.

options.text: Body mass index 33 kg/m²
options.rationale: A body mass index above 30 kg/m² is obesity, a modifiable risk factor.

options.text: A parent had a myocardial infarction at 52 years of age
options.rationale: Family history matters and is part of the history, but it is a nonmodifiable risk factor.

options.text: Walks for 20 minutes once each week
options.rationale: This is far below 150 minutes of moderate exercise each week. Physical inactivity is a modifiable risk factor.

options.text: Reports feeling angry and hostile whenever there is a wait
options.rationale: Psychological factors such as anger and hostility are modifiable risk factors.

options.text: Is 58 years of age
options.rationale: The risk of coronary artery disease rises with age, but age is a nonmodifiable risk factor.

questions.takeaway: Modifiable risk factors are lifestyle habits: smoking, physical inactivity, obesity, and psychological factors such as stress, anger, and hostility. Age, sex assigned at birth, ethnic origin, and family history are nonmodifiable.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask of each finding whether the client could change it. Family history and age both raise risk, which makes them tempting, but neither can be changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The client can stop: modifiable.
Both can change: modifiable.
Psychological factors are modifiable.
Both raise risk but cannot be changed.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, E.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a client, 72 years old, who is seen for fatigue. Heart rate is 84 beats per minute and regular. Which findings require further assessment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Point of maximal impulse palpated at the left fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line
options.rationale: This is the expected location of the point of maximal impulse.

options.text: An extra sound heard just after S2, during rapid ventricular filling
options.rationale: This is an S3. It may be normal under 35 years of age, but at 72 it may indicate decreased ventricular compliance or heart failure.

options.text: S1 and S2 heard clearly
options.rationale: S1 and S2 are the normal heart sounds.

options.text: Skin warm and pink on both hands
options.rationale: Warm, pink skin is an expected finding of skin color and temperature.

options.text: A whooshing sound heard between S1 and S2 at the apex, not recorded at the last visit
