options.rationale: A whooshing sound between S1 and S2 is a systolic murmur from turbulent flow, and it is new since the last visit.

options.text: Radial pulses equal on the right and left
options.rationale: Pulses that are equal on both sides are expected.

questions.takeaway: An S3 may be normal before 35 years of age but in an older adult may mean decreased ventricular compliance or heart failure. A murmur is a whooshing sound from turbulent flow, and a systolic murmur falls between S1 and S2.
questions.strategy: The S3 is the trap: it can be normal, so students leave it unselected. Read the client's age. At 72 the same sound points to the ventricle.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Point of maximal impulse location, S1 and S2, skin, and pulses are all expected.

steps.action: Read the age with the S3
steps.detail: At 72 years an S3 is not expected.
The systolic murmur was not present at the last visit.

elimination.verdict: B, E.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A client, 64 years old, has had hypertension for 10 years. Blood pressure today is 158/96 mm Hg. While auscultating at the apex with the bell, the nurse hears a short, low pitched extra sound just before S1. Which interpretation is accurate?

options.text: An S3 gallop, reflecting decreased ventricular compliance from long standing hypertension
options.rationale: An S3 can also reflect decreased compliance, but it is heard during rapid ventricular filling, just after S2. A sound just before S1 is timed to atrial contraction.

options.text: An S4 gallop, reflecting a stiff, noncompliant ventricle from long standing hypertension
options.rationale: An S4 is heard during atrial contraction, just before S1, and reflects a stiff, noncompliant ventricle. It may occur with hypertension.

options.text: A pericardial friction rub from movement of an inflamed pericardium
options.rationale: A friction rub comes from an inflamed pericardium. It is not tied to atrial contraction, and nothing in the stem suggests pericarditis.

options.text: A diastolic murmur from turbulent blood flow through a narrowed valve
options.rationale: A murmur is a whooshing or swishing sound from turbulent flow, not a short, low pitched extra sound.

questions.takeaway: S3 comes during rapid ventricular filling, just after S2. S4 comes during atrial contraction, just before S1, and reflects a stiff, noncompliant ventricle, as seen with hypertension, ventricular hypertrophy, myocardial infarction, or advancing age.
questions.strategy: A and B give the same cause, so the cause cannot decide. Time the sound: just before S1 is atrial contraction, which is an S4.

steps.detail: Just before S1, which is atrial contraction.
A is an S3 after S2; B is an S4 before S1.
A rub comes from the pericardium, and a murmur is whooshing.

elimination.verdict: B. A sound just before S1 is an S4, which fits a stiff ventricle from long standing hypertension.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: During a procedure, a small air bubble enters a pulmonary vein of a client. The client's family asks how air in the lungs could reach the brain. Which sequence correctly lists the structures the air would pass through?

options.text: Pulmonary veins, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, arteries of the head
options.rationale: Blood from the lungs enters the left atrium through the pulmonary veins, crosses the mitral valve into the left ventricle, and leaves through the aortic valve toward the arteries of the head.

options.text: Pulmonary veins, left atrium, tricuspid valve, left ventricle, pulmonic valve, arteries of the head
options.rationale: The chambers are in the right order, but both valves belong to the right side of the heart. On the left side the atrioventricular valve is the mitral valve and the semilunar valve is the aortic valve.

options.text: Pulmonary veins, left ventricle, mitral valve, left atrium, pulmonic valve, arteries of the head
options.rationale: Two errors. The chambers are reversed, because the pulmonary veins empty into the left atrium, and the pulmonic valve leads from the right ventricle to the lungs, not from the left ventricle.

options.text: Pulmonary veins, left ventricle, tricuspid valve, left atrium, aortic valve, arteries of the head
options.rationale: Two errors. The chambers are reversed, because the pulmonary veins empty into the left atrium, and the tricuspid valve sits on the right side of the heart, not between the left chambers.

questions.takeaway: Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, crosses the mitral valve into the left ventricle, and leaves through the aortic valve to the arteries of the head, arms, and lower body.
questions.strategy: Start where blood from the lungs enters the heart, then alternate chamber and valve. On the left side the atrioventricular valve is the mitral and the semilunar valve is the aortic. Check each link on its own: chamber order, then each valve.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Blood from the lungs enters through the pulmonary veins into the left atrium, so the atrium comes before the ventricle. Eliminate C and D.
Mitral between the left chambers, aortic leaving the left ventricle. Tricuspid and pulmonic belong to the right side. Eliminate B.

elimination.verdict: A. Pulmonary veins, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, arteries of the head.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: A nurse auscultating a client, 66 years old, hears a murmur that falls between S1 and S2. Which events of the cardiac cycle are taking place while this murmur is heard? Select all that apply.

options.text: The aortic and pulmonic valves are open
options.rationale: Between S1 and S2 is ventricular ejection, when the aortic and pulmonic valves open.

options.text: The ventricles eject blood into the arteries
options.rationale: This interval is systole. The ventricles eject blood and ventricular pressure peaks.

options.text: The mitral and tricuspid valves are closed
options.rationale: The mitral and tricuspid valves close at S1 and do not open again until ventricular filling, after S2.

options.text: The ventricles fill as the mitral and tricuspid valves open
options.rationale: Ventricular filling with the mitral and tricuspid valves open happens in diastole, between S2 and the next S1.

options.text: The atria contract while the P wave appears
options.rationale: Atrial contraction with the P wave comes at the end of diastole, before S1.

options.text: The aortic and pulmonic valves close to make the second sound
options.rationale: Closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves is S2 itself, which ends this interval. It does not happen during the murmur.

questions.takeaway: S1 is closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves and starts systole. Between S1 and S2 the aortic and pulmonic valves are open and the ventricles eject. S2 is closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves and starts diastole, when the ventricles fill.
questions.strategy: Picture the interval as systole. Anything that belongs to filling, atrial contraction, or the closing that makes S2 belongs outside it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Between S1 and S2 is ventricular ejection, which is systole.
Aortic and pulmonic open; mitral and tricuspid closed.
Ventricular filling and atrial contraction come after S2 or before S1.
The closing that makes S2 ends the interval.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: A client has a clot blocking a deep vein in the right calf. The right calf is swollen, and the right foot is warm and pink with a pedal pulse equal to the left. Which function of the vascular system is directly impaired in the right leg?

options.text: Returning blood from the capillaries to the right side of the heart
options.rationale: The primary function of the venous system is to complete the circulation by returning blood from the capillaries to the right side of the heart. A blocked vein impairs this.

options.text: Delivering oxygen and nutrients from the heart to the tissues
options.rationale: This is the arterial system's function. The warm, pink foot with an equal pulse shows that arterial delivery is working.

options.text: Draining tissue fluid from the swollen calf back to the circulation through lymphatic flow
options.rationale: The calf swells because blood cannot return past the clot, not because lymphatic vessels are blocked. The structure that is directly impaired is the vein.

options.text: Carrying cell wastes from the tissues to the excretory organs
options.rationale: The vascular system does carry wastes, but the specific function lost when a vein is blocked is the return of blood to the heart.

questions.takeaway: The arterial system delivers oxygen and nutrients to body tissues. The venous system completes the circulation by returning blood from the capillaries to the right side of the heart.
questions.strategy: Match the blocked vessel to its job. The warm, pink foot and equal pulse tell you the arteries are delivering, so the problem is return.

steps.detail: The clot is in a vein.
Return blood from the capillaries to the right side of the heart.
A warm, pink foot with an equal pulse shows that delivery is intact.

elimination.verdict: A. A blocked vein impairs the return of blood to the right side of the heart.

questions.objective: Describe the basic functions of the arterial and venous systems.

questions.stem: A client is admitted after blood loss from a fall. Heart rate is 125 beats per minute, and stroke volume is 32 mL per beat. The reference range for cardiac output is 3 to 6 L/min. Which statement about this client's cardiac output is accurate?

options.text: It is 4.0 L/min, which shows the blood loss has not yet affected the heart
options.rationale: The number is correct, but the low stroke volume shows the blood loss has affected the heart. The output is held up only by the fast rate.

options.text: It is below range, because a stroke volume under 60 mL always lowers output
options.rationale: Output depends on both factors. A fast heart rate can offset a low stroke volume, and here 125 times 32 mL gives 4.0 L/min.

options.text: It is 4.0 L/min, kept in range by the fast rate offsetting low stroke volume
options.rationale: Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume: 125 times 32 mL is 4,000 mL, or 4.0 L/min. The fast rate is offsetting the low stroke volume.

options.text: It cannot be judged until the heart rate is back below 100 beats per minute
options.rationale: Cardiac output can be calculated at any heart rate with the formula.

questions.takeaway: Cardiac output is the amount of blood pumped from the left ventricle per minute, equal to heart rate times stroke volume. When stroke volume falls, a faster heart rate can keep output within range.
questions.strategy: Two options give the right number; only one gives the right meaning. A normal output with a low stroke volume and a fast rate means the heart is offsetting, not unaffected.

steps.detail: 125 times 32 mL is 4,000 mL per minute, or 4.0 L/min.
B says always; output depends on both factors.
Both say 4.0 L/min; only C explains why it is within range.

elimination.verdict: C. The fast heart rate is offsetting the low stroke volume.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.stem: A client has blood pressure 186/108 mm Hg and arteries narrowed by long standing hypertension. Heart rate is 88 beats per minute. Which statement best explains the effect on the left ventricle?

options.text: Preload rises, so the stretched muscle fibers contract with less force
options.rationale: Preload is the stretch from the volume in the ventricle at the end of diastole. High arterial pressure and narrow vessels change the resistance, not the filling volume.

options.text: Afterload rises, so the stretched fibers contract harder and stroke volume rises
options.rationale: Afterload does rise, but a stronger contraction from added stretch is Starling's law, which describes preload. A rise in afterload without compensation lowers stroke volume.

options.text: Preload falls, because high arterial pressure blocks blood returning to the heart
options.rationale: Preload depends on blood returning from the venous and pulmonary systems. Arterial pressure is the resistance against ejection.

options.text: Afterload rises, so stroke volume can fall unless the heart compensates
options.rationale: Afterload is the resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood. It rises with arterial pressure and narrow vessels, and a rise without compensation lowers stroke volume.

questions.takeaway: Preload is the stretch of the muscle fibers from the volume in the ventricle at the end of diastole. Afterload is the resistance the ventricle pumps against, which rises with arterial pressure and narrower vessels and can lower stroke volume.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort the cue first: high pressure and narrow arteries describe resistance, which is afterload. Then pick the effect: more afterload means more resistance to eject against, so stroke volume can fall.

steps.detail: High arterial pressure and narrowed arteries are resistance.
A and C both blame volume, the shared wrong fact.
B and D both say afterload rises; only D gives the correct effect on stroke volume.

elimination.verdict: D. Higher afterload makes the ventricle work harder and can lower stroke volume.

questions.objective: Explain cardiac output, stroke volume, preload, afterload, and mean arterial pressure.

questions.scenario: A client, 61 years old, arrives at the emergency department with pressure in the chest that began 5 hours ago and is now 6 of 10. Blood pressure 146/90 mm Hg, heart rate 104 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. The point of care troponin I is 0.48 ng/mL.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Wait for the repeat troponin before reporting the first result
options.rationale: Repeat testing is planned, but a value this far above the reference is reported now, not after the next result.

options.text: Notify the provider of the troponin result now
options.rationale: A troponin I above 0.03 ng/mL indicates myocardial injury or infarction and is reported at once.

options.text: Prepare the client for an exercise ECG to look for silent disease
options.rationale: An exercise ECG stops when chest pain appears. This client has chest pressure now and a troponin showing injury.

options.text: Walk the client to the restroom before testing begins
options.rationale: Activity raises the heart's oxygen demand in a client with ongoing chest pressure and evidence of injury.

options.text: Obtain a 12 lead ECG
options.rationale: Troponin is evaluated together with the symptoms and ECG changes, and a 12 lead ECG is obtained for chest pain.

options.text: Orthostatic hypotension
options.rationale: No positional blood pressure change is described, and the pressure is above normal.

options.text: Pericarditis from an inflamed pericardium
options.rationale: Pericarditis may produce a friction rub, but the troponin result points to injury of the heart muscle.

options.text: Elevated serum lipids
options.rationale: Lipids estimate long term risk. No lipid result is given, and they do not explain an acute rise in troponin.

options.text: Myocardial injury
options.rationale: Troponin is a heart muscle protein released into the blood when heart muscle is injured. A value above the reference with ongoing chest pressure points to myocardial injury.

options.text: Troponin repeated in 3 to 6 hours
options.rationale: After the first troponin, levels are assessed again in 3 to 6 hours.

options.text: Location of the point of maximal impulse
options.rationale: The point of maximal impulse is part of the physical assessment but does not track acute injury.

options.text: Chest pressure rating
options.rationale: The pain rating tracks whether the ischemic pain continues or eases.

options.text: Total cholesterol level
options.rationale: Cholesterol guides long term risk reduction, not the course of acute injury.

questions.takeaway: A troponin T or I above its reference indicates myocardial injury or infarction. Report it, obtain an ECG, and repeat troponin in 3 to 6 hours while tracking the pain.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Name the condition from the troponin result with the ongoing pressure, then choose actions that treat it as injury now and parameters that follow its course over hours.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0.48 ng/mL is far above the reference of below 0.03 ng/mL.
Myocardial injury.
Report now and obtain a 12 lead ECG.
Repeat troponin in 3 to 6 hours and the chest pressure rating.

elimination.verdict: Myocardial injury; notify the provider and obtain a 12 lead ECG; monitor the repeat troponin and the chest pressure rating.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: A client, 55 years old, arrives at the emergency department 40 minutes after chest pressure began while shoveling snow. The pressure is now 5 of 10. The point of care troponin I is 0.01 ng/mL. The client says, "The blood test is normal, so I want to go home." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Your troponin is normal, so an exercise ECG is next to look for hidden disease."
options.rationale: An exercise ECG does detect silent coronary disease, but it stops when chest pain appears. This client still has pressure rated 5 of 10.

options.text: "Troponin can take hours to rise, so it will be rechecked in 3 to 6 hours here."
options.rationale: The pressure began only 40 minutes ago. Troponin is repeated in 3 to 6 hours, so one early normal value does not rule out injury.

options.text: "Your first troponin is normal; an ECG will be done so the provider can decide about discharge."
options.rationale: An ECG is part of the evaluation, but this response presents one normal troponin as reassuring. Only 40 minutes have passed, so the troponin is repeated in 3 to 6 hours before injury can be excluded.

options.text: "Troponin stays raised a long time, so a normal level means it is not your heart."
options.rationale: Troponin stays raised for a long time after injury, which helps clients who arrive hours later. It does not mean an early normal value excludes injury.

questions.takeaway: Troponin is the preferred marker of heart muscle injury and is repeated 3 to 6 hours after the first result. A single normal value soon after symptoms begin does not rule out injury.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: B and C both keep the client for evaluation. The cue that decides is time: 40 minutes after onset, one normal troponin cannot exclude injury, so the repeat in 3 to 6 hours is what the client needs to hear.

steps.detail: 40 minutes since onset, with pressure still at 5 of 10.
D treats one normal troponin as ruling out injury, and A stresses the heart during ongoing pain.
C reassures with one early value; B explains why the marker is repeated.

elimination.verdict: B. One early normal troponin does not rule out injury, so it is repeated in 3 to 6 hours.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for several clients who returned within the past 2 hours from a left heart catheterization through the right femoral artery. Before each procedure, the right dorsalis pedis pulse was present and equal to the left. Which findings require immediate action? Select all that apply.

options.text: New chest pressure rated 4 of 10
options.rationale: Chest pain after catheterization is a critical rescue finding. The nurse stays with the client and obtains a 12 lead ECG.

options.text: Urine output 240 mL over the past hour
options.rationale: The contrast acts as an osmotic diuretic, so a high urine output is expected. The nurse keeps oral and intravenous fluids going so the contrast is excreted.

options.text: The right dorsalis pedis pulse is now absent, and the right foot is cool and pale
options.rationale: A dramatic change in the pulses of the affected limb is a critical rescue finding. The rapid response team or provider is contacted at once.

options.text: Blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg and heart rate 80 beats per minute, both matching the values before the procedure
options.rationale: The values match the client's own baseline, so they do not signal bleeding or another complication.

options.text: The right foot is warm and pink, with a right dorsalis pedis pulse equal to the left
options.rationale: Pulses, temperature, and color in the affected limb match the baseline, which shows circulation below the site is intact.

options.text: Firm swelling that is growing under the right groin dressing
options.rationale: A forming hematoma calls for steady, firm pressure on the site and the rapid response team or provider at once.

questions.takeaway: After catheterization, check the site and the limb below it with every vital sign check. Chest pain, dysrhythmias, bleeding, hematoma, or a dramatic change in the limb pulses call for the rapid response team or provider at once. High urine output from the contrast is expected.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Compare each finding with the baseline from before the procedure. Anything that matches the baseline or follows from the contrast is expected; anything new at the site, in the limb, or in the chest is acted on now.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New chest pressure is a critical rescue finding.
Osmotic diuresis from contrast is expected.
A lost pulse with a cool, pale foot is a dramatic change; a pulse matching baseline is expected.
Growing firm swelling is a hematoma.

elimination.verdict: A, C, F.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for a left heart catheterization through the right femoral artery at 1300. At 1100 the nurse reviews the checklist. The client ate toast at 0600, drank clear apple juice at 0930, and took the usual warfarin dose at 0800. The signed consent is complete, and the client reports no allergies. Which action by the nurse is most important?

options.text: Report that the client drank apple juice this morning, so the procedure is delayed
options.rationale: Clear liquids are allowed up to 2 hours before the procedure. The juice at 0930 was 3.5 hours before 1300.

options.text: Report that the client ate toast this morning, so the procedure is delayed
options.rationale: Solids are held for 6 hours before the procedure. The toast at 0600 was 7 hours before 1300.

options.text: Report the warfarin dose taken at 0800 to the provider before the procedure
options.rationale: Warfarin and other oral anticoagulants are held when the femoral artery will be used, because of the bleeding risk at the site.

options.text: Ask whether the client has ever reacted to iodine based contrast before the procedure
options.rationale: Contrast allergy is questioned before the procedure, and the client already reports no allergies. A warfarin dose before femoral arterial access is the finding that puts the client at risk and must reach the provider.

questions.takeaway: Before catheterization, clear liquids are allowed up to 2 hours before and solids are held for 6 hours. Warfarin and other oral anticoagulants are held when the femoral artery will be used, so a dose taken that morning is reported.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The juice is the defensible trap because many clients are told to take nothing by mouth. Count the hours: 0930 to 1300 is 3.5 hours, beyond the 2 hour limit for clear liquids. The femoral access is the cue that makes the warfarin the problem.

steps.detail: Juice 3.5 hours before and toast 7 hours before are both within the rules.
A and B both delay the procedure for intake that meets the rules.
The femoral artery will be used, so warfarin should have been held.
Useful, but the client reports no allergies; the warfarin is the unaddressed risk.

elimination.verdict: C. Warfarin is held when femoral access is planned, so the morning dose is reported.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: An echocardiogram for a client, 69 years old, shows that the tricuspid valve does not open fully, so blood cannot move forward through it normally. Where does the blood back up first, and which finding does the nurse expect from that backup?

options.text: Into the left atrium and pulmonary veins, causing crackles in both lung bases
options.rationale: This is the backup from a narrowed mitral valve, which sits between the left atrium and left ventricle. The tricuspid valve is on the right side of the heart.

options.text: Into the right ventricle and pulmonary arteries, causing a lower oxygen saturation
options.rationale: The right ventricle and pulmonary arteries lie downstream of the tricuspid valve. A valve that does not open fully reduces flow into them; blood backs up behind the valve, not in front of it.

options.text: Into the right atrium and venae cavae, causing neck vein distention and ankle edema
options.rationale: The tricuspid valve sits between the right atrium and right ventricle. Blood that cannot pass it backs up into the right atrium and then into the superior and inferior venae cavae, raising venous pressure in the neck and lower body. Tricuspid stenosis is a listed cause of jugular venous distention.

options.text: Into the right atrium and pulmonary veins, causing crackles in both lung bases
options.rationale: The right atrium is correct, but the pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Blood behind the tricuspid valve backs into the venae cavae, not the pulmonary veins.

questions.takeaway: Blood backs up behind a valve that will not open. The tricuspid valve sits between the right atrium and right ventricle, so backup goes into the right atrium and the venae cavae, which drain the upper and lower body.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Place the valve on the 12 step flow, then look upstream. The structure just before the valve fills first, and the vessels draining into it come next.

steps.detail: The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and the right ventricle.
Before the valve are the right atrium and the venae cavae.
The right ventricle and pulmonary arteries lie after the valve.
Pulmonary veins drain into the left atrium, so they belong to the mitral valve picture.

elimination.verdict: Right atrium and venae cavae, with neck vein distention and ankle edema.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: A client, 71 years old, has diabetes and smokes 1 pack of cigarettes per day. The left lower leg is cool and pale with sparse hair, the left dorsalis pedis pulse is weak, and the client reports left calf pain after walking 1 block. The right lower leg is warm and pink with a strong right dorsalis pedis pulse, 2+ pitting edema to the mid shin, and a heavy feeling at the end of each day. Which interpretation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: Left leg: impaired venous return; right leg: impaired arterial delivery of oxygen and nutrients
options.rationale: This reverses the two legs. A cool, pale, hairless leg with a weak pulse is not getting enough arterial blood; a warm, pink, swollen leg with a strong pulse is getting arterial blood but not returning it.

options.text: Both legs: impaired venous return, because pain and swelling each reflect blood pooling in the veins
options.rationale: Only the right leg shows pooling. The left leg has a weak pulse, coolness, pallor, and pain with walking, which point to low arterial delivery.

options.text: Left leg: impaired arterial delivery; right leg: excess arterial inflow raising pressure in the tissues
options.rationale: The left leg is read correctly. The right leg has a strong pulse and warm skin because arterial flow is intact, but the edema comes from blood not leaving the leg, not from extra blood entering it.

options.text: Left leg: impaired delivery of oxygen and nutrients by the arteries; right leg: impaired venous return
options.rationale: The arterial system delivers oxygen and nutrients, so its failure shows as coolness, pallor, hair loss, a weak pulse, and pain with activity. The venous system returns blood from the capillaries to the right side of the heart, so its failure shows as edema in a leg that stays warm and pink with a strong pulse.

questions.takeaway: Arteries deliver oxygen and nutrients; veins return blood to the right heart. Low arterial delivery looks cool, pale, hairless, and painful with a weak pulse. Poor venous return looks swollen and heavy in a leg that stays warm with a strong pulse.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Judge each leg separately by asking whether blood is failing to arrive or failing to leave. The pulse and skin temperature answer the first; edema answers the second.

steps.detail: Cool, pale, sparse hair, weak pulse, and pain with walking: blood is not arriving.
Warm, pink, strong pulse, pitting edema: blood arrives but does not leave.
Arrival is the arterial system; return is the venous system.

steps.action: Reject the swap and the extras
steps.detail: A swapped pair, a single cause for both legs, and excess inflow each misread one leg.

elimination.verdict: Left leg arterial, right leg venous.

questions.objective: Describe the basic functions of the arterial and venous systems.

questions.stem: A client, 54 years old, has a lipid panel drawn after a 12 hour fast. Results: total cholesterol 242 mg/dL, LDL 164 mg/dL, HDL 36 mg/dL, triglycerides 128 mg/dL. Which interpretations by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: The LDL of 164 mg/dL raises the risk for coronary artery disease
options.rationale: LDL is mainly cholesterol and is the bad cholesterol. A level above the desired value of less than 130 mg/dL is positively linked with coronary artery disease.

options.text: The HDL of 36 mg/dL raises the risk, because HDL protects against coronary artery disease
options.rationale: HDL is the good cholesterol, and higher levels are protective. A level of 36 mg/dL is below the desired value for any adult, so the client loses that protection.

options.text: The triglycerides of 128 mg/dL raise the risk for coronary artery disease
options.rationale: A triglyceride level of 128 mg/dL falls within the desired range, so this value does not add risk. Elevated triglycerides would.

options.text: The total cholesterol of 242 mg/dL raises the risk for coronary artery disease
options.rationale: Total cholesterol above the desired value of less than 200 mg/dL indicates increased risk for coronary artery disease.

options.text: The low HDL balances the high LDL, so the overall risk is unchanged
options.rationale: The two values do not cancel. High LDL raises risk and low HDL removes protection, so both push the risk in the same direction.

options.text: A higher HDL on the next panel would add to the client's risk
options.rationale: This reverses the role of HDL. A rise in HDL would lower the risk, because elevated HDL is negatively correlated with coronary artery disease.

questions.takeaway: High LDL, high total cholesterol, and high triglycerides raise the risk for coronary artery disease. HDL works the other way: a high level protects, and a low level removes that protection.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each lipid by direction first. For LDL, total cholesterol, and triglycerides, higher is worse; for HDL, lower is worse. Then compare each value with the level you know is desired.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: LDL, total cholesterol, and triglycerides: high is risk. HDL: low is risk.
LDL 164 mg/dL, total cholesterol 242 mg/dL, and HDL 36 mg/dL.
Triglycerides 128 mg/dL do not add risk.
Low HDL does not offset high LDL, and a higher HDL lowers risk.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.nursesNote: Client, 77 years old, 3 days after a myocardial infarction. Reports sharp chest pain, 5 of 10, that eases when sitting upright. Oral temperature 38.2 °C. Blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg in the right arm and 122/76 mm Hg in the left arm. Radial pulses strong and equal on the right and left. Skin on both hands warm and dry, with pink nail beds. Point of maximal impulse palpated over the left fifth and sixth intercostal spaces, lateral to the midclavicular line. S1 and S2 heard clearly. A high pitched, scratchy sound heard over the precordium with each heartbeat.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow up.

segments.text: Reports sharp chest pain, 5 of 10, that eases when sitting upright
segments.rationale: New chest pain after a myocardial infarction always needs follow up. Sharp pain that eases when sitting upright fits pericarditis rather than ischemia, but it still must be reported and assessed.

segments.text: Oral temperature 38.2 °C
segments.rationale: A fever points to inflammation. Together with the sharp chest pain and the scratchy sound, it supports an inflamed pericardium.

segments.text: Blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg in the right arm and 122/76 mm Hg in the left arm
segments.rationale: The two arms differ by only 2 mm Hg, and neither value calls for action.

segments.text: Radial pulses strong and equal on the right and left
segments.rationale: Strong, equal pulses show intact arterial flow to both arms. This is an expected finding.

segments.text: Skin on both hands warm and dry, with pink nail beds
segments.rationale: Warm, pink skin and nail beds show adequate perfusion. Decreased perfusion would appear cool, pale, and moist.

segments.text: Point of maximal impulse palpated over the left fifth and sixth intercostal spaces, lateral to the midclavicular line
segments.rationale: The point of maximal impulse belongs at the left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line. An impulse felt over more than one space and shifted lateral to that line can mean left ventricular hypertrophy.

segments.text: S1 and S2 heard clearly
segments.rationale: Clear first and second heart sounds are the normal finding.

segments.text: A high pitched, scratchy sound heard over the precordium with each heartbeat
segments.rationale: A scratchy sound with each beat suggests a pericardial friction rub, which comes from movement of an inflamed pericardium and may occur with pericarditis after a myocardial infarction. Rubs are often transient, so document it and report it now.

questions.takeaway: After a myocardial infarction, sharp chest pain that eases sitting upright, a fever, and a scratchy sound with each beat together point to an inflamed pericardium. A point of maximal impulse that is spread over two spaces and lateral to the midclavicular line suggests an enlarged left ventricle.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Compare each finding with the normal you expect: the point of maximal impulse at the left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line, only S1 and S2, warm pink skin, and equal pulses. Anything that departs from those normals, or any chest pain, needs follow up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sharp pain 5 of 10 easing upright and a temperature of 38.2 °C.
A scratchy sound with each beat suggests a friction rub.
Felt over two spaces and lateral to the midclavicular line.
Equal arm pressures, strong equal pulses, warm pink skin, clear S1 and S2.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A client, 86 years old, is admitted for observation after tripping on a rug and falling. Cardiac monitor: regular rhythm, heart rate 54 beats per minute, no premature beats. Blood pressure 126/74 mm Hg lying and 122/72 mm Hg standing. The client is alert, denies dizziness, and walked 50 meters in the hallway without stopping. Clinic records show resting heart rates of 52 to 56 beats per minute at every visit for the past 4 years. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: Report the heart rate to the provider now, because a rate below 60 limits cardiac output during activity
options.rationale: A slow rate can limit output, but this client walked 50 meters without stopping and has no dizziness. There is no sign of low output to report urgently.

options.text: Record the rate as the client's baseline and continue routine monitoring, since it matches 4 years of readings
options.rationale: With age, pacemaker cells decrease and conduction time increases, so a rate below 60 is common. The deciding cue is that this rate matches 4 years of clinic readings, the rhythm is regular, and the client has no symptoms. It is the client's baseline, not a new change.

options.text: Request a 12 lead ECG before the next walk, because a rate below 60 can signal a new conduction block
options.rationale: Assessing the rhythm when the rate is below 60 is the right instinct, and it would be the choice for a new slow rate. Here the monitor already shows a regular rhythm, and 4 years of matching readings show the rate is not new.

options.text: Teach the client to rise slowly, because the slow rate shows the baroreceptors have lost sensitivity
options.rationale: Rising slowly is good teaching for older adults, but heart rate is a conduction system finding. The lying and standing pressures differ by only 4 mm Hg, so there is no orthostatic change here.

questions.takeaway: A heart rate below 60 is common in older adults because pacemaker cells decrease with age. The question is whether it is new. A rate that matches years of readings, with a regular rhythm and no symptoms, is the baseline.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options assess or report a rate below 60, which is sound in general. Look for the cue that tells you whether the rate is new: here, 4 years of matching readings.

steps.detail: A slow rate in an older adult comes from fewer pacemaker cells and longer conduction time.
Alert, no dizziness, walked 50 meters, and only a 4 mm Hg drop on standing.
The rate matches clinic readings of 52 to 56 beats per minute for 4 years.
A 12 lead ECG fits a new slow rate; the monitor already shows a regular rhythm without premature beats.
Baroreceptors explain pressure changes with position, not heart rate.

elimination.verdict: Record the rate as baseline and continue routine monitoring.

questions.objective: Identify important cardiovascular changes associated with aging.

questions.stem: A client, 63 years old, had heart surgery 2 days ago. An echocardiogram now shows fluid collecting in the pericardial space. Blood pressure is 92/64 mm Hg, was 124/78 mm Hg at 0800. Heart rate is 118 beats per minute, was 84 beats per minute at 0800. The family asks where the fluid is and why the blood pressure is falling. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: The fluid sits between the endocardium and the myocardium, and it weakens each contraction from the inside
options.rationale: The endocardium lines the chambers and lies directly against the myocardium; there is no fluid space between them. The pericardial space is outside the heart muscle.

options.text: The fluid sits between the parietal and visceral pericardium, and it squeezes the heart so the chambers cannot fill
options.rationale: The pericardial space lies between the parietal pericardium and the visceral pericardium (the epicardium). Fluid that collects there presses on the heart from outside, the ventricles fill less, stroke volume falls, and blood pressure drops while the heart rate rises to compensate.

options.text: The fluid sits between the parietal and visceral pericardium, and it stretches the heart muscle so it contracts harder
options.rationale: The location is right, but the effect is reversed. Fluid around the heart limits filling, so less blood is stretched into the ventricles and less is pumped out.

options.text: The fluid sits between the myocardium and the epicardium, and it blocks blood flow through the coronary arteries
options.rationale: The epicardium is the visceral pericardium attached to the heart muscle; there is no fluid space between it and the myocardium. The fluid is in the pericardial space, outside the epicardium.

questions.takeaway: From outside in: parietal pericardium, pericardial space, visceral pericardium (epicardium), myocardium, endocardium. Fluid in the pericardial space compresses the heart and limits filling, so stroke volume and blood pressure fall.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from your sources.
questions.strategy: Two options place the fluid correctly. Decide on the effect: fluid outside the heart cannot make the muscle stretch more; it limits how much blood can enter the chambers.

steps.detail: The pericardial space lies between the two pericardial layers. Options that put fluid next to the myocardium are out.
One says the fluid squeezes the heart, the other says it stretches the muscle.
A falling blood pressure with a rising heart rate fits less filling and lower stroke volume.

elimination.verdict: Between the parietal and visceral pericardium, squeezing the heart so the chambers cannot fill.

questions.objective: Review the basic anatomy, blood flow, and valves of the heart.

questions.stem: A client, 67 years old, has had hypertension for 20 years. Blood pressure today is 162/98 mm Hg in the right arm. With the client supine and the head of the bed slightly raised, the nurse inspects the precordium and sees the apical impulse at the left sixth intercostal space, lateral to the midclavicular line, spread over two intercostal spaces. No movement is seen over the aortic, pulmonic, or tricuspid areas. Which interpretation is accurate?

options.text: The impulse is in the mitral area at the apex, so this is the expected point of maximal impulse
options.rationale: Pulsation in the mitral area is normal, but the expected point is the left fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line, in one space. This impulse is lower, lateral, and spread over two spaces.

options.text: The impulse is displaced, and with no movement over the other areas this suggests right ventricular enlargement
options.rationale: The impulse is displaced, but the apex is formed by the left ventricle. Movement in the tricuspid area, not a shifted apical impulse, would point toward the right side.

options.text: The impulse is displaced lateral and over more than one space, which suggests left ventricular hypertrophy
options.rationale: The point of maximal impulse belongs at the left fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line. An impulse shifted lateral to that line and felt in more than one space suggests left ventricular hypertrophy, which fits years of pumping against high afterload.

options.text: The impulse position changes with the head of the bed, so it cannot be interpreted until the client lies flat
options.rationale: The client is positioned as recommended: supine with the head slightly raised. The finding can be interpreted now.

questions.takeaway: The point of maximal impulse is at the left fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line. A PMI shifted lateral and spread over more than one space suggests left ventricular hypertrophy; movement over the aortic, pulmonic, or tricuspid areas is abnormal.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Compare the finding with the normal landmark first, then ask which chamber forms the apex. Long standing hypertension raises the work of the left ventricle.

steps.detail: Normal is left fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line, one space. This impulse is displaced, so it is not expected.
Supine with the head slightly raised is the standard position, so the finding stands.
The apex is left ventricle, and 20 years of hypertension makes left ventricular hypertrophy the fit.

elimination.verdict: The impulse is displaced lateral and over more than one space, suggesting left ventricular hypertrophy.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A client, 46 years old, is seen for palpitations that began 3 weeks ago. The nurse hears a new murmur between S1 and S2 at the apex. The client works as a roofer and has no health insurance. Which history questions are appropriate for this client? Select all that apply.

options.text: "Did you have rheumatic fever or repeated strep throat infections as a child?"
options.rationale: Recurrent tonsillitis, streptococcal infections, and rheumatic fever can lead to valve abnormalities, and a new murmur raises that question.

options.text: "Have you recently used cocaine or any other drugs that were not prescribed for you?"
options.rationale: Cocaine and illicit drugs are often associated with heart disease, including rhythm problems that cause palpitations. The drug history includes them.

options.text: "Which over the counter products, herbal products, or supplements do you take?"
options.rationale: The drug history covers prescription, over the counter, and herbal or natural products, along with any drug sensitivities.

options.text: "Can you do the same work on the roof that you could do a year ago?"
options.rationale: The functional history compares current activity with past activity. Patients often limit activity gradually and do not notice until asked.

options.text: "Your palpitations are from the stress of roofing in the heat, aren't they?"
options.rationale: Stress and heat are worth asking about, but this is a leading question that supplies the cause. The current problem is explored openly: onset, duration, frequency, and precipitating, aggravating, and relieving factors.

options.text: "Did any of your grandparents have heart disease after they turned 80 years old?"
options.rationale: Family history belongs in the history, but it focuses on immediate family: the age, health status, and cause of death of parents, siblings, and children. A first degree relative with coronary artery disease is the major risk factor.

questions.takeaway: A cardiovascular history goes beyond risk factors: medical history (including rheumatic fever and strep infections), drug history (prescription, over the counter, herbal, illicit), social history (work, support, ability to pay), nutrition, family and genetic history, current problems, and function.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Match each question to a part of the history and ask whether this client's symptoms or situation make it relevant. A leading question, or one aimed at the wrong people, is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A new murmur links to childhood strep infections and rheumatic fever: true.
Illicit drugs and over the counter or herbal products both belong: true, true.
Comparing work tolerance with a year ago: true.
A leading question and a family question aimed at the wrong relatives do not collect an accurate history: false, false.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.stem: A client, 58 years old, had lymph nodes removed from the left axilla 6 months ago. The left arm has been swelling slowly over 4 weeks. The left hand is warm and pink, the left radial pulse is strong and equal to the right, capillary refill in the left fingers is 2 seconds, and an ultrasound shows no clot in the left arm veins. The right arm and both legs have no edema. Which explanation of the swelling is most accurate?

options.text: Blood is not returning through the left arm veins to the right side of the heart
options.rationale: Returning blood to the heart is a vascular function, and a venous clot can cause swelling in one arm. The ultrasound found no clot, so venous return is not the impaired function here.

options.text: Tissue fluid in the left arm is not draining back into the circulation through lymphatic flow
options.rationale: The vascular system allows lymphatic flow to drain tissue fluid back into the circulation. After lymph nodes are removed, that drainage can fail, and fluid collects in one extremity (lymphedema) while arterial and venous flow are intact.

options.text: Arterial flow to the left arm is reduced, so tissues are not receiving oxygen and nutrients
options.rationale: Reduced arterial flow causes a cool, pale limb with weak pulses. This hand is warm and pink with a strong pulse and brisk refill.

options.text: The heart is not pumping enough, so excess fluid is collecting in the tissues of the body
options.rationale: Fluid from heart failure usually collects on both sides and in dependent areas, such as both legs. Swelling limited to the left arm points to a local cause.

questions.takeaway: The vascular system carries blood out to nourish tissues, carries wastes to excretory organs, lets lymphatic flow drain tissue fluid back into the circulation, and returns blood to the heart. Edema in one limb with intact arterial and venous flow points to lymphatic blockage.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Use the findings to rule out each function in turn: pulses and color test arterial delivery, the ultrasound tests venous return, and the pattern of edema tests a whole body cause.

steps.detail: Warm, pink, strong pulse, 2 second refill: arterial delivery is intact.
No clot on ultrasound: venous return is not blocked.

steps.action: Test for a whole body cause
steps.detail: Only one arm swells, so heart failure does not fit.
Lymph nodes removed from the same side: lymphatic drainage is the function impaired.

elimination.verdict: Tissue fluid in the left arm is not draining back through lymphatic flow.

questions.objective: Describe the basic functions of the arterial and venous systems.

questions.stem: A client, 52 years old, is in the emergency department with a fracture of the right wrist and rates the pain 9 of 10. The client is shouting at a family member. Blood pressure is 168/98 mm Hg in the left arm, heart rate 112 beats per minute. At a clinic visit 2 weeks ago, blood pressure was 126/78 mm Hg and heart rate 74 beats per minute. Which explanation of the blood pressure is most accurate?

options.text: Parasympathetic stimulation through the vagus nerve from the pain is raising the heart rate and blood pressure
options.rationale: Pain does change autonomic activity, but vagus (parasympathetic) stimulation slows the heart rate. It does not explain a rise.

options.text: Baroreceptors in the aortic arch are stretched by the higher pressure and are now driving the pressure higher
options.rationale: Baroreceptors are stretched by a higher pressure, but their impulses inhibit the vasomotor center, which lowers blood pressure. They work against this rise.

options.text: The kidneys sensed less blood flow and activated the renin angiotensin aldosterone mechanism to retain fluid
options.rationale: This mechanism raises blood pressure when renal blood flow or pressure falls. Nothing here lowered renal flow, and fluid retention does not explain a rise over minutes after an injury.

options.text: Pain and anger stimulate the sympathetic nervous system, which raises the heart rate and blood pressure
options.rationale: Emotional behaviors such as pain and anger stimulate the sympathetic nervous system to raise blood pressure and heart rate. With a normal reading 2 weeks ago, the nurse treats the pain and rechecks before labeling this hypertension.

questions.takeaway: Blood pressure is regulated by the autonomic nervous system, the kidneys, and the endocrine system. Pain, anger, and excitement stimulate the sympathetic nervous system and raise blood pressure and heart rate; baroreceptors respond to a rise by lowering the pressure.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Check the direction of each mechanism. Only one of them pushes the pressure up in response to what is happening to this client right now.

steps.detail: Parasympathetic stimulation slows the heart: wrong direction.
Stretch inhibits the vasomotor center and lowers pressure: wrong direction.
This responds to falling renal flow and acts through fluid retention: wrong trigger and wrong timing.
126/78 mm Hg 2 weeks ago fits a sympathetic response to pain and anger, so treat the pain and recheck.

elimination.verdict: Pain and anger stimulate the sympathetic nervous system; recheck the blood pressure once the pain is treated.

questions.objective: Describe the basic functions of the arterial and venous systems.

questions.stem: A client, 74 years old, with dark brown skin is admitted with heart failure. Oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. The nurse is assessing for decreased perfusion and cyanosis. Which assessment approach is best?

options.text: Inspect the conjunctivae, oral mucosa, and nail beds for ash gray color; compare skin temperature side to side with the back of the hand
options.rationale: Small vessels lie near the surface in the nail beds, mucous membranes, and conjunctivae, so these areas show perfusion best. In dark skin, decreased perfusion and cyanosis appear as an ash gray color, and skin temperature is compared side to side with the dorsal surface of the hand.

options.text: Inspect the skin of the face, arms, and lips for a bluish tinge; compare skin temperature side to side with the back of the hand
options.rationale: The temperature technique is right, but a bluish color is how cyanosis shows in light skin. In dark brown skin it appears as graying, best seen in the mucous membranes, conjunctivae, and nail beds.

options.text: Inspect the conjunctivae, oral mucosa, and nail beds for ash gray color; feel skin temperature on one side only with the fingertips
options.rationale: The sites and color are right, but skin temperature is checked for symmetry by touching different areas with the back of the hand or fingers, comparing both sides.

options.text: Inspect the palms and soles for a yellow brown color; rely on the oxygen saturation trend to show any changes in perfusion over time
options.rationale: A yellow brown color can signal decreased perfusion in brown skin, but the oxygen saturation measures oxygenation, not skin perfusion. The skin, mucous membranes, and temperature still need direct assessment.

questions.takeaway: Assess perfusion where small vessels are near the surface: nail beds, mucous membranes, and conjunctivae. In dark skin, decreased perfusion and cyanosis show as ash gray; check skin temperature for symmetry with the back of the hand.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options name the right sites. Decide on technique: temperature is compared on both sides with the back of the hand.

steps.detail: Nail beds, mucous membranes, and conjunctivae show perfusion in any skin tone. The face and arms are not the best sites in dark skin.
Ash gray in dark brown skin; bluish is the light skin presentation.
Back of the hand, both sides. One side with the fingertips misses symmetry.
Oxygen saturation does not replace a skin and perfusion assessment.

elimination.verdict: Inspect the conjunctivae, oral mucous membranes, and nail beds for ash gray color, and compare skin temperature on both sides with the back of the hand.

questions.objective: Perform a focused cardiovascular history and physical assessment.

questions.scenario: A nurse on a cardiac unit reviews the laboratory plan for several clients.
questions.stem: For each client, indicate the laboratory test the nurse uses to monitor the problem described.

rows.text: Takes warfarin each evening for atrial fibrillation; the dose was changed 3 days ago
rows.rationale: PT and INR are used when starting and maintaining oral anticoagulants such as warfarin. The INR is the most reliable way to monitor warfarin.

rows.text: Receives a continuous intravenous heparin infusion for a clot in the left leg
rows.rationale: The PTT is assessed in clients receiving heparin. It shows whether the infusion is reaching the prescribed level of anticoagulation.

rows.text: Takes a loop diuretic for heart failure and now has new premature ventricular beats on the monitor
rows.rationale: Diuretics can lower potassium, and hypokalemia increases electrical instability and ventricular dysrhythmias. The basic metabolic panel includes potassium.

rows.text: Has pulmonary edema, a respiratory rate of 32 breaths per minute, and new confusion
rows.rationale: Arterial blood gases show tissue oxygenation, carbon dioxide removal, and acid base status. Severe breathlessness with new confusion calls for that information.

rows.text: Has heart failure, the loop diuretic dose was doubled 2 days ago, and the provider wants kidney function checked
rows.rationale: Blood urea nitrogen and creatinine show kidney function, and a larger diuretic dose can also shift sodium and potassium. All of these are on the basic metabolic panel.

rows.text: Had a mechanical heart valve placed last year and takes warfarin to prevent clots on the valve
rows.rationale: Clients with prosthetic valves tend to form thrombi and often take warfarin. PT and INR monitor that therapy, whatever the reason for the anticoagulant.

questions.takeaway: Match the lab to what it monitors: PT and INR for warfarin, PTT for heparin, arterial blood gases for oxygenation, carbon dioxide, and acid base status, and the basic metabolic panel for electrolytes such as potassium and sodium.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Name the drug or the problem first, then the test that tracks it. Heparin and warfarin are monitored by different tests, and rhythm changes on a diuretic point to an electrolyte.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Warfarin: PT and INR, for any reason it is taken. Heparin: PTT.
Pulmonary edema with confusion needs arterial blood gases.
A diuretic with new ventricular beats points to potassium; a diuretic dose increase calls for kidney function, blood urea nitrogen and creatinine. Both are on the basic metabolic panel.

elimination.verdict: PT and INR; PTT; basic metabolic panel; arterial blood gases; basic metabolic panel; PT and INR.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: A client, 59 years old, is scheduled for an exercise electrocardiogram (stress test) on a treadmill at 1300 tomorrow to screen for coronary artery disease. The client takes a beta blocker each morning, and the cardiologist has written to hold it on the day of the test. Which instruction by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Take your beta blocker tomorrow morning as usual so your heart rate stays controlled on the treadmill."
options.rationale: Keeping the usual routine sounds safe, but beta blockers are usually withheld on the day of the test so the heart rate can rise during exercise. The cardiologist ordered it held.

options.text: "Do not eat or drink anything after midnight, and plan to stay flat in bed for several hours after the test."
options.rationale: Fasting and bed rest describe preparation and follow up for cardiac catheterization. A stress test allows a light meal 2 hours before and has no bed rest.

options.text: "You may eat a light meal by 1100, and do not drink coffee or smoke tomorrow; take a hot shower after the test."
options.rationale: The meal, caffeine, and smoking instructions are right, but a hot shower is avoided for 1 to 2 hours after the test because it may cause hypotension.

options.text: "You may eat a light meal by 1100, and do not drink coffee or smoke tomorrow; skip your beta blocker that morning."
options.rationale: Before a stress test the client may have a light meal 2 hours before, avoids smoking, alcohol, and caffeine on the day of the test, and follows the cardiologist's direction on cardiac drugs, here holding the beta blocker so the heart rate can rise.

questions.takeaway: Before an exercise stress test: rest the night before, a light meal up to 2 hours before, no smoking, alcohol, or caffeine that day, and cardiac drugs such as beta blockers held only as the cardiologist directs. Avoid a hot shower for 1 to 2 hours afterward.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two options share the meal and caffeine instructions. Decide on the second half: holding the beta blocker follows the order, while a hot shower after the test risks hypotension.

steps.detail: The order says hold the beta blocker, so taking it is wrong.
Fasting after midnight and bed rest belong to catheterization.
Both give the right meal and caffeine teaching. Only one keeps the drug order; the other adds a hot shower, which is avoided.

elimination.verdict: Light meal by 1100, no coffee or smoking, and skip the beta blocker that morning.

questions.objective: Recognize common laboratory and diagnostic tests used to evaluate the cardiovascular system.

questions.stem: A nurse on a cardiac unit reviews findings documented for several clients who have heart failure. Which findings indicate right sided heart failure? Select all that apply.

options.text: Neck veins distended with the head of the bed raised to 45 degrees
options.rationale: Jugular venous distention reflects systemic venous congestion. When the right ventricle fails, blood backs up into the systemic veins.

options.text: Sleeps on 3 pillows and becomes short of breath within minutes of lying flat
options.rationale: Orthopnea comes from pulmonary congestion. Blood backs up into the lungs when the left ventricle fails, so this is a left sided finding.

options.text: New confusion, with cool hands and feet bilaterally
options.rationale: Confusion and cool extremities reflect decreased cardiac output and decreased perfusion, a left sided pattern.

options.text: Reports no appetite and nausea at meals, with a liver edge palpable below the right costal margin
options.rationale: Anorexia, nausea, and hepatomegaly come from systemic venous congestion of the liver and gut, a right sided pattern.

options.text: Abdominal girth up 4 cm in 3 days with a distended, tight abdomen
options.rationale: Ascites and abdominal distention reflect systemic venous congestion, a right sided pattern.

options.text: Urine output 22 mL per hour for 3 hours
options.rationale: Lower urine output is a decreased cardiac output finding. The failing left ventricle sends less blood to the kidneys.

questions.takeaway: Left sided failure backs blood into the lungs and lowers output: dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, cough, fatigue, tachycardia, confusion, cool extremities, lower urine output. Right sided failure backs blood into the systemic veins: dependent edema, JVD, weight gain, ascites, hepatomegaly, anorexia and nausea.
questions.strategy: Ask where the blood is backing up. Lungs or low output points left. Neck veins, belly, liver, and legs point right.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Distended neck veins, ascites, and the liver and gut findings are systemic congestion: right. Orthopnea is lung congestion: left.
Low urine output, confusion, and cool extremities come from decreased cardiac output: left.
Nausea and poor appetite sound like low perfusion of the gut, but they come from venous congestion: right.

elimination.verdict: A, D, E.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.nursesNote: Client admitted with heart failure. Reports shortness of breath walking to the bathroom and waking at night gasping for air. Coughing frequently. Heart rate 112 beats per minute. Respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. Blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg. SpO2 91% on room air. Crackles in both lung bases. Abdomen soft, not distended. No edema in either ankle. Neck veins flat with the head of the bed at 45 degrees.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that indicate left sided heart failure.

segments.text: waking at night gasping for air
segments.rationale: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea is a pulmonary congestion finding of left sided failure.

segments.text: Coughing frequently
segments.rationale: Cough is a pulmonary congestion finding of left sided failure.

segments.text: Blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg
segments.rationale: Above 120/80 mm Hg, but elevated blood pressure is a cause of heart failure, not one of the pulmonary congestion or decreased cardiac output findings of left sided failure.

segments.text: Heart rate 112 beats per minute
segments.rationale: Tachycardia above 100 beats per minute is a decreased cardiac output finding of left sided failure.

segments.text: SpO2 91% on room air
segments.rationale: Below 95 to 100%. Fluid in the lungs impairs gas exchange.

segments.text: Crackles in both lung bases
segments.rationale: Crackles are a pulmonary congestion finding of left sided failure.

segments.text: Abdomen soft, not distended
segments.rationale: No ascites or abdominal distention, so no sign of systemic venous congestion here.

segments.text: Neck veins flat with the head of the bed at 45 degrees
segments.rationale: No jugular venous distention. This is an expected finding.

questions.takeaway: This client shows left sided failure: paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, cough, crackles, and low SpO2 from pulmonary congestion, plus tachycardia from decreased cardiac output. The absence of edema, ascites, and JVD argues against right sided involvement.
questions.strategy: An abnormal value is not automatically a left sided finding. For each abnormal finding, ask whether it shows blood backing into the lungs or low output, or whether it is a cause of heart failure instead.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Night gasping, cough, crackles, and SpO2 91% all point to fluid in the lungs.
Heart rate 112 beats per minute.

steps.action: Abnormal but not a finding of left sided failure
steps.detail: Blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg is a cause of heart failure.
Soft abdomen, flat neck veins.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure is newly confused at 1000 after being oriented at 0700. Blood pressure 94/60 mm Hg, heart rate 108 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 97% on room air. Hands and feet are cool bilaterally. Urine output was 60 mL over the last 3 hours. Fine crackles are heard in both lung bases. Which explanation best accounts for the confusion?

options.text: Decreased cerebral perfusion from low cardiac output
options.rationale: Correct. The low blood pressure, tachycardia, cool extremities, and urine output of 20 mL per hour all show low output, and the brain is underperfused the same way the kidneys are.

options.text: Hypoxemia from fluid in the lungs
options.rationale: Crackles in the bases show some pulmonary congestion, so this is the right idea, but SpO2 97% on room air is inside 95 to 100%. The brain is getting oxygenated blood; it is not getting enough of it.

options.text: Systemic venous congestion from right sided failure
options.rationale: Systemic venous congestion produces edema, JVD, ascites, and liver findings, none of which are described. It does not explain confusion.

options.text: Fluid volume deficit from excess fluid removal
options.rationale: Low urine output and low blood pressure can fit a deficit, but crackles show the client still has fluid in the lungs, which argues against a deficit.

questions.takeaway: Confusion in heart failure can come from decreased cardiac output or from hypoxemia. Check the SpO2: when it is in range and the output findings (low blood pressure, tachycardia, cool extremities, low urine output) cluster, the cause is perfusion, not oxygenation.
questions.strategy: Hypoxemia and low output both cause confusion, and crackles make hypoxemia tempting. The deciding cue is SpO2 97% on room air.

steps.detail: Low output and hypoxemia both explain confusion.
SpO2 97% on room air is inside 95 to 100%, so hypoxemia is out.
Blood pressure 94/60 mm Hg, heart rate 108, cool hands and feet, 20 mL per hour of urine: low output.
No systemic congestion findings; crackles argue against a deficit.

elimination.verdict: Decreased cerebral perfusion from low cardiac output.

questions.objective: Differentiate left and right sided heart failure and identify their key clinical findings.

questions.stem: A client is admitted with worsening heart failure. Heart rate 104 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 92% on room air, 2+ edema in both ankles. Which actions belong in the nurse's ongoing assessment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Auscultate lung sounds and note how far up the crackles are heard
options.rationale: Lung sounds are a core heart failure assessment and show whether pulmonary congestion is spreading or clearing.

options.text: Weigh the client daily at the same time, on the same scale, in similar clothing
options.rationale: Daily weight with a consistent technique tracks fluid gained or lost.

options.text: Record intake and output each shift
options.rationale: Intake and output show whether fluid is being retained or removed.

options.text: Assess the apical heart rate and rhythm
options.rationale: Heart rate and rhythm are part of the nursing assessment; tachycardia is a low output finding.

options.text: Delegate auscultation of lung sounds to assistive personnel at each vital sign check
options.rationale: Assistive personnel can measure vital signs, but auscultating and interpreting lung sounds is a nursing assessment and is not delegated.

options.text: Weigh the client once a week on the same scale to limit day to day variation
options.rationale: Same scale is right, but heart failure weights are daily. A weekly weight misses a gain of 2 to 3 lb in 24 hours.

questions.takeaway: Heart failure assessment: respiratory status and SpO2, lung sounds, heart rate and rhythm, JVD and edema, activity tolerance, intake and output, and daily weight at the same time, on the same scale, in similar clothing.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option keeps one correct detail (lung sounds, same scale) and breaks another (who assesses, how often).

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Belongs, and the level of crackles matters.

steps.action: Weight, intake and output, heart rate and rhythm
steps.detail: All belong.
Auscultating and interpreting lung sounds stays with the nurse.
Heart failure weights are daily; weekly misses a 24 hour gain.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with dyspnea and 2+ edema in both ankles has a B type natriuretic peptide (BNP) of 860 pg/mL. An echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 35%, and the chest x ray shows an enlarged heart. Which interpretation of these results is correct?

options.text: The BNP reflects ventricular stretch, the ejection fraction shows a relaxation problem, and the film confirms the ejection fraction
options.rationale: Two errors. An ejection fraction of 35% is reduced, which is a contraction problem; a relaxation problem is heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Ejection fraction comes from the echocardiogram, not the chest x ray.

options.text: The BNP reflects heart muscle damage, the ejection fraction shows a contraction problem, and the film confirms the ejection fraction
options.rationale: Two errors. Troponin is the marker of heart muscle damage, while a BNP of 860 pg/mL reflects ventricular stretch. Ejection fraction comes from the echocardiogram, not the chest x ray.

options.text: The BNP reflects ventricular stretch, the ejection fraction shows a contraction problem, and the film may show congestion
options.rationale: BNP rises with ventricular stretch from fluid overload. An ejection fraction of 35% is heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, a contraction problem. The chest x ray in heart failure shows cardiomegaly and congestion.

options.text: The BNP reflects heart muscle damage, the ejection fraction shows a relaxation problem, and the film may show congestion
options.rationale: Two errors. A BNP of 860 pg/mL reflects ventricular stretch, not muscle damage, which troponin marks. An ejection fraction of 35% is reduced, a contraction problem.

questions.takeaway: BNP rises with ventricular stretch and fluid overload. The echocardiogram shows structure and ejection fraction: HFrEF is a contraction problem with an EF typically below 40%; HFpEF is a relaxation problem with a relatively preserved EF. The chest x ray shows cardiomegaly and congestion.
questions.strategy: Match each test to the question it answers: how stretched (BNP), how well it squeezes (echocardiogram), how big and how wet (chest x ray). Judge each part on its own; the key is the only option with all three parts right.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 860 pg/mL reflects stretch and fluid overload, not muscle damage. Eliminate B and D.
Reduced: a contraction problem. Eliminate A.
Cardiomegaly and congestion; ejection fraction comes from the echocardiogram. C remains.

elimination.verdict: C. Ventricular stretch, a contraction problem, and congestion on the film.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure has received a diuretic for 2 days. Today: weight 2 lb lower than yesterday on the same scale, urine output 1900 mL in 24 hours with intake of 1400 mL, crackles now heard only at the right base, SpO2 95% on 2 L nasal cannula, heart rate 88 beats per minute. Which finding best shows that the diuretic is achieving its purpose?

options.text: SpO2 95% on 2 L of oxygen by nasal cannula
options.rationale: SpO2 is in range, but it is measured on supplemental oxygen, so it reflects the oxygen as much as the fluid removal.

options.text: Heart rate of 88 beats per minute at rest
options.rationale: A rate in range is welcome, but many things affect heart rate. It does not directly show fluid removal.

options.text: Crackles now heard only at the right lung base
options.rationale: Fewer crackles do suggest less lung fluid, but crackles are one location on one exam. The weight and output measure the fluid removed.

options.text: Weight down 2 lb and output 500 mL above intake
options.rationale: A diuretic removes excess fluid. Weight down on the same scale and output exceeding intake measure that removal directly.

questions.takeaway: Diuretics remove excess fluid. The most direct evidence is a falling daily weight and output exceeding intake; fewer crackles, less dyspnea, and better SpO2 support it.
questions.strategy: Several options are good news. The key word is best: pick the finding that measures what the drug does.

steps.detail: Remove excess fluid.
Weight and the output to intake balance.
Fewer crackles is supportive, not a measure of volume.
SpO2 on oxygen and heart rate are influenced by other factors.

elimination.verdict: A 2 lb weight loss with output above intake.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.stem: A nurse receives report on four clients with heart failure. Client 1 reports new chest pain at rest, 6 of 10, with SpO2 96% on room air. Client 2 asks how much sodium is in canned soup before lunch. Client 3 has SpO2 86% on room air, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, and crackles halfway up both lungs. Client 4 has a weight up 3 lb since yesterday on the same scale, with ankle edema now 2+ from 1+. In which order does the nurse see the clients, from first to last?

options.text: Client 1, client 3, client 2, client 4
options.rationale: Two errors. Client 3 has a breathing problem with severe hypoxemia and spreading crackles and comes before chest pain with SpO2 in range, and a weight gain with more edema comes before a teaching question.

options.text: Client 3, client 1, client 4, client 2
options.rationale: Severe hypoxemia with crackles halfway up both lungs is a breathing problem and comes first. Chest pain at rest may be ischemia and comes next. The weight gain with more edema must be addressed today but is not an emergency. The teaching question is last.

options.text: Client 3, client 4, client 1, client 2
options.rationale: Client 3 is first, but chest pain at rest outranks a weight gain with more edema, which shows worsening heart failure without a breathing or circulation emergency.

options.text: Client 3, client 1, client 2, client 4
options.rationale: The first two are right, but a gain of 3 lb in 24 hours with more edema is a physiologic change and comes before a teaching question.

questions.takeaway: Prioritize by ABCs: severe hypoxemia with spreading crackles first, chest pain at rest next, a reportable weight gain with more edema next, and a teaching question last.
questions.strategy: Apply the ABCs, then separate an emergency from a finding that is reportable but not immediately dangerous. A physiologic change always outranks a teaching need.

steps.detail: SpO2 86% with crackles halfway up both lungs: first. Eliminate A.
Chest pain at rest: second. Eliminate C.
3 lb in 24 hours with more edema before the sodium question. Eliminate D.

elimination.verdict: B. Client 3, client 1, client 4, client 2.

questions.objective: Describe priority assessment, treatment, and patient teaching interventions for heart failure.

questions.scenario: A client with heart failure is sitting in a chair at 1400.
