elimination.verdict: D. Injury, lipid entry and oxidation, fatty streak, fibrous plaque, narrowing, ischemia.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: A client with coronary artery disease has had chest pressure only while climbing stairs for 1 year, relieved within minutes by rest. Today the client comes to the emergency department with chest pressure that began while reading in a chair and has lasted 40 minutes, rated 8 of 10, with diaphoresis. Blood pressure 154/92 mm Hg, heart rate 108 beats per minute. Which change in the coronary artery best explains the new pattern?

options.text: The plaque has grown slowly, narrowing the artery a little more each month
options.rationale: Slow narrowing produces the predictable pattern with exertion that the client had for a year. It does not explain sudden pressure at rest.

options.text: The arteriole walls have thickened from long periods of high blood pressure
options.rationale: Thickening of the arteriole walls is how primary hypertension damages organs over time. It does not explain a sudden change.

options.text: The plaque has narrowed the artery past a critical point, so flow is now too low even at rest
options.rationale: Narrowing builds over months. It would not jump suddenly from a year of pressure with stairs to 40 minutes of pressure at rest with diaphoresis.

options.text: A plaque has ruptured, and a clot has formed on it that is blocking flow
options.rationale: Plaque rupture and thrombosis can cause an acute coronary syndrome or acute myocardial infarction. Pressure at rest lasting 40 minutes with diaphoresis fits a sudden blockage.

questions.takeaway: Plaque that narrows a coronary artery causes ischemia with exertion. When plaque ruptures, a clot forms quickly and can cause an acute coronary syndrome or a myocardial infarction, so pressure that begins at rest and lasts is a sudden, not a gradual, change.
questions.strategy: Every option describes something real in atherosclerosis. Pick the one whose speed matches the stem: a year of exertional pressure, then sudden pressure at rest.

steps.detail: A year of pressure with stairs, now 40 minutes at rest.
Slow growth and wall thickening are gradual. Critical narrowing builds over months and would not jump suddenly from stair pressure to 40 minutes at rest.
Rupture with a clot.

elimination.verdict: A plaque has ruptured and a clot is blocking flow.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: A client, 46 years old, has no history of hypertension. Over 3 clinic visits, with a cuff sized to the arm and after 5 minutes of seated rest, readings in the right arm average 126/84 mm Hg. At the first visit, the left arm read within 2 mm Hg of the right. The client says, "My top number is under 130, so I only have elevated blood pressure, right?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Your bottom number places you in stage 1 hypertension, because either number can set the category."
options.rationale: Stage 1 is a systolic of 130 to 139 or a diastolic of 80 to 89 mm Hg. A diastolic of 84 mm Hg meets stage 1 even though the systolic of 126 mm Hg alone would not.

options.text: "Yes, a top number under 130 means elevated blood pressure, so the plan is a yearly recheck."
options.rationale: Elevated blood pressure is a systolic of 120 to 129 mm Hg and a diastolic below 80 mm Hg. Both conditions must be met, and a diastolic of 84 mm Hg rules it out.

options.text: "Your average falls in stage 2 hypertension, because both numbers are above the goal for adults."
options.rationale: Both numbers are above the goal of below 130/80 mm Hg, but stage 2 starts at a systolic of 140 or a diastolic of 90 mm Hg. Neither value reaches stage 2.

options.text: "Yes, the top number sets the category, and the bottom number counts only once it reaches stage 2."
options.rationale: Every category above normal is defined by the systolic or the diastolic. The higher category reached by either number is the one that applies.

questions.takeaway: Blood pressure categories use "or" above the elevated level: the higher category reached by either the systolic or the diastolic number is the one that applies. Elevated blood pressure requires a diastolic below 80 mm Hg.
questions.strategy: The client anchors on the systolic. Check the diastolic of 84 mm Hg separately before accepting the client's label.

steps.detail: Systolic 126 mm Hg alone would be elevated; diastolic 84 mm Hg alone is stage 1.
The higher category reached by either number wins, so stage 1.
B and D both say the top number decides.
Neither 126 nor 84 mm Hg reaches stage 2, so C is out.

elimination.verdict: Stage 1 hypertension, set by the diastolic of 84 mm Hg.

questions.objective: Recognize common manifestations, complications, and priority nursing assessments for hypertension.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client, 70 years old, has had vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days and has no history of kidney disease or hypertension. Lying blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg in the right arm with heart rate 80 beats per minute. Within 30 seconds of standing, blood pressure is 94/60 mm Hg and heart rate is 106 beats per minute. Urine output is 20 mL per hour for the past 4 hours, was 60 mL per hour yesterday. Serum creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL, the same as at a clinic visit 1 month ago. The rise in heart rate within 30 seconds of standing is driven mainly by [[1]].

The low urine output is best explained by [[2]].

Of the mechanisms named, the one that raises blood pressure by increasing both peripheral vascular resistance and blood volume is [[3]].

options.text: The renin angiotensin aldosterone system responding to the fluid loss
options.rationale: The fluid loss does activate this system, but its effects come through hormones over minutes to hours. A heart rate rise within 30 seconds of standing is a reflex.

options.text: Arterial baroreceptors sensing the fall in pressure on standing
options.rationale: Baroreceptors sense changes in arterial pressure and respond within seconds, speeding the heart and constricting vessels. The 30 second timing is the cue.

options.text: Vascular autoregulation in the body tissues
options.rationale: Autoregulation adjusts local flow to keep each tissue perfused. It does not sense arterial pressure and drive the heart rate.

options.text: Chemoreceptors sensing the oxygen level of the blood
options.rationale: Chemoreceptors respond to oxygen and carbon dioxide levels. Nothing in the stem describes a change in oxygenation.

options.text: Kidney damage from long standing high blood pressure
options.rationale: Kidney damage can lower urine output, but the creatinine is unchanged from 1 month ago and there is no kidney or hypertension history, so the kidneys are responding, not failing.

options.text: Vascular autoregulation closing off kidney flow to protect the brain
options.rationale: Autoregulation works to maintain each organ's own perfusion. It does not divert flow away from the kidneys.

options.text: Sodium and water retention after low kidney blood flow activates the renin angiotensin aldosterone system
options.rationale: Fluid loss lowers kidney perfusion, which triggers renin release. Aldosterone then holds sodium and water, so less urine is made. The unchanged creatinine points to a kidney response, not kidney damage.

options.text: Vasoconstriction from the baroreceptor reflex alone
options.rationale: The reflex does constrict vessels, but it does not explain the kidneys holding sodium and water over hours. That is the work of the renin angiotensin aldosterone system.

options.text: The baroreceptor reflex
options.rationale: The reflex raises pressure through a faster heart rate and vasoconstriction, so it raises resistance, but it does not add to blood volume.

options.text: Vascular autoregulation
options.rationale: Autoregulation maintains local tissue perfusion. It does not raise systemic resistance and volume.

options.text: The renin angiotensin aldosterone system
options.rationale: Angiotensin II constricts vessels, raising peripheral vascular resistance, and aldosterone retains sodium and water, raising blood volume. The cue is both.

questions.takeaway: Baroreceptors sense arterial pressure and respond in seconds through heart rate and vessel tone. The renin angiotensin aldosterone system responds to low kidney flow with vasoconstriction plus sodium and water retention, which lowers urine output and raises both resistance and volume.
questions.strategy: Each blank has two defensible answers. Let the timing decide blank 1 (seconds means a reflex), the unchanged creatinine decide blank 2 (a kidney response, not damage), and the word both decide blank 3.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Within 30 seconds of standing: the baroreceptor reflex, not a hormonal system.
Creatinine unchanged from 1 month ago and no kidney history: retention from the renin angiotensin aldosterone system, not damage.
Resistance and volume together: only the renin angiotensin aldosterone system adds volume.

elimination.verdict: Arterial baroreceptors; sodium and water retention from the renin angiotensin aldosterone system; the renin angiotensin aldosterone system.

questions.objective: Explain the basic mechanisms that regulate blood pressure and contribute to hypertension.

questions.stem: A client, 66 years old, has had hypertension for 14 years and often skips doses. Blood pressure today is 164/98 mm Hg in the right arm and 162/96 mm Hg in the left arm, and heart rate is 80 beats per minute. The nurse reviews the record. Which finding shows that the hypertension has already damaged a target organ?

options.text: A morning headache, 3 of 10, that eases by midday
options.rationale: Headache can occur with significantly elevated pressure, but it is a manifestation of the high reading, not evidence that an organ has been damaged.

options.text: LDL cholesterol 172 mg/dL on the latest lipid panel
options.rationale: A high LDL level is a risk factor for atherosclerosis. It raises future risk but does not show organ damage from hypertension.

options.text: Serum creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, was 1.0 mg/dL 3 years ago
options.rationale: Persistent hypertension damages vessels and lowers kidney perfusion. A creatinine that has nearly doubled shows falling kidney function, which is target organ damage.

options.text: Readings of 160/90 mm Hg or higher at 3 of the last 4 visits
options.rationale: Repeated high readings show that pressure is poorly controlled. They describe the cause of damage, not a damaged organ.

questions.takeaway: Target organ damage is the end result of persistent hypertension: stroke in the brain, left ventricular hypertrophy, CAD or heart failure in the heart, chronic kidney disease, and peripheral vascular disease. A rising creatinine is kidney damage, while symptoms, high readings and lipids are not.
questions.strategy: Sort each option: is it a symptom, a risk factor, a measure of control, or a sign that an organ has changed?

steps.detail: Brain, heart, kidneys and vessels.
Headache is a symptom, LDL is a risk factor, repeated readings are control.
Creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, was 1.0 mg/dL, shows kidney decline.

elimination.verdict: The rising creatinine shows kidney damage.

questions.objective: Recognize common manifestations, complications, and priority nursing assessments for hypertension.

questions.stem: A client, 62 years old, started hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension 3 weeks ago and takes no other drugs. Which findings does the nurse recognize as possible adverse effects of this drug? Select all that apply.

options.text: Potassium 3.1 mEq/L
options.rationale: Thiazide diuretics increase potassium excretion, and hypokalemia is their most frequent side effect.

options.text: Weakness in both legs when climbing stairs
options.rationale: Muscle weakness can signal hypokalemia from potassium loss in the urine.

options.text: A persistent dry cough that began 2 weeks ago
options.rationale: A nagging dry cough is the most common side effect of ACE inhibitors, which the client does not take.

options.text: Lying blood pressure 132/80 mm Hg and standing 110/72 mm Hg, with lightheadedness
options.rationale: Diuresis can cause hypovolemia and orthostatic hypotension, shown by a 22 mm Hg systolic drop with symptoms.

options.text: Weight up 2 kg in 1 week with swelling in both ankles
options.rationale: A diuretic removes fluid. Weight gain with edema points away from a diuretic effect and needs a separate cause.

options.text: Heart rate 52 beats per minute, regular, at the right radial pulse
options.rationale: Thiazides do not slow the heart. Low potassium is linked to an irregular pulse and dysrhythmias, not a slow, regular rate.

questions.takeaway: Thiazide and loop diuretics cause potassium loss and fluid loss: watch for low potassium, muscle weakness, irregular pulse, dizziness and orthostatic drops. Cough belongs to ACE inhibitors.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Tie each finding to the drug's action. A drug that removes sodium, water and potassium causes low potassium and low volume, not fluid gain, cough or a slow heart.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Loss in the urine explains 3.1 mEq/L and leg weakness.
Diuresis explains the orthostatic drop.
Cough is an ACE inhibitor effect; edema and a slow regular rate do not fit a diuretic.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D.

questions.objective: Describe lifestyle changes and common medication classes used to manage hypertension.

questions.stem: A nurse at an urgent care clinic receives four clients with hypertension at the same time. Which client does the nurse assess first?

options.text: Blood pressure 168/102 mm Hg in the right arm, with chest pressure that began 20 minutes ago at rest and sweating
options.rationale: Chest pressure at rest with sweating suggests the heart is not getting enough oxygen now. Hypertension damages the heart through CAD and MI, and this client shows signs of that damage happening, so this client is seen first.

options.text: Blood pressure 188/122 mm Hg in the right arm after missing 2 days of doses, alert, and denying headache, chest pain or vision changes
options.rationale: This reading is at the crisis level and needs prompt care, but the client reports no symptoms of organ injury. A client with active chest pressure at rest comes before a high number without symptoms.

options.text: Blood pressure 154/96 mm Hg in the right arm, with a dull headache, 3 of 10, since waking
options.rationale: Headache can occur with elevated pressure, but this reading is below the crisis level and the headache is mild and present for hours.

options.text: Lying blood pressure 126/80 mm Hg and standing 108/72 mm Hg in the right arm, lightheaded on standing after a dose increase 2 days ago
options.rationale: An orthostatic drop raises the risk of falls and needs follow up, but it is not a threat to the heart or brain right now.

questions.takeaway: A crisis level reading is urgent, but symptoms of organ injury now, such as chest pressure at rest, decide priority over the number alone. Treat the client whose heart is showing ischemia before the client whose reading is highest.
questions.strategy: B tempts because 188/122 mm Hg is the highest reading and meets the crisis level. The deciding cue is that client A has chest pressure at rest with sweating, while client B denies every symptom.

steps.detail: A has chest pressure at rest; B has the highest reading.
B denies headache, chest pain and vision changes.
Chest pressure at rest with sweating signals ischemia now.
C is mild; D is a fall risk, not an organ threat.

elimination.verdict: Assess the client with chest pressure at rest first.

questions.objective: Recognize common manifestations, complications, and priority nursing assessments for hypertension.

questions.stem: A client, 50 years old, has readings averaging 142/90 mm Hg in the right arm over 3 clinic visits, with a cuff sized to the arm after 5 minutes of seated rest. The client says, "I feel completely well and have never had a headache, so my pressure cannot be hurting anything. I will start treatment when I get symptoms." Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Your readings are only a little above the goal, so rechecking once a year is enough for as long as you feel well."
options.rationale: Readings averaging 142/90 mm Hg are above the goal of below 130/80 mm Hg, and waiting a year leaves the pressure damaging vessels and organs without treatment.

options.text: "High pressure usually causes no symptoms while it damages vessels, and over time it can lead to stroke, heart attack, heart failure, or kidney failure."
options.rationale: Hypertension is often asymptomatic, and chronic elevation damages vessels and organs. Its major complications are stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, and kidney failure, so feeling well is not a reason to wait.

options.text: "High pressure usually causes no symptoms, and the harm it does is limited to the heart, so a yearly heart tracing will show any damage it causes."
options.rationale: Asymptomatic is correct, but hypertension damages the brain, kidneys, and vessels as well as the heart, and a tracing would not show kidney damage or stroke risk.

options.text: "You are right that headaches are the first warning of damage, so call as soon as you notice one and we will start treatment then."
options.rationale: Most clients have no symptoms, and headache appears only with significantly elevated pressure. Damage can be well advanced before any symptom appears.

questions.takeaway: Hypertension is often asymptomatic while it damages vessels and organs. Its major complications are stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, and kidney failure, and the ACC/AHA goal for all people is below 130/80 mm Hg.
questions.strategy: Two options agree that hypertension has no symptoms. Read on to which organs it harms; the one that limits the damage to the heart is the right idea with one thing off.

steps.detail: 142/90 mm Hg is above the ACC/AHA goal of below 130/80 mm Hg, the goal for all people.
Hypertension is usually silent; headache comes only with significantly elevated pressure.
Both say no symptoms; only one names all four major complications.
A pressure above goal is not left untreated for a year.

elimination.verdict: High pressure is usually silent while it damages the brain, heart, and kidneys.

questions.objective: Explain the basic mechanisms that regulate blood pressure and contribute to hypertension.

questions.stem: A client, 48 years old, has readings averaging 146/92 mm Hg in both arms over 3 clinic visits. Body mass index 32 kg/m2. Smokes 1 pack a day and has a high stress job. A parent has hypertension. Urinalysis is negative for protein and red blood cells, potassium is 4.2 mEq/L, creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL, and the client takes no drugs. The client asks, "What kind of high blood pressure is this, and how does it damage my body?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "This is secondary hypertension caused by your weight, and losing weight will cure it."
options.rationale: Obesity is a risk factor for primary hypertension, not a condition that causes secondary hypertension. Weight loss lowers pressure but is not described as a cure.

options.text: "This is primary hypertension. Over time the high pressure stretches and thins the walls of your large arteries, which lowers blood flow to your organs."
options.rationale: Primary is correct, but continuous elevation thickens the walls of the small arteries (medial hyperplasia). It does not thin the large arteries.

options.text: "This is primary hypertension, the most common type. Over time the pressure thickens the walls of your small arteries, which lowers blood flow to your organs."
options.rationale: With normal kidney tests, no drugs, and risk factors of obesity, smoking, stress, and family history, this fits primary hypertension. Continuous elevation causes medial hyperplasia, a thickening of the arteriole walls, which reduces perfusion and damages vital organs.

options.text: "This is primary hypertension, the most common type. Over time cholesterol plaque builds up inside your small arteries, which lowers blood flow to your organs."
options.rationale: Primary is correct, but plaque from lipid laden macrophages is atherosclerosis. The organ damage of primary hypertension comes from thickening of the arteriole walls.

questions.takeaway: Primary (essential) hypertension is the most common type and has no single underlying condition. Its risk factors include obesity, smoking, stress, and family history, and it damages vital organs through medial hyperplasia, a thickening of the arteriole walls.
questions.strategy: Three options agree it is primary hypertension, so the mechanism decides. Thickened arteriole walls is the slide's mechanism; plaque belongs to atherosclerosis.

steps.detail: Normal urinalysis, potassium, and creatinine, no drugs, and classic risk factors: primary.
Obesity is a risk factor, not a secondary cause.
Thickening of arteriole walls, not thinning of large arteries.
Plaque from lipid laden macrophages is a different process.

elimination.verdict: Primary hypertension; the arteriole walls thicken and organ perfusion falls.

questions.objective: Differentiate primary and secondary hypertension and identify major risk factors.

questions.nursesNote: 1030. Client, 60 years old, at a walk in clinic. Blood pressure 176/108 mm Hg in the right arm and 174/106 mm Hg in the left arm. Reports a headache at the back of the head since waking, 4 of 10. States vision has been blurry in both eyes since yesterday. Face appears flushed. Becomes short of breath climbing one flight of stairs, which began this week. Reports cramping in the right calf after walking 2 blocks that stops with standing still. Reports heartburn after spicy meals for 1 year. Reports pain in the right knee after gardening for 1 month.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that may be manifestations of significantly elevated blood pressure.

segments.text: Reports a headache at the back of the head since waking, 4 of 10.
segments.rationale: Headache is a possible manifestation of significantly elevated pressure.

segments.text: States vision has been blurry in both eyes since yesterday.
segments.rationale: Blurred vision is a possible manifestation of significantly elevated pressure.

segments.text: Face appears flushed.
segments.rationale: Facial flushing is a possible manifestation of significantly elevated pressure.

segments.text: Becomes short of breath climbing one flight of stairs, which began this week.
segments.rationale: Dyspnea is a possible manifestation of significantly elevated pressure.

segments.text: Reports cramping in the right calf after walking 2 blocks that stops with standing still.
segments.rationale: This pattern points to reduced arterial flow to the leg, a vascular problem, not a manifestation of the elevated pressure itself.

segments.text: Reports heartburn after spicy meals for 1 year.
segments.rationale: Heartburn tied to meals for a year is a digestive finding and is not a manifestation of elevated blood pressure.

segments.text: Reports pain in the right knee after gardening for 1 month.
segments.rationale: Knee pain after gardening is a joint finding with a clear mechanical explanation, not a manifestation of elevated blood pressure.

questions.takeaway: Most clients with hypertension have no symptoms. With significantly elevated pressure, possible manifestations are headache, dizziness, facial flushing, blurred vision, and dyspnea.
questions.strategy: Check each finding against the five possible manifestations of significantly elevated pressure. Findings with another clear explanation, such as a meal pattern or knee pain after gardening, are not selected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Headache, blurred vision, flushing, and dyspnea are on it.
Calf cramping with walking that stops with rest is a flow problem in the leg.
Heartburn after meals and knee pain after gardening have digestive and joint explanations.

questions.objective: Recognize common manifestations, complications, and priority nursing assessments for hypertension.

questions.stem: A client, 64 years old, has type 2 diabetes and smokes. The health record lists both arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis. The client asks, "Are those two words for the same thing?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Yes. Both mean the artery wall stiffens with age, and neither involves any buildup inside the wall."
options.rationale: Arteriosclerosis is thickening and hardening of the arterial wall, but atherosclerosis specifically involves plaque in the wall.

options.text: "No. Atherosclerosis is one form of hardening of the arteries, in which blood clots stick to the inner lining and harden into plaque."
options.rationale: One form of arteriosclerosis is correct, but the plaque forms from lipid laden macrophages building up in the wall, not from clots. A clot can form later if a plaque ruptures.

options.text: "No. Atherosclerosis is stretching and thinning of the artery wall from high pressure, and arteriosclerosis is the plaque."
options.rationale: This reverses the terms and the process. Atherosclerosis is the plaque forming type, and the wall thickens rather than thins.

options.text: "No. Atherosclerosis is one form of hardening of the arteries, in which fat filled immune cells build up in the wall and form plaque."
options.rationale: Atherosclerosis is a form of arteriosclerosis: the wall thickens and hardens as lipid laden macrophages accumulate and plaque develops. Diabetes and smoking are both risk factors.

questions.takeaway: Atherosclerosis is a form of arteriosclerosis: thickening and hardening of the arterial wall from lipid laden macrophages and plaque. Risk factors are diabetes, smoking, hyperlipidemia or dyslipidemia, hypertension, and autoimmunity.
questions.strategy: Two options agree it is one form of hardening of the arteries. Read on to what forms the plaque: fat filled cells in the wall, not clots on the lining.

steps.detail: Atherosclerosis is one form of arteriosclerosis.
Atherosclerosis involves plaque; plain stiffening does not.
The wall thickens, and atherosclerosis is the plaque type.
Plaque comes from lipid laden macrophages, not clots.

elimination.verdict: One form of hardening of the arteries, with plaque from fat filled cells in the wall.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: A client, 61 years old, has a coronary artery narrowed by plaque and asks why chest pressure comes on while climbing stairs. Which statements by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: "The plaque takes up space inside the artery, so less blood can reach your heart muscle."
options.rationale: Coronary narrowing restricts blood flow to the myocardium.

options.text: "Climbing stairs makes your heart work harder, and its need for oxygen can outgrow what the narrowed artery delivers."
options.rationale: Exertion raises myocardial oxygen demand; a narrowed artery cannot increase flow enough, so ischemia develops.

options.text: "The pressure is a sign that your heart muscle is getting less oxygen than it needs."
options.rationale: Ischemia is reduced oxygen delivery relative to the muscle's need, and chest pressure is its main manifestation.

options.text: "Each episode means a small part of your heart muscle has died and cannot recover."
options.rationale: Ischemia from narrowing is reversible when demand falls. Death of heart muscle is infarction, which usually follows plaque rupture and thrombosis.

options.text: "A narrowed artery causes chest pressure only once a clot has fully blocked it."
options.rationale: Narrowing alone causes ischemia when demand rises. A clot on a ruptured plaque causes an acute coronary syndrome, which is a different event.

options.text: "Resting makes the problem worse, because a slower heart pushes less blood through the narrowed artery."
options.rationale: Rest lowers the heart's oxygen demand, which brings demand back within what the narrowed artery can supply.

questions.takeaway: Plaque narrows the coronary artery and restricts flow. When exertion or stress raises demand, oxygen delivery falls short and ischemia results; rest lowers demand. A clot on a ruptured plaque is the separate event behind an acute coronary syndrome.
questions.strategy: Treat ischemia as a mismatch between supply and demand. True statements explain the supply limit or the demand rise; false ones confuse ischemia with infarction or a clot.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Plaque narrows the lumen and restricts flow.
Stairs raise the oxygen need above what the artery delivers.
Less oxygen than the muscle needs.
Muscle death is infarction; a full clot is an acute coronary syndrome; rest lowers demand.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: A client receiving treatment that suppresses the immune system is on neutropenic precautions. This morning the client develops frequent liquid stools, and the provider suspects C. difficile. The stool test result will not be available until tomorrow. Which action does the nurse take when preparing to give care?

options.text: Continue neutropenic precautions today and add contact precautions when the result is confirmed
options.rationale: Contact precautions are right, but the timing is wrong. They are started for suspected as well as confirmed C. difficile.

options.text: Replace neutropenic precautions with contact precautions and wear a gown and gloves for all contact
options.rationale: Gown and gloves are right, but precautions are added, not swapped. The client still needs protective precautions.

options.text: Continue neutropenic precautions and start contact precautions now, with gown and gloves for all contact
options.rationale: Contact precautions are initiated for suspected or confirmed C. difficile, with gown and gloves during all client contact. The client's protective precautions continue.

options.text: Continue neutropenic precautions and add a mask for all care until the result is available
options.rationale: A mask is for droplet spread. C. difficile calls for contact precautions with gown and gloves.

questions.takeaway: Start contact precautions for suspected or confirmed C. difficile, with gown and gloves for all contact. Precautions are added to what the client already needs, never swapped.
questions.strategy: Two decisions are packed into each option: what happens to the precautions the client already has, and when and how the new ones start.

steps.detail: Neutropenic precautions in place. C. difficile suspected, result tomorrow.
Suspected or confirmed, so start now.
Contact: gown and gloves, not a mask.

steps.action: Check what happens to the first set
steps.detail: It continues.

elimination.verdict: Continue neutropenic precautions and start contact precautions now.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission-based precautions

questions.stem: A nurse finishes care for a client on neutropenic precautions and contact precautions for suspected C. difficile. Facility policy states that soap and water is used after care of clients with suspected or confirmed C. difficile. The nurse's gloves are intact and the hands are not visibly soiled. How does the nurse complete hand hygiene?

options.text: Remove the gown and gloves, then wash with soap and water before going on to the next client
options.rationale: Hands are cleaned after gloves are removed, and for C. difficile soap and water is used when facility policy indicates it.

options.text: Remove the gown and gloves, then use alcohol based sanitizer because the hands are not visibly soiled
options.rationale: Sanitizer is preferred in most routine situations when hands are not visibly soiled. Here the facility policy for C. difficile directs soap and water.

options.text: Wash the gloved hands with soap and water, then remove the gown and gloves and go to the next client
options.rationale: Soap and water is right, but the order is wrong. Hands are cleaned after the gloves come off.

options.text: Remove the gown and gloves, use alcohol based sanitizer now, and wash with soap and water before eating
options.rationale: Washing before eating is correct in general, but it does not replace the hand hygiene the policy requires now.

questions.takeaway: Clean hands after removing gloves. Sanitizer is preferred for routine care when hands are not visibly soiled, but for C. difficile use soap and water when facility policy indicates it.
questions.strategy: "Not visibly soiled" and "gloves intact" both point toward sanitizer. The stated policy for C. difficile overrides the routine choice, and the order of glove removal settles the rest.

steps.detail: Not visibly soiled: sanitizer is usually preferred.

steps.action: Find the exception in the stem
steps.detail: Facility policy: soap and water after C. difficile care.
Gloves come off first, then hands are cleaned.

elimination.verdict: Remove gown and gloves, then wash with soap and water.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission-based precautions

questions.stem: A client receiving treatment that suppresses the immune system is on neutropenic precautions and contact precautions for suspected C. difficile. The client is tearful and asks to see a family member. The family member arrives and says, "My allergies are acting up, so I have had a runny nose and a little cough since yesterday. I brought a mask and I will stay only a few minutes." Which action is best?

options.text: Have the family member put on a mask, gown, and gloves and clean the hands, then allow a visit of a few minutes
options.rationale: Protective equipment does not make an ill visitor safe for this client. The visitor reports new symptoms, and the nurse cannot confirm the cause. A short visit still exposes the client.

options.text: Explain that visitors are screened for illness, ask the family member to wait until well, and offer a phone call now
options.rationale: Neutropenic precautions include screening visitors and staff for illness. The nurse explains this in plain language and still responds to the client's wish for contact.

options.text: Ask the client to decide, because the client understands the risk and has asked for the visit
options.rationale: Involving the client is usually right, but screening visitors for illness is part of the precautions that protect this client.

options.text: Allow the family member to stand in the doorway in a mask, away from the bed, for a few minutes
options.rationale: Distance and a mask do not make an ill visitor safe for a client on neutropenic precautions.

questions.takeaway: Neutropenic precautions protect the client: protective precautions as indicated, meticulous hand hygiene, and screening visitors and staff for illness.
questions.strategy: Protective equipment sounds like enough, and the client's distress pulls toward allowing the visit. The visitor's own explanation, allergies, makes the symptoms sound harmless. The deciding cue is that screening is for symptoms, and this visitor has a runny nose and a cough that began yesterday.

steps.detail: The client, by the neutropenic precautions.
Runny nose and cough since yesterday, whatever the visitor thinks the cause is.
Equipment, distance, and client choice do not remove the exposure.

steps.action: Meet the client's need another way
steps.detail: Explain plainly and offer contact that carries no exposure.

elimination.verdict: Explain the screening, ask the family member to wait until well, and offer a phone call.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission-based precautions

questions.nursesNote: 1400, day 2 of admission for pneumonia: Restless and pulling at bed linen, was calm and alert at 1000. Respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, was 18 at 1000. Oxygen saturation 95% on room air, same as at 1000. Oral temperature 37.1 °C. Urine output 25 mL per hour, was 60 mL per hour at 1000. Productive cough, unchanged since admission.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that suggest possible sepsis.

segments.text: Restless and pulling at bed linen, was calm and alert at 1000
segments.rationale: A new change in mental status in a client with an infection is an early cue of sepsis.

segments.text: Respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, was 18 at 1000
segments.rationale: A respiratory rate above 20 breaths per minute is concerning, and this is a rise from baseline.

segments.text: Oxygen saturation 95% on room air, same as at 1000
segments.rationale: The value matches baseline.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.1 °C
segments.rationale: This reading is not a cue by itself, and it does not rule sepsis out. The nurse does not rely on fever alone.

segments.text: Urine output 25 mL per hour, was 60 mL per hour at 1000
segments.rationale: Decreased urine output signals deterioration.

segments.text: Productive cough, unchanged since admission
segments.rationale: The cough is an expected finding of pneumonia and has not changed.

questions.takeaway: Early cues of sepsis in a client with an infection: new confusion or restlessness, a respiratory rate above 20 breaths per minute, temperature changes, and decreased urine output. Fever is not required.
questions.strategy: Look for change from the 1000 baseline in mentation, breathing, and urine output. An unchanged finding of the pneumonia itself is not a new cue.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pneumonia.
Mentation, respiratory rate, urine output.
Oxygen saturation and cough.

steps.action: Do not lean on the temperature
steps.detail: 37.1 °C neither adds a cue nor removes the others.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: A client with pneumonia has become restless over the past 4 hours. The respiratory rate has risen from 18 to 26 breaths per minute and urine output has fallen from 60 to 25 mL per hour. The nurse has just completed an assessment, found these changes, and suspects sepsis. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Obtain the ordered specimens and check that the intravenous access works
options.rationale: Specimens and working access matter, but they come after help and orders are on the way. Doing them first delays escalation.

options.text: Notify the provider or activate the rapid response process
options.rationale: The assessment is already done and the cues are in hand. When sepsis is suspected, the nurse escalates immediately so that help and orders are on the way.

options.text: Reassess breathing, circulation, mentation, and vital signs before calling
options.rationale: Reassessment is right while help is on the way, but the stem says the assessment is complete. Repeating it before calling delays escalation.

options.text: Give the prescribed treatment promptly and then reassess the response
options.rationale: Treatment is given once it is prescribed, after specimens are obtained and access is checked. It cannot be the first step.

questions.takeaway: When sepsis is suspected and the assessment is done: escalate immediately, reassess while help is on the way, obtain ordered specimens and check intravenous access, then give prescribed treatment promptly and reassess.
questions.strategy: The stem says the assessment has been done and the cues are in hand, so the first move is to escalate. Reassessment follows while help is on the way, and treatment comes after the specimens.

steps.detail: The stem says the nurse just assessed and found the changes.
Restlessness, a respiratory rate of 26, and urine output of 25 mL per hour with suspected sepsis call for the provider or rapid response.

steps.action: Place the rest after the call
steps.detail: Reassess while help comes, then specimens and access, then treatment and reassessment.

elimination.verdict: B. Notify the provider or activate the rapid response process.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.scenario: A client is on day 2 of admission for pneumonia. At 1000 the client was calm and alert with a heart rate of 88 beats per minute, a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation of 95% on room air, and urine output of 60 mL per hour. At 1400 the client is restless and pulling at the bed linen, the heart rate is 112 beats per minute, the respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 95% on room air, urine output is 25 mL per hour, and the oral temperature is 37.1 °C. The cough is unchanged since admission. No new orders have been written.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Reassess breathing, circulation, mentation, and vital signs
options.rationale: The nurse reassesses these while help is on the way.

options.text: Recheck the oral temperature in 1 hour and escalate if a fever develops
options.rationale: The nurse does not wait for fever. Several cues are already present.

options.text: Apply oxygen and recheck the respiratory rate in 30 minutes before calling
options.rationale: Oxygen would fit worsening oxygenation, but the saturation is 95% on room air, the same as at 1000. Waiting 30 minutes delays escalation of a client with new organ dysfunction.

options.text: Notify the provider or activate the rapid response process now
options.rationale: When sepsis is suspected, the nurse escalates immediately.

options.text: Expected course of pneumonia
options.rationale: New restlessness and a fall in urine output are changes from baseline, not expected findings. The cough, the expected finding, is unchanged.

options.text: Anxiety about the hospital stay
options.rationale: Restlessness with faster breathing and less urine in a client with an infection is not treated as anxiety.

options.text: Possible sepsis
options.rationale: A client with an infection has new restlessness, a faster heart rate, a respiratory rate above 20, and decreased urine output. The changes reach beyond the lungs to mentation and kidney perfusion.

options.text: Worsening pneumonia causing hypoxemia
options.rationale: Restlessness and a faster respiratory rate can come from low oxygen, but the saturation is 95% on room air, unchanged from 1000. Hypoxemia does not explain the change, and the fall in urine output points to a whole body response.

options.text: Amount and color of sputum
options.rationale: Sputum describes the pneumonia. It does not show whether perfusion is getting better.

options.text: Mental status compared with the 1000 baseline
options.rationale: Mental status moving toward baseline is a marker of response to treatment.

options.text: Urine output each hour
options.rationale: Urine output is a key marker of adequate perfusion.

options.text: Oxygen saturation as the single measure of response
options.rationale: Oxygenation is watched, but the nurse judges the whole trend rather than one number, and the saturation never changed here.

questions.takeaway: New changes in mentation, breathing, heart rate, and urine output in a client with an infection are possible sepsis, even with no fever and an unchanged oxygen saturation. Escalate and reassess, then follow the whole trend, especially mental status and urine output.
questions.strategy: Worsening pneumonia is the defensible rival. Use the oxygen saturation: 95% on room air at both times means low oxygen does not explain the restlessness, and the falling urine output shows a response beyond the lungs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Saturation 95% at 1000 and 1400 rules out hypoxemia as the cause.
Known infection plus new changes in mentation, heart rate, breathing, and urine output: possible sepsis.
Escalate now and reassess. Options that wait for oxygen effect or for fever are out.
Choose perfusion and mentation markers, not one number or a description of the pneumonia.

elimination.verdict: Possible sepsis; escalate and reassess; monitor hourly urine output and mental status against 1000.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: A client with pneumonia was treated for suspected sepsis 2 hours ago with the prescribed antimicrobial and intravenous fluids. By the time treatment began the client was restless and confused, blood pressure was 96/58 mm Hg, the respiratory rate was 26 breaths per minute, both feet were cool and mottled, and urine output was 20 mL per hour. Now blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg and the respiratory rate is 22 breaths per minute. The client is still confused, both feet are still cool and mottled, and urine output is still 20 mL per hour. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Continue the current plan and reassess in 15 minutes, because blood pressure and breathing are both better
options.rationale: Two numbers are better, but the nurse judges the whole trend. Mentation, skin, and urine output have not changed.

options.text: Report the better blood pressure and breathing now, and hold the other findings for the next update
options.rationale: A report that leaves out the unchanged findings hides the reason for concern.

options.text: Warm both feet with blankets and recheck the skin before deciding whether the other findings need a call
options.rationale: Warming addresses one finding and delays action on persistent poor perfusion.

options.text: Notify the provider of the current findings now and ask for the plan to be reviewed
options.rationale: Mentation, skin findings, and urine output are considered together with blood pressure and breathing. Persistent signs of poor perfusion require further escalation.

questions.takeaway: Judge the whole trend rather than one number: mentation, blood pressure, skin findings, breathing, and urine output together. Persistent signs of poor perfusion require further escalation.
questions.strategy: A better blood pressure is the most reassuring number there is, and breathing is better too. The deciding cue is that the three findings that show perfusion at the tissues have not moved.

steps.detail: Better: blood pressure, respiratory rate. Unchanged: mentation, skin, urine output.
Mentation, skin color and temperature, urine output.
A recheck in 15 minutes fits a client improving across the board. Two hours after treatment, this client is not.
Persistent poor perfusion: escalate further.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider of the current findings now.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.stem: A client with pneumonia was treated for suspected sepsis 6 hours ago. By the time treatment began the client was restless and confused, the respiratory rate was 26 breaths per minute, both feet were cool and mottled, and urine output was 20 mL per hour. Which set of findings now shows that the client is improving?

options.text: Oral temperature is 37.0 °C, the client is still confused, and urine output is 20 mL per hour
options.rationale: One number in range does not show improvement when mentation and urine output have not changed.

options.text: Client is alert and oriented, respiratory rate is 20 breaths per minute, and urine output is 55 mL per hour
options.rationale: Mental status has moved toward baseline, breathing has slowed from 26 to 20, and urine output has risen from 20 to 55 mL per hour. Every finding given points the same way.

options.text: Client is alert and oriented, respiratory rate is 20 breaths per minute, and both feet are cool and mottled
options.rationale: Mentation and breathing are better, but cool, mottled skin is a sign of poor perfusion. The whole trend has to improve.

options.text: Respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, and the client now responds only when shaken
options.rationale: A slower rate with a drop in responsiveness is not improvement. Mental status has moved away from baseline.

questions.takeaway: Judge the whole trend: mental status toward baseline, blood pressure and perfusion improving, urine output improving, breathing and oxygenation stabilizing.
questions.strategy: Two options start with the same good findings. Read to the end of each: one finishes with a sign of poor perfusion and one with a better urine output.

steps.detail: Confusion, respiratory rate 26, cool mottled feet, urine 20 mL per hour.

steps.action: Check each option to the end
steps.detail: Only one has every finding moving the right way.
A normal temperature, a slower rate, or two good findings with mottled skin is not improvement.

elimination.verdict: Alert and oriented, respiratory rate 20, urine output 55 mL per hour.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.stem: A client had surgery on the right lower leg 4 days ago and has had an indwelling urinary catheter since the operation. The provider's orders include strict intake and output. The unit has no nurse driven protocol for catheter removal. The client now walks to the bathroom with one person assisting and is eating and drinking. During morning care the nurse reviews the client's devices. Which action does the nurse take about the catheter?

options.text: Leave the catheter in place, because the order for strict intake and output requires accurate measurement
options.rationale: The order is for measurement, not for a catheter. A client who walks to the bathroom can have output measured another way.

options.text: Leave the catheter in place, and increase catheter care to twice each shift to lower the risk
options.rationale: Catheter care helps prevent exposure, but it does not answer whether the device is still needed.

options.text: Raise with the provider whether the catheter is still needed, and offer to measure output another way
options.rationale: The nurse reassesses whether urinary catheters are still needed. This client walks and drinks, and the reason given for the catheter can be met without it.

options.text: Remove the catheter this morning, because the nurse decides when a device is no longer needed
options.rationale: Questioning the device is right. Removing it without an order or a protocol goes beyond what the situation supports.

questions.takeaway: Invasive devices bypass natural barriers. Reassess whether urinary catheters and vascular access devices are still needed, and raise it when the reason for the device can be met another way.
questions.strategy: The order for strict intake and output makes keeping the catheter look required. Separate what was ordered, which is measurement, from the device, and then stay within the nurse's role.

steps.detail: Day 4, walks to the bathroom, drinking.

steps.action: Separate the order from the device
steps.detail: Output can be measured without a catheter.

steps.action: Compare the two options that question the device
steps.detail: One raises it with the provider. One removes it without an order.

elimination.verdict: Raise whether the catheter is still needed and offer another way to measure output.

questions.objective: Identify patient factors that increase infection risk

questions.stem: A client had surgery on the right lower leg 5 days ago, and the surgical wound is now draining. The provider orders a wound culture and a first dose of an antimicrobial, both to be done this morning. The antimicrobial is at the bedside and due now, and the culture swab has to be brought from the supply room. The client is alert, with a respiratory rate of 16 breaths per minute and a blood pressure of 124/76 mm Hg, which matches the readings from the past 2 days. In which order does the nurse carry out the orders?

options.text: Obtain the wound culture, then give the first dose of the antimicrobial
options.rationale: The culture identifies the organism and guides treatment. It is collected before the antimicrobial is started.

options.text: Give the first dose of the antimicrobial, then obtain the wound culture
options.rationale: Both actions are right, but the order is reversed. The specimen is collected before the antimicrobial is started.

options.text: Obtain the wound culture and hold the antimicrobial until the result is reported
options.rationale: The culture comes first, but treatment is not held for the result. Treatment of the suspected cause is given as ordered.

options.text: Give the first dose of the antimicrobial and obtain the culture only if the wound does not improve
options.rationale: The culture was ordered to guide treatment from the start. It is not kept in reserve.

questions.takeaway: Culture and susceptibility identifies the organism and guides treatment. Collect the specimen before the antimicrobial is started when that causes no meaningful delay, and do not hold treatment for the result. In probable sepsis the antimicrobial is not delayed for cultures.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The drug is ready and the swab is not, which pulls toward giving the dose first. The client's vital signs match baseline, so there is time to collect the specimen first.

steps.detail: Options that hold or skip an order are out.

steps.action: Compare the two that do both
steps.detail: Culture first, or antimicrobial first.
The specimen is collected before the antimicrobial is started.

elimination.verdict: Culture first, then the antimicrobial.

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.stem: A client has cellulitis of the right leg with a draining wound, and the wound culture is positive for MRSA. A second client, in the next room, has a central venous catheter in the right chest and receives treatment that suppresses the immune system. The nurse cares for both clients today. Which actions interrupt the method of transmission link in the chain of infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Performing hand hygiene after removing gloves in the first client's room
options.rationale: Hands carry organisms from one client to the next. Clean hands break that route, even though the second client is the one who will be touched next.

options.text: Keeping the draining wound on the first client's right leg covered with an intact dressing
options.rationale: This blocks the organism, but at the portal of exit. Organisms leave the reservoir through the wound, and containing the drainage closes that exit.

options.text: Using a blood pressure cuff kept only for the first client's room
options.rationale: Shared equipment carries organisms between clients. Dedicated equipment removes the vehicle.

options.text: Giving the first client the prescribed antimicrobial for the MRSA cellulitis
options.rationale: Treating the infection acts on the agent and reservoir, the organism where it lives in the first client's wound.

options.text: Asking the provider whether the second client's central venous catheter is still needed
options.rationale: A central line gives organisms a direct path into the bloodstream. Removing an unneeded device closes the portal of entry, not the route between clients.

options.text: Offering the second client the recommended vaccines before discharge
options.rationale: Vaccination lowers the second client's risk for the infections the vaccines cover. It acts on the susceptible host.

questions.takeaway: The chain runs agent and reservoir, portal of exit, method of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host. Every infection control action works by breaking one link, and naming the link tells you why the action matters.
questions.strategy: Follow the organism's path from the first client's wound to the second client. Ask where the organism is at the moment each action happens: still in the wound, leaving it, traveling, entering, or meeting a host. Only the actions on the traveling step are transmission.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It lives in the first client's wound: treating it acts on the agent and reservoir.
The draining wound; a covered dressing contains it, which is the portal of exit.
Hands and the cuff both carry organisms between rooms: these are transmission.

steps.action: Find the entry and the host
steps.detail: The central line is the entry. Vaccination changes the host.

elimination.verdict: A, C.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.stem: A client is on day 2 of admission for cellulitis of the right lower leg. The wound culture is positive for MRSA, and the client is receiving the prescribed antimicrobial. At admission the client was alert and oriented, with a heart rate of 84 beats per minute. The 0800 assessment findings are listed below. Which findings does the nurse report promptly? Select all that apply.

options.text: Redness now extends 3 cm beyond the skin marking drawn at admission
options.rationale: The infection is spreading past the border marked at admission while the client receives the antimicrobial. A worsening site is reported.

options.text: Right calf warm and swollen, unchanged since admission
options.rationale: Warmth and swelling are expected with cellulitis, and they match admission.

options.text: Heart rate 108 beats per minute
options.rationale: The heart rate is above the reference range and has risen from 84 at admission, a change in circulation in a client with an infection.

options.text: Small amount of yellow drainage on the dressing, same as yesterday
options.rationale: The drainage has not changed from yesterday.

options.text: Oral temperature 37.1 °C
options.rationale: The reading is within the reference range. It is not a cue by itself, and it does not cancel the other changes, because the nurse does not rely on fever alone.

options.text: Asks the same question three times in 10 minutes
options.rationale: This is a new change in mental status compared with the alert and oriented baseline at admission, a change that matters in a client with an infection.

questions.takeaway: Compare each finding with the client's baseline. A spreading site, a rising heart rate, and new confusion are reported even when the temperature is within range.
questions.strategy: Sort every finding into changed or unchanged since admission. Expected findings of cellulitis that have not changed are not new cues, and a normal temperature does not cancel the findings that have changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Redness past the marking, heart rate 84 to 108, new repeated questions.
Warmth and swelling, and drainage the same as yesterday.

steps.action: Do not lean on the temperature
steps.detail: 37.1 °C neither adds a cue nor removes the others.

elimination.verdict: A, C, F.

questions.objective: Assess for infection and recognize clinical deterioration

questions.stem: A client with cellulitis of the right leg is being discharged with a dressing over a draining wound. The wound culture was positive for MRSA, and the client has a prescription for an oral antibiotic. The client lives with a partner and a 6 year old child. Which statements by the client indicate that the teaching has been effective? Select all that apply.

options.text: "This germ spreads by touch, from the wound or from things the drainage has touched."
options.rationale: MRSA is spread by contact: touching the person, the wound, or contaminated items.

options.text: "Because this germ spreads by touch, my family only needs to clean their hands if they touch the wound itself."
options.rationale: Contact is the right route, but it is too narrow. Items the drainage has touched also spread MRSA, so hands are cleaned after touching those too.

options.text: "I will clean my hands after I touch the dressing, even if I wore gloves."
options.rationale: Hands are cleaned after gloves are removed, because gloves do not replace hand hygiene.

options.text: "When my hands look dirty after a dressing change, hand sanitizer is enough."
options.rationale: Cleaning the hands is right, but the method is wrong. Visibly soiled hands are washed with soap and water.

options.text: "I will take every dose of the antibiotic, even once my leg looks better."
options.rationale: The whole course is completed. Stopping early when the leg looks better leaves organisms behind.

options.text: "I will save any leftover pills in case my child catches a cold this winter."
options.rationale: Antibiotics do not treat viral infections such as a cold, unnecessary use adds to resistance, and leftover pills mean the course was not finished.

questions.takeaway: Teach MRSA as a contact organism: clean hands after touching the wound or dressing and after removing gloves, soap and water when hands are visibly soiled, finish the whole antibiotic course, and never use antibiotics for a viral illness.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two wrong statements have the right idea with one fact off: contact limited to the wound in one, the hand hygiene method in the other. Check the reach of contact, the method, and the antibiotic use in each statement.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Contact includes items the drainage touched, not only the wound.
Visibly dirty hands need soap and water.
Finish the course; a cold is viral.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E.

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client who is 84 years old has chronic kidney disease, receives immunosuppressive treatment, and has a central venous catheter in the right chest and an abdominal surgical incision from 3 months ago that is closed with no redness or drainage. The nurse identifies [[1]] as the factors that increase this client's risk for infection by lowering the body's defenses.

The nurse identifies [[2]] as the factor that bypasses the body's natural barriers.

If this client develops an infection, the nurse expects that [[3]].

options.text: the client's age, the immunosuppressive treatment, and the central venous catheter
options.rationale: Age and the treatment lower immune status, but the catheter does not lower defenses. It bypasses the barriers, and chronic kidney disease is left out.

options.text: the chronic kidney disease, the immunosuppressive treatment, and the abdominal incision
options.rationale: Chronic illness and the treatment lower immune status, but the incision is closed with no redness or drainage, so the skin barrier is intact, and age is left out.

options.text: the client's age, the chronic kidney disease, and the immunosuppressive treatment
options.rationale: Age extremes, chronic illness, and immunosuppressive treatment all lower immune status.

options.text: the abdominal incision
options.rationale: Broken skin gives direct access to pathogens, but this incision is closed with no redness or drainage.

options.text: the central venous catheter
options.rationale: Invasive devices bypass natural barriers and give organisms a direct path into the bloodstream.

options.text: the immunosuppressive treatment
options.rationale: The treatment raises risk by lowering immune status, not by bypassing a barrier.

options.text: a fever will be the first sign, so the temperature is checked every 2 hours
options.rationale: Checking temperature is part of assessment, but fever is not relied on as the first or only sign.

options.text: a fever may not appear, so changes in behavior and function from baseline matter
options.rationale: Immune status shapes the response. The nurse does not rely on fever alone and watches for changes from baseline.

options.text: the white blood cell count will rise before other findings appear
options.rationale: A count is interpreted together with the assessment, and a client with low immune status may not mount the usual rise, so no single lab result is waited on.

questions.takeaway: Immune status drives infection risk: age extremes, chronic illness, and immunosuppressive treatment. Invasive devices and broken skin open a direct path in. In a client with low immune status, do not wait for a fever.
questions.strategy: Sort the client's factors into two groups: those that weaken the defenses and those that open a path past them. A factor belongs in only one group. Then ask what weak defenses do to the signs you expect to see.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Age 84, chronic kidney disease, and the treatment all lower immune status.
The central line bypasses them. The incision is closed with no redness or drainage, so the skin is intact.
Fever may be absent, so compare with baseline. No single lab result replaces the assessment.

elimination.verdict: Age, chronic kidney disease, and the treatment; the central venous catheter; fever may not appear.

questions.objective: Identify patient factors that increase infection risk

questions.stem: A nurse reviews four clients at 1200. Which client's findings fit sepsis rather than infection alone or an inflammatory response alone?

options.text: Acute pancreatitis, no source of infection found: oral temperature 38.4 °C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, alert, urine output 50 mL per hour
options.rationale: Temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate are all outside the reference ranges, which is an inflammatory response. No infection has been found, and sepsis requires infection plus organ dysfunction.

options.text: Urinary tract infection and dementia: oral temperature 38.1 °C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, confused as on admission, urine output 45 mL per hour
options.rationale: Infection with a fever is present, but the confusion matches the admission baseline, and the other findings are within range. No new organ dysfunction is shown.

options.text: Cellulitis of the left leg, redness spread 2 cm since 0800: oral temperature 37.1 °C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, alert, urine output 50 mL per hour
options.rationale: The local infection is worsening, which raises the risk for sepsis, but every finding outside the leg is within range. No organ dysfunction is shown.

options.text: Urinary tract infection: oral temperature 37.0 °C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, confused since 1000 after being alert, urine output 40 mL per hour
options.rationale: Infection plus a new change in mental status is evidence of organ dysfunction. Sepsis can be present without a fever or abnormal vital signs.

questions.takeaway: Sepsis is infection plus organ dysfunction, such as new confusion. An inflammatory response alone does not establish sepsis, and sepsis can occur without abnormal temperature, heart rate, or respiratory rate.
questions.strategy: The client with the most abnormal numbers looks sickest, and the client with dementia also has an infection and confusion. The deciding cue is the word new: only one client's confusion began today after being alert.

steps.detail: Pancreatitis with no infection found shows inflammation, not sepsis.
Mental status, oxygenation, urine output.
One is confused as on admission. One became confused since 1000.
Infection with a fever and fast heart rate meets SIRS but is not sepsis without new organ dysfunction.
Spreading redness alone with every other finding in range is not organ dysfunction.

elimination.verdict: The client with a urinary tract infection and new confusion since 1000.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: A client with a respiratory infection coughs into both hands and then presses the call light. The nurse answers the call and touches the call light without gloves. The nurse later develops the same infection. By which route did the organism reach the nurse?

options.text: Droplet, because the organism left the client in a cough
options.rationale: The organism started in a cough, but the route is named by how it reaches the next person. No droplets reached the nurse's mucous membranes.

options.text: Contact, because the nurse touched an item the client contaminated
options.rationale: The organism reached the nurse on a contaminated item. Touching a person or a contaminated item is the contact route.

options.text: Contact, because the client touched the nurse during the call
options.rationale: Contact is the right route, but the stem describes no touch between the two people. The organism traveled on the call light.

options.text: Airborne, because particles from the cough stayed in the room air
options.rationale: Airborne spread explains illness without touch or close range. Here the nurse touched a contaminated item, which accounts for the spread.

questions.takeaway: Contact spreads by touching a person or a contaminated item, droplet by respiratory droplets reaching nearby mucous membranes, and airborne by particles that stay suspended in the air. Name the route by how the organism reaches the next person, not by where it came from.
questions.strategy: A cough does not make the route droplet. Ask how the organism reached the next person: by touch, by droplets at close range, or by particles still in the air.

steps.detail: The cough is where the organism came from, not how it reached the nurse.
The call light carried the organism from the client's hands to the nurse's hands.
The stem shows touch of an item, not touch between people.

elimination.verdict: B. Contact, because the nurse touched an item the client contaminated.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.stem: A client, 78 years old, is admitted from the emergency department with a cough and suspected pneumonia. The client lives at home with a family member. Oral temperature 37.0 °C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Which actions belong in the nurse's admission infection assessment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask when the cough started and how it has changed since then
options.rationale: Symptoms and their onset are part of the history in an infection assessment.

options.text: Ask whether anyone the client lives or works with has been ill recently
options.rationale: Exposures are part of the history and can point to the source.

options.text: Ask whether any devices are in place, such as a urinary catheter used at home
options.rationale: Devices are part of the history. They bypass natural barriers and can be a source of infection.

options.text: Ask the family member how the client's alertness and activity compare with usual
options.rationale: Findings are compared with the client's baseline. Changes in behavior and function matter, and the family member knows what is usual.

options.text: Obtain a sputum specimen for culture before finishing the history, so the organism is identified quickly
options.rationale: The nurse obtains ordered specimens. No culture has been ordered, and the history is part of the assessment, not a step to cut short.

options.text: Record the oxygen saturation of 93% as expected for a client who is 78 years old
options.rationale: 93% is below the reference range of 95 to 100%. Decreased oxygen saturation is a concerning cue, and age does not make it expected.

questions.takeaway: The infection assessment gathers symptoms, onset, exposures, recent treatment, and devices; assesses overall appearance, the likely site, and respiratory status; and compares every finding with baseline. Do not rely on fever alone.
questions.strategy: The two wrong options each sound like good practice: one rushes to identify the organism, and one explains a low value by age. Ask whether the specimen was ordered and whether the value is inside its reference range.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Onset, exposures, and devices all belong.
Comparing with usual alertness and activity belongs.
No culture was ordered, and the history is not cut short.
93% is below 95 to 100%, whatever the age.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Assess for infection and recognize clinical deterioration

questions.stem: A client has a draining wound on the left foot. The provider ordered a wound culture and susceptibility, a complete blood count with differential, and an intravenous antimicrobial. On day 2, the susceptibility report shows that the organism is resistant to the antimicrobial the client is receiving. The next dose is due in 1 hour. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the next dose on time, because a missed dose lowers the drug level, then report
options.rationale: On time dosing matters, but this drug may not treat the organism. The provider needs the report before the dose so the order can change.

options.text: Hold the next dose and wait for the provider to see the report on rounds
options.rationale: Questioning the dose is right, but holding it without reporting leaves the client with no treatment and no new plan.

options.text: Report the susceptibility result to the provider before the next dose is due
options.rationale: The culture and susceptibility test identifies the organism and guides the drug choice. The nurse supports appropriate antimicrobial use by following culture results, and the provider needs this result to change the treatment.

options.text: Check the complete blood count with differential to decide whether the drug is working
options.rationale: The blood count adds information about the immune response, read together with the assessment. It does not answer which drug the organism responds to.

questions.takeaway: Culture and susceptibility identifies the organism and guides the antimicrobial choice. The complete blood count with differential adds information about the immune response. Read every result together with the assessment, and act on a susceptibility report that does not match the drug being given.
questions.strategy: Match each test to the question it answers: which organism and which drug, or how the body is responding. Then look for the choice that both protects the client from an ineffective drug and gets a new plan.

steps.detail: Susceptibility answers which drug works. The blood count answers how the body is responding.
Giving the dose first and holding it silently both leave the client without an effective plan.

steps.action: Choose the action that changes the plan
steps.detail: Report before the dose is due.

elimination.verdict: C. Report the susceptibility result to the provider before the next dose is due.

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.stem: A client admitted with a urinary tract infection was alert at 0700 and is confused at 0900. Oral temperature 38.6 °C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg. At 0915 the provider examines the client, documents probable sepsis without shock, and orders blood cultures and an intravenous antimicrobial. Facility policy states that laboratory staff draw blood cultures, and they report that they can reach the unit at 1115. The antimicrobial arrives at 0930, and the intravenous access works. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the antimicrobial at 1115 right after the laboratory staff draw the blood cultures
options.rationale: Specimens are obtained before the antimicrobial when that causes no delay, and 1115 is within 3 hours. The 3 hour window is for possible sepsis without shock. Probable sepsis calls for the antimicrobial immediately, ideally within 1 hour, and waiting for cultures until 1115 delays it 2 hours.

options.text: Hold the antimicrobial, recheck vital signs every 30 minutes, and give it if the blood pressure falls
options.rationale: Rechecking vital signs is right, but waiting for a falling blood pressure waits for shock. The provider has documented probable sepsis, which calls for the antimicrobial now.

options.text: Draw blood for culture from the existing intravenous line, then give the antimicrobial now
options.rationale: Getting the specimen first is the right idea, but facility policy assigns blood cultures to laboratory staff, and the existing line is not the way the specimen is obtained.

options.text: Give the antimicrobial now, and have the blood cultures drawn when the laboratory staff arrive
options.rationale: For probable sepsis the antimicrobial is given immediately, ideally within 1 hour. Cultures come first only when drawing them delays the antimicrobial by no more than 45 minutes; here the delay would be 2 hours.

questions.takeaway: Probable or definite sepsis, or septic shock: give the antimicrobial immediately, ideally within 1 hour. Possible sepsis without shock: investigate rapidly and begin treatment within 3 hours if concern persists. Obtain cultures first only when that does not delay the antimicrobial.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: "Without shock" and the culture first habit both point toward waiting until 1115, which is still inside 3 hours. The deciding cue is the provider's word probable: the 3 hour window belongs only to possible sepsis without shock.

steps.detail: The provider documented probable sepsis, not possible sepsis.
Probable sepsis: antimicrobial immediately, ideally within 1 hour.
Cultures first is right only when it causes no delay. A 2 hour wait is a delay.
A falling blood pressure is not required to act.
Policy assigns blood cultures to laboratory staff.

elimination.verdict: Give the antimicrobial now and draw cultures when the laboratory staff arrive.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.stem: A client admitted for a planned replacement of the right hip has a nasal swab screening result that is positive for MRSA. The client has no redness, swelling, or drainage anywhere on the body. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C, and the white blood cell count is 7000 per mm3. Which statement by the nurse to the team is accurate?

options.text: "The client is colonized, so the nose is not a reservoir until an infection develops."
options.rationale: Colonization is correct, but the organism is still present and can still leave the client and reach others. A colonized client is a reservoir.

options.text: "The client is colonized, and the nose can spread MRSA mainly by droplets."
options.rationale: Colonization is correct, but MRSA spreads by contact, on hands and shared equipment, not mainly by droplets.

options.text: "The client has an MRSA infection that has not yet caused a fever."
options.rationale: The nurse does not rely on fever alone, but this client has no signs at any site and a white blood cell count within range. Nothing shows the organism invading and growing.
