options.text: "The client is colonized, and the nose can be a source that hands or equipment carry."
options.rationale: Colonization differs from infection: the organism is present without symptomatic disease. A reservoir is where the agent lives, so hands and shared equipment can carry it to the next client.

questions.takeaway: Colonization means the organism is present without disease. A colonized client is still a reservoir, and an infection that develops during care can come from the client's own organisms or an outside source.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Separate carrying an organism from being infected by it, then follow the organism: where it lives and how it leaves. Three options agree on colonization, so the decision rests on the reservoir and the route.

steps.detail: Positive screen, no signs at any site, white blood cell count in range: colonization. This removes the infection option.
Colonized still means a reservoir, which removes the option that says it is not one.
MRSA travels by contact on hands and equipment, which removes the droplet option.

elimination.verdict: D. The client is colonized, and the nose can be a source that hands or equipment carry.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.stem: A client who had a stroke coughs, and the voice sounds wet, each time thin liquids are swallowed. Which portal of entry does this finding place at risk?

options.text: Respiratory tract, because the swallowed liquid is entering the airway
options.rationale: Coughing and a wet voice with thin liquids mean the liquid is going into the airway. Aspiration leads to respiratory infection such as pneumonia.

options.text: Gastrointestinal tract, because the client is swallowing the liquids
options.rationale: The liquid is swallowed, but the cough and wet voice show it is not staying in the gastrointestinal tract. Ask where the organism actually gets in.

options.text: Damaged mucous membrane, because repeated coughing injures the throat
options.rationale: Damaged mucous membranes in the throat do allow entry, but nothing in the stem shows a damaged membrane. The finding points to the airway.

options.text: Respiratory tract, because the stroke has weakened the immune response
options.rationale: The portal is right, but the reason is not. The stem shows liquid entering the airway, not a change in immunity.

questions.takeaway: Infections enter through the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts, through broken skin or damaged mucous membranes, and through vascular access and other invasive devices that bypass natural barriers.
questions.strategy: Ask where the organism would actually get in, not which body part is named first. A swallow that ends in a cough enters the airway.

steps.detail: A wet cough with thin liquids is aspiration, so respiratory tract.
Swallowing names the gastrointestinal tract, but the liquid is not staying there.
Two options name the respiratory tract; only one gives the reason the stem supports.

elimination.verdict: A. Respiratory tract, because the swallowed liquid is entering the airway.

questions.objective: Identify patient factors that increase infection risk

questions.stem: A client is on day 1 after abdominal surgery, with a wound drain on the right side and no diagnosed infection. The nurse will empty the drain, irrigate the incision as ordered, count the radial pulse at the intact right wrist, and give a subcutaneous injection. Which actions by the nurse follow standard precautions? Select all that apply.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene before touching the client and after care is finished
options.rationale: Hand hygiene before and after client contact is part of standard precautions for every client.

options.text: Wear a gown and gloves to empty the drain, because drainage may splash onto clothing
options.rationale: Equipment is chosen for the exposure expected. Gloves protect from body fluids, and a gown is worn when drainage may reach clothing or skin.

options.text: Wear gloves to count the radial pulse at the intact right wrist
options.rationale: Gloves are right for body fluids and broken skin, but counting a pulse on intact skin carries no expected exposure.

options.text: Place the used needle in the sharps container without recapping it
options.rationale: Sharps are handled safely: needles are not recapped and go into a puncture resistant container.

options.text: Skip eye protection while irrigating the incision, because no infection has been diagnosed
options.rationale: Standard precautions apply whether or not an infection has been diagnosed. Irrigation can splash, so eye protection is worn.

options.text: Clean the hands with alcohol based sanitizer after removing gloves if drainage soiled the hands
options.rationale: Cleaning the hands after removing gloves is right, but visibly soiled hands are washed with soap and water.

questions.takeaway: Standard precautions apply to every client: hand hygiene before and after contact, protective equipment matched to the expected exposure, safe sharps handling, and soap and water when hands are visibly soiled.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: For each task, ask what exposure is expected, not what the client is diagnosed with. More equipment is not safer when no exposure is expected, and a missing diagnosis never lowers the precautions.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Drain: gown and gloves. Irrigation: eye protection. Pulse on intact skin: no gloves needed.
No recapping, into the container.
Soiled hands need soap and water, even after gloves.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission-based precautions

questions.stem: A nurse receives report at 0700 on four clients with infections. Which client does the nurse assess first?

options.text: Urinary tract infection, day 1: heart rate 98 beats per minute and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, were 74 and 14 at 0300; oral temperature 37.0 °C; alert
options.rationale: Every value is still inside its range, but the heart rate rose 24 beats per minute and the respiratory rate rose 6 breaths per minute in 4 hours. A trend away from baseline is the earliest sign of deterioration.

options.text: Pneumonia, day 3: oral temperature 38.3 °C, the same at each check since admission; heart rate 96 beats per minute; alert and oriented as on admission
options.rationale: This is the only fever, but it has not changed since admission, and mental status matches baseline. The nurse does not rank clients by fever alone.

options.text: Cellulitis of the left leg, day 2: heart rate 106 beats per minute, between 104 and 108 at every check since admission; respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute; alert
options.rationale: The heart rate is above range, but it has not moved since admission. Compared with baseline, nothing has changed.

options.text: Infected abdominal wound, day 4: pain 3 of 10, was 6 of 10 at 0300 before a prescribed analgesic; oral temperature 37.4 °C, was 37.6 °C at 0300
options.rationale: Pain and temperature are both moving toward baseline after treatment.

questions.takeaway: Compare every finding with the client's baseline and look at the trend. Values that are moving away from baseline over hours outrank values that are out of range but unchanged.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The fever in the pneumonia client and the heart rate above range in the cellulitis client look most abnormal. The deciding cue is the 0300 values: only one client's findings have moved away from baseline in 4 hours.

steps.action: Mark what is out of range
steps.detail: Fever in the pneumonia client, heart rate in the cellulitis client, a temperature slightly above range in the wound client.
Only the urinary tract infection client has worsened since 0300.
Pain and temperature are both falling.
A worsening trend comes before an abnormal value that has not changed.

elimination.verdict: The client with the urinary tract infection whose heart rate and respiratory rate rose since 0300.

questions.objective: Assess for infection and recognize clinical deterioration

questions.scenario: A nurse cares for two clients in adjacent rooms. One client, 70 years old, has a draining wound on the right leg whose culture grew MRSA. The other client receives immunosuppressive treatment, has a closed abdominal incision with no drainage, and has a central venous catheter in the right chest.
questions.stem: For each nursing action, indicate the link in the chain of infection that the action interrupts.

rows.text: Covering the draining MRSA wound on the right leg with an intact dressing
rows.rationale: This wound holds the organism, so the dressing contains drainage at the point where organisms leave the reservoir. The same action on a clean wound would protect entry instead.

rows.text: Covering the closed abdominal incision of the client on immunosuppressive treatment with a sterile dressing
rows.rationale: This incision holds no known organism. The dressing protects a break in the skin where organisms could get in, so it acts on entry, not exit.

rows.text: Performing hand hygiene before touching the central venous catheter in the right chest
rows.rationale: Hands carry organisms from one person or surface to the next. Clean hands remove the vehicle before it reaches the catheter, so the action works on transmission.

rows.text: Using sterile technique and placing a sterile dressing over the central venous catheter insertion site in the right chest
rows.rationale: The catheter is a direct pathway into the bloodstream. A sterile dressing at the insertion site protects the entry point itself, not what carries organisms to it.

rows.text: Giving the prescribed antimicrobial to the client with the MRSA wound on the right leg
rows.rationale: Treatment acts on the organism where it lives, in the wound of the client who is the reservoir.

rows.text: Offering the client with the MRSA wound, 70 years old, a recommended vaccine before discharge
rows.rationale: This client is the reservoir for MRSA, but the vaccine does nothing to that organism. It lowers this client's risk for the infections the vaccine covers, so it acts on the client as a host.

questions.takeaway: The same action can break different links. A dressing over a wound that holds the organism blocks the exit; over a clean wound it protects the entry. Hand hygiene stops the carrier; a sterile dressing at the insertion site protects the entry. A vaccine always acts on the host, even in a client who is also a reservoir.
questions.strategy: For each row, ask whether the action works on the organism's source, on what carries it, or on the place it would get in. The cue is in the row: does the wound hold the organism, and does the action clean the carrier or protect the entry point?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The MRSA wound holds the organism: portal of exit. The clean incision on an immunosuppressed client: portal of entry.
Hand hygiene cleans the carrier: method of transmission. A sterile dressing at the insertion site protects the entry: portal of entry.

steps.action: Place the antimicrobial and the vaccine
steps.detail: The antimicrobial acts on the agent in its reservoir. The vaccine changes the person's susceptibility: susceptible host.

elimination.verdict: Portal of exit; portal of entry; method of transmission; portal of entry; agent and reservoir; susceptible host.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.stem: A nurse gives a subcutaneous injection and, while placing the uncapped needle in the sharps container at the bedside, sticks the left index finger with it. The client's record lists no known bloodborne infection. Two other clients have oral medications due now. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Finish giving the oral medications that are due now, then report the injury to the supervisor
options.rationale: Reporting is right, but needlestick injuries are reported immediately. Delaying the report for routine medications delays evaluation and follow up care.

options.text: Report the injury to the supervisor, and skip the exposure protocol because no infection is known
options.rationale: Reporting at once is right, but the record lists no known infection, which does not mean no infection. The facility exposure protocol is followed for every needlestick.

options.text: Report the injury to the supervisor now, and follow the facility exposure protocol for evaluation
options.rationale: Needlestick injuries and blood exposures are reported to supervisors immediately, documented at the scene, and followed through the facility exposure protocol for evaluation and follow up care. First aid is washing the site with soap and water; the report follows at once.

options.text: Ask the client to consent to blood testing first, so the report to the supervisor is complete
options.rationale: The nurse does not hold the report while collecting more information. The exposure protocol directs evaluation, and the report comes first.

questions.takeaway: Report a needlestick injury or blood exposure to the supervisor immediately, document it at the scene, and follow the facility exposure protocol whatever the client's known history.
questions.strategy: Two options report at once. The difference is whether the client's record changes the protocol. A record with no known infection never cancels the exposure protocol.

steps.detail: Finishing medications first puts routine work ahead of an exposure.
Waiting for the client's blood test is another delay.

steps.action: Compare the two that report now
steps.detail: No known infection is not the same as no infection, so the protocol still applies.

elimination.verdict: Report the injury to the supervisor now, and follow the facility exposure protocol.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission-based precautions

questions.stem: A client who is 81 years old and has diabetes mellitus is on day 3 of admission for an infected pressure injury over the sacrum. At 0200 the client was alert and oriented, with a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute. At 0600 the client is lethargic, the respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute, the heart rate is 114 beats per minute, the oral temperature is 35.8 °C, the skin is cool and clammy, and sacral pain is 2 of 10, the same as at 0200. Blood cultures drawn on admission showed no growth. The nurse suspects sepsis. Which statements by the nurse about this client are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sepsis can be present even though the admission blood cultures showed no growth
options.rationale: An organism does not need to be found in the bloodstream for sepsis to be present. The diagnosis is clinical, based on signs of organ dysfunction.

options.text: The temperature of 35.8 °C makes sepsis less likely, because sepsis causes a fever
options.rationale: Temperature changes are common early signs, and they include feeling cold and clammy as well as fever. A low temperature with cool, clammy skin is a cue, not reassurance.

options.text: Blood vessels that dilate and leak can lower blood flow and oxygen delivery to the tissues
options.rationale: In sepsis the widespread response makes vessels dilate and become more permeable, so circulation and oxygen delivery to tissues may fall, and organ dysfunction may follow.

options.text: New lethargy, compared with alert and oriented at 0200, can be a sign of organ dysfunction
options.rationale: A sudden change in mental status from baseline is an early cue. New confusion or decreased alertness is evidence of organ dysfunction.

options.text: These findings fit an infection that is still confined to the pressure injury over the sacrum
options.rationale: The wound is the likely source, but new lethargy, a respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute, and cool, clammy skin show a response affecting the whole body.

options.text: The respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute is explained by the sacral pain of 2 of 10
options.rationale: A respiratory rate above 20 breaths per minute is concerning. The pain has not changed since 0200, while the respiratory rate rose from 18 breaths per minute, so pain does not explain it.

questions.takeaway: Sepsis is a clinical diagnosis based on organ dysfunction. It does not need a positive blood culture or a fever, and new changes in mentation and breathing from baseline are early cues.
questions.strategy: Test each statement against the client's own baseline. Anything that waits for a fever or a positive blood culture, or explains a new change with a finding that has not changed, is false.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No growth in the blood does not rule out sepsis: true.
Cold and clammy is a sepsis cue: false.
Dilated, leaky vessels lower tissue perfusion: true.
Lethargy is new: true. Pain is unchanged, so it cannot explain the new respiratory rate: false. A whole body response is not a confined infection: false.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: A client who is 81 years old is on day 3 of admission for an infected pressure injury over the sacrum. At 0200 the client was alert and oriented, with a heart rate of 90 beats per minute, a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, and urine output of 50 mL per hour. At 0600 the client is lethargic, the heart rate is 114 beats per minute, the respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute, urine output is 20 mL per hour, and the oral temperature is 35.8 °C. The nurse activates the rapid response process. Which statement best begins the nurse's report to the team?

options.text: "Infected sacral pressure injury. Heart rate 114 beats per minute, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, temperature 35.8 °C, urine 20 mL per hour. Please assess."
options.rationale: The current values are accurate, but without the 0200 values the team cannot see the change, the new lethargy is left out, and no concern is stated.

options.text: "Infected sacral pressure injury. The client is lethargic with low urine output but has no fever, so I think the infection is likely not spreading beyond the wound."
options.rationale: The findings are right, but the conclusion is wrong. The nurse does not rely on fever alone, and the change from baseline points toward sepsis.

options.text: "The client looks septic and needs antimicrobials and fluids right away. Please come to the room as soon as you can, because this is urgent and cannot wait."
options.rationale: The concern is right, but the statement gives no findings. The team needs the changes that led the nurse to escalate.

options.text: "Infected sacral pressure injury. Since 0200: alert to lethargic, heart rate 90 to 114 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 to 26 breaths per minute. I suspect sepsis."
options.rationale: This names the likely source, gives the change from baseline in mentation and vital signs, and states the concern. Trends from baseline make the deterioration clear.

questions.takeaway: When escalating care, give the likely source, the change from the client's baseline in breathing, mentation, circulation, and urine output, and the concern itself.
questions.strategy: Every option names something true. Pick the one that lets the team see the trend: current values alone hide how far the client has moved from baseline.

steps.detail: No fever does not mean the infection is not spreading.
Urgency without findings gives the team nothing to act on.
Current values alone versus values with their 0200 baseline: the trend shows the deterioration.

elimination.verdict: The report that gives the source, the change since 0200, and the concern for sepsis.

questions.objective: Assess for infection and recognize clinical deterioration

questions.stem: At 0930 a nurse has intravenous antimicrobial doses ready for four clients and can start only one at a time. Each order states to give the dose now. Which client does the nurse give the antimicrobial to first?

options.text: Urinary tract infection: the provider documented possible sepsis without shock at 0900; blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg, heart rate 108 beats per minute; alert
options.rationale: This client was documented first and has the lower blood pressure, but possible sepsis without shock calls for rapid investigation and treatment within 3 hours if concern persists. That window allows this dose to follow the client who needs it within 1 hour.

options.text: Pneumonia: the provider documented infection without signs of sepsis at 0850; oral temperature 38.9 °C, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute; alert
options.rationale: This is the highest temperature, but the provider found no sepsis. The nurse does not rank clients by fever alone.

options.text: Cellulitis of the right leg: the provider documented probable sepsis at 0920; blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg, heart rate 102 beats per minute; alert
options.rationale: For probable or definite sepsis, the antimicrobial is given immediately, ideally within 1 hour. The provider's category, not the blood pressure, sets the time limit, so this client is first.

options.text: Infected left foot wound: day 3 of treatment, dose due at 0930; oral temperature 37.4 °C, heart rate 88 beats per minute; alert
options.rationale: A dose on time matters, but this client shows no sepsis and is on day 3 of treatment. It can follow the clients who have a sepsis time limit.

questions.takeaway: The Hour 1 bundle sets the time limit by category: septic shock or probable or definite sepsis gets the antimicrobial immediately, ideally within 1 hour; possible sepsis without shock is investigated rapidly and treated within 3 hours if concern persists.
questions.strategy: The urinary tract infection client looks sicker and was documented first. The deciding cue is the provider's category: possible sepsis without shock versus probable sepsis, which carries the shorter time limit.

steps.detail: Pneumonia without sepsis and the day 3 foot wound have no sepsis time limit.
One has possible sepsis without shock, the other probable sepsis.
Probable sepsis: within 1 hour. Possible sepsis without shock: within 3 hours if concern persists. A lower blood pressure that is not shock does not change the category.

elimination.verdict: The client with cellulitis and probable sepsis documented at 0920.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.stem: A client, 79 years old, is admitted for dehydration. The lips are dry and cracked, there is a skin tear on the left forearm, and an indwelling urinary catheter was placed in the emergency department. The record shows none of the recommended vaccines. Which nursing actions use the body's defenses or prevent exposure to lower this client's infection risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Giving mouth care and moistening the lips so the oral mucous membranes stay intact
options.rationale: Intact skin and mucous membranes form barriers. Cracked lips and a dry mouth are breaks in that barrier, and mouth care helps restore it.

options.text: Covering the skin tear on the left forearm and protecting the skin from further tears
options.rationale: Broken skin gives organisms direct access. Covering the tear and preventing new ones protects the skin barrier.

options.text: Performing hand hygiene before and after handling the urinary catheter or drainage bag
options.rationale: Hand hygiene and care of invasive devices help prevent exposure. The catheter bypasses natural barriers, so clean hands at every contact matter.

options.text: Offering the recommended vaccines before discharge, following facility protocol
options.rationale: Vaccination reduces risk for the infections covered by recommended vaccines. It strengthens the host's own defenses.

options.text: Asking the provider for an antibiotic now so that an infection does not develop
options.rationale: No infection has been identified. Antibiotics given without an indication do not strengthen defenses, and unnecessary use contributes to resistance.

options.text: Using alcohol based sanitizer on hands that are visibly soiled with the client's stool
options.rationale: Hand hygiene is right, but hands that are visibly soiled need soap and water. Alcohol based sanitizer is preferred only when hands are not visibly soiled.

questions.takeaway: The body defends itself with intact skin and mucous membranes and with inflammation and immune responses. Nurses support those defenses, offer recommended vaccines, and prevent exposure with hand hygiene and device care.
questions.strategy: For each action, ask whether it protects a barrier, strengthens the host, or blocks exposure. An action that only looks protective, or uses the wrong hand hygiene method, is false.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cracked lips and a skin tear are broken barriers: mouth care and covering the tear are true.
Hand hygiene around the catheter prevents exposure: true.
Recommended vaccines lower risk: true.
An antibiotic with no infection is not prevention; visibly soiled hands need soap and water: false, false.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.stem: A nurse receives report on four clients. Which client does the nurse identify as having the highest risk for developing sepsis?

options.text: Age 84 years, cellulitis of the left leg on day 3 of antimicrobials, redness now inside the border marked on admission, no invasive devices
options.rationale: Older age is a risk factor, but this infection is shrinking on treatment and there are no devices. A worsening infection, not an older age alone, is the stronger warning.

options.text: Age 61 years, on chemotherapy for cancer, a central venous port in the right chest, urinary tract infection with new flank pain since 0800
options.rationale: This client combines reduced immune function, an invasive device, chronic illness, and an infection that is getting worse. Each is a listed risk factor for sepsis, and together they make this client the highest risk.

options.text: Age 35 years, nasal swab positive for MRSA, admitted for an elective procedure, no signs of infection and no invasive devices
options.rationale: A resistant organism sounds dangerous, but this is colonization, not infection. Sepsis is a response to an infection, and none is present.

options.text: Age 52 years, type 2 diabetes mellitus, a small blister on the right heel with no redness, warmth, or drainage, no invasive devices
options.rationale: Chronic illness is a risk factor, but the blister shows no sign of infection, and sepsis needs an infection to start.

questions.takeaway: Risk factors for sepsis: older adults, reduced immune function, chronic illness or serious wounds, invasive devices or recent procedures, and anyone whose infection is worsening. Risk rises as factors add up on top of an active infection.
questions.strategy: Sepsis starts with an infection. Remove the clients who have none, then compare an improving infection with a worsening one in a client with several risk factors.

steps.detail: MRSA colonization and an uninfected blister cannot lead to sepsis yet.
Cellulitis is shrinking on treatment; the urinary tract infection is worsening.
Chemotherapy, cancer, and a central port add reduced immunity, chronic illness, and a device.

elimination.verdict: The client receiving chemotherapy with a central venous port and a worsening urinary tract infection.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.scenario: A client, 76 years old, is on day 2 after surgery on the right hip. At 0700 the client was alert and oriented, heart rate 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, urine output 50 mL per hour. At 1100 the client is confused, heart rate 116 beats per minute, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, blood pressure 98/58 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 93% on room air, oral temperature 38.6 °C, and urine output 20 mL per hour. The hip incision is red with cloudy drainage. The client has an indwelling urinary catheter and a peripheral intravenous catheter in the left forearm. The nurse has activated the rapid response process, and the provider has ordered blood cultures and a serum lactate.
questions.stem: For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated for this client now.

rows.text: Trend vital signs, oxygen saturation, mental status, and hourly urine output against the 0700 values
rows.rationale: Sepsis assessment trends vital signs, oxygenation, mental status, and urine output. The 0700 values are the baseline that shows how far the client has moved.

rows.text: Inspect the hip incision, the urinary catheter, and the intravenous site for a likely source of infection
rows.rationale: The nurse assesses for a likely infection source. The cloudy drainage is a strong lead, but the catheter and the intravenous site are also possible sources.

rows.text: Prepare for the ordered blood cultures and serum lactate, and check that the intravenous access works
rows.rationale: The nurse anticipates ordered cultures and lactate testing, obtains ordered specimens, and assesses intravenous access so treatment is not delayed.

rows.text: Hold further assessments until the lactate result shows whether the client has sepsis
rows.rationale: Clinical assessment remains essential alongside diagnostic information. No single test confirms sepsis, and the findings are already changing.

rows.text: Treat a single lactate result that is not elevated as ruling out sepsis
rows.rationale: No single test confirms or rules out sepsis, and a lactate result is interpreted with the assessment, not instead of it. New confusion, a respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute, and low urine output remain signs of organ dysfunction.

rows.text: Wait for organisms to grow in the blood cultures before treating the condition as sepsis
rows.rationale: An organism does not need to be found in the bloodstream for sepsis to be present. The diagnosis is clinical, based on signs of organ dysfunction.

questions.takeaway: In suspected sepsis, trend vital signs, oxygenation, mental status, and urine output; look for the source; anticipate cultures and lactate. Tests support the clinical assessment and never replace it.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each action by whether it keeps the clinical assessment going or waits on a test result. Waiting on a lactate or a culture is the trap.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Trending against 0700 and searching for the source are indicated.
Ordered cultures, lactate, and working intravenous access are indicated.
Holding assessment for a lactate, trusting one lactate value, or waiting for culture growth are not indicated.

elimination.verdict: Indicated: trend against 0700, find the source, prepare for cultures and lactate. Not indicated: holding assessment, trusting one lactate value, waiting for culture growth.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

chapters.title: Acute Coronary Syndromes: Coronary Artery Disease

questions.stem: A client, 57 years old, with hypertension and dyslipidemia asks how these conditions can lead to coronary artery disease. The nurse explains that hypertension and dyslipidemia injure the endothelium of the coronary artery, and that low density lipoprotein then enters the artery wall and is oxidized. Which event does the nurse describe next?

options.text: Macrophages are drawn into the wall and a fatty streak forms
options.rationale: Oxidized LDL attracts macrophages. They fill with lipid and form the fatty streak, the first visible lesion.

options.text: The fatty streak develops into a fibrous plaque in the wall
options.rationale: This is the right process one step too late. The fatty streak must form before it can mature into a fibrous plaque.

options.text: The narrowed coronary artery restricts blood flow to the heart
options.rationale: Narrowing comes after the plaque has formed and takes up room in the lumen.

options.text: Reduced oxygen delivery to the heart muscle causes ischemia
options.rationale: Ischemia is the end of the chain, after the artery has narrowed and flow is restricted.

questions.takeaway: Atherosclerosis becomes coronary artery disease in four steps: endothelial injury, plaque formation (LDL enters and is oxidized, macrophages form a fatty streak, then a fibrous plaque), narrowing of the coronary artery, and ischemia from reduced oxygen delivery.
questions.strategy: Build the plaque in the order it grows. Nothing can mature into a fibrous plaque until a fatty streak exists, and nothing narrows the artery until the plaque is there.

steps.detail: Endothelial injury, then LDL enters and is oxidized.
Fatty streak comes before fibrous plaque.
Narrowing and ischemia come after the plaque is formed.

elimination.verdict: A. Macrophages are drawn into the wall and a fatty streak forms.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.nursesNote: Client, 59 years old, seen for a wellness visit. Parent died of a myocardial infarction at 62 years old. Has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes per day for 30 years. Blood pressure 148/94 mm Hg. LDL cholesterol 172 mg/dL. Works at a desk and does not exercise. Body mass index 23 kg/m2. Fasting blood glucose 118 mg/dL. Eats fried food or fast food 5 days each week.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that are modifiable risk factors for coronary artery disease.

segments.text: Client, 59 years old
segments.rationale: Increasing age is a risk factor, but it is nonmodifiable. The client cannot change it.

segments.text: Parent died of a myocardial infarction at 62 years old
segments.rationale: Family history is a nonmodifiable risk factor. It raises risk but cannot be changed.

segments.text: Has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes per day for 30 years
segments.rationale: Cigarette smoking is a modifiable risk factor. It injures the endothelium, and the client can stop.

segments.text: Blood pressure 148/94 mm Hg
segments.rationale: 148/94 mm Hg is above the normal range of below 120/80 mm Hg. Hypertension is modifiable with lifestyle change and medication.

segments.text: LDL cholesterol 172 mg/dL
segments.rationale: 172 mg/dL is above the reference of below 100 mg/dL. Dyslipidemia is a modifiable risk factor.

segments.text: Works at a desk and does not exercise
segments.rationale: A sedentary lifestyle is a modifiable risk factor.

segments.text: Fasting blood glucose 118 mg/dL
segments.rationale: 118 mg/dL is above the reference of 70 to 99 mg/dL, which points to insulin resistance. Diabetes and insulin resistance are modifiable risk factors.

segments.text: Eats fried food or fast food 5 days each week
segments.rationale: An atherogenic diet, high in fat, is a modifiable risk factor.

segments.text: Body mass index 23 kg/m2
segments.rationale: A body mass index of 23 kg/m2 is inside the reference range of 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m2, so obesity is not present.

questions.takeaway: Modifiable risk factors for coronary artery disease are dyslipidemia, hypertension, cigarette smoking, diabetes and insulin resistance, obesity and a sedentary lifestyle, and an atherogenic diet. Age and family history raise risk but cannot be changed.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions of each finding: does it raise risk, and can the client change it? Age and family history pass the first test and fail the second. A value inside its range fails the first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Age 59 and a parent's myocardial infarction cannot be changed.

steps.action: Check each value against its range
steps.detail: Blood pressure, LDL, and glucose are above range. Body mass index 23 kg/m2 is inside 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m2.
Smoking, no exercise, and frequent fried or fast food are all changeable.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client, 52 years old, has blood pressure readings of 164/98 mm Hg and 160/96 mm Hg at two clinic visits. LDL cholesterol is 92 mg/dL, and the client has never smoked. The client asks, "My cholesterol is in range, so how could my blood pressure put plaque in my heart arteries?" Which response by the nurse answers the client's question?

options.text: "High pressure makes your heart work harder and need more oxygen, so plaque in your heart arteries starts to cause chest pressure."
options.rationale: This is true about hypertension and the heart, but it explains why existing plaque causes symptoms. The client asked how plaque forms.

options.text: "High pressure thickens the heart muscle until it presses on the coronary arteries and narrows them from the outside."
options.rationale: Hypertension can thicken the left ventricle, but plaque narrows a coronary artery from inside the wall, not by outside pressure.

options.text: "High pressure makes the artery walls thicken and stiffen over time, and that thickened wall is the plaque."
options.rationale: Hypertension does thicken arteriole walls (medial hyperplasia), but plaque is a buildup of lipid laden macrophages inside the wall that starts with endothelial injury, not the thickened muscle layer.

options.text: "High pressure damages the inner lining of your heart arteries, which lets cholesterol get into the wall and start plaque."
options.rationale: Endothelial injury from hypertension is the first step of atherosclerosis. Once the lining is injured, LDL enters the wall, is oxidized, and starts plaque.

questions.takeaway: Hypertension contributes to coronary artery disease two ways: it injures the endothelium, which starts plaque formation, and it raises myocardial oxygen demand. The question asked decides which one is the answer.
questions.strategy: Two options are true about hypertension and the heart. The deciding cue is the client's exact question: how pressure puts plaque in the arteries. Only the endothelial injury answer explains plaque.

steps.action: Read the question the client asked
steps.detail: The client asks how blood pressure causes plaque, not why chest pain happens.

steps.action: Set aside the true but off target option
steps.detail: Higher oxygen demand explains angina, not plaque formation.
Plaque grows inside the wall.
Medial thickening from hypertension is not plaque. Plaque starts with injury to the lining.
Endothelial injury lets LDL into the wall.

elimination.verdict: Hypertension injures the lining, which lets LDL enter the wall and start plaque.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: A client with coronary artery disease reports chest pressure that starts after walking uphill for about 5 minutes and goes away within 3 minutes of sitting down. Blood pressure 134/82 mm Hg, heart rate 78 beats per minute. The client asks why the pressure comes and goes. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: A plaque narrows the artery so that flow meets the heart's needs at rest but falls short during exertion
options.rationale: The narrowed artery restricts flow. At rest the supply is enough. Walking uphill raises demand, oxygen delivery falls short, and ischemia causes the pressure until rest lowers demand again.

options.text: A clot fully blocks the artery while the client walks and then dissolves each time the client sits down
options.rationale: Plaque rupture with a clot causes an acute coronary syndrome. A clot does not form and dissolve on a predictable schedule with each walk.

options.text: Walking sends blood to the leg muscles and away from the heart, and sitting returns the flow to the heart
options.rationale: Exertion raises the heart's own demand; it does not divert coronary flow to the legs. The pressure comes from a narrowed artery that cannot raise supply to match.

options.text: A spasm of the coronary artery closes it during walking, and the spasm relaxes once the client sits down
options.rationale: Vasospastic angina usually occurs at rest or in the early morning, not on a predictable exertion schedule. A fixed narrowing that cannot meet higher demand fits this pattern.

questions.takeaway: A fixed narrowing restricts coronary flow. When exertion raises oxygen demand beyond what the narrowed artery can supply, the muscle becomes ischemic, and rest ends the shortfall. That is the predictable pattern of chronic angina.
questions.strategy: Every option offers a mechanism for pressure that comes and goes. Choose the one that fits a predictable trigger and relief with rest: a fixed narrowing that cannot raise supply when demand rises.

steps.detail: Pressure with uphill walking that ends within 3 minutes of sitting.

steps.action: Match it to supply and demand
steps.detail: Narrowing limits supply, exertion raises demand, rest lowers it.
Exertion raises the heart's own demand; it does not divert coronary flow to the legs.
A clot is the acute event, not a predictable pattern.
Spasm angina comes at rest, not predictably with exertion.

elimination.verdict: Narrowed artery: supply meets demand at rest but not during exertion.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: A client has had chronic angina for 2 years. The chest pressure has always started after climbing two flights of stairs and ended within 3 minutes of rest. Over the past 2 weeks, the same pressure starts after walking from the bedroom to the kitchen, and it still ends within 3 minutes of rest. No pressure now. Blood pressure 128/78 mm Hg, heart rate 82 beats per minute. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Reinforce the plan to rest at the first sign of pressure, because rest still ends it within 3 minutes
options.rationale: Relief with rest fits chronic angina, and teaching rest is reasonable. But the pressure now starts with far less exertion. That is a worsening pattern, and reinforcing the old plan leaves it unevaluated.

options.text: Teach the client to take sublingual nitroglycerin before walking to the kitchen to prevent the pressure
options.rationale: Taking nitroglycerin before a known trigger is reasonable teaching for a predictable pattern. This pattern is no longer predictable: the threshold has dropped from two flights of stairs to a short walk, and that change needs evaluation, not prevention.

options.text: Report the change in the pattern to the provider today for urgent evaluation
options.rationale: Angina that is new, worsening, or at rest is unstable and needs urgent evaluation. Pressure that once needed two flights of stairs and now comes with walking to the kitchen is worsening.

options.text: Document the episodes and review the pattern again at the routine clinic visit in 3 months
options.rationale: Documenting is part of care, but waiting 3 months delays evaluation of angina that is getting worse.

questions.takeaway: Chronic angina is predictable: the same trigger, the same relief. A change in the pattern, such as pressure that now starts with less exertion, means unstable angina and urgent evaluation, even when rest still relieves it.
questions.strategy: Relief with rest makes the old plan look right. The deciding cue is the trigger: two flights of stairs before, a walk to the kitchen now. A lower threshold is a worsening pattern.

steps.action: Compare the trigger then and now
steps.detail: Two flights of stairs, now bedroom to kitchen.
Worsening angina is unstable, even with relief by rest.
Reinforcing rest and waiting 3 months both leave the change unevaluated.

steps.action: Reject prevention of the old pattern
steps.detail: Nitroglycerin before exertion treats a predictable pattern. The pattern has changed.

elimination.verdict: Report the worsening pattern for urgent evaluation.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client, 74 years old, with coronary artery disease and type 2 diabetes mellitus calls the clinic to describe symptoms from the past week. Which reports may be manifestations of myocardial ischemia? Select all that apply.

options.text: An ache in the jaw that starts while raking leaves and stops with rest
options.rationale: Angina may radiate to the jaw. Onset with exertion and relief with rest fit ischemia.

options.text: Unusual fatigue and weakness while making the bed
options.rationale: Fatigue and weakness can accompany ischemia, and some clients have atypical symptoms rather than chest pain.

options.text: Shortness of breath and sweating while carrying groceries up the stairs
options.rationale: Dyspnea and diaphoresis can occur with ischemia, and they came on with exertion.

options.text: Cramping in the right calf after walking one block that stops when standing still
options.rationale: The exertion and rest pattern looks like angina, but the discomfort is in the right calf. Angina radiates to the jaw, neck, shoulder, arm, or back, not the leg.

options.text: Pressure across the upper back that comes on with exertion
options.rationale: Angina may radiate to the back, and pressure is a common description.

options.text: Pain in the left shoulder that began after lifting a heavy box and worsens when the arm moves
options.rationale: The shoulder is a site angina can reach, but this pain began with a lift and changes with arm movement, which points to the muscle or joint rather than the heart.

questions.takeaway: Angina is pressure, heaviness, squeezing, or pain that may radiate to the jaw, neck, shoulder, arm, or back, and it may come with dyspnea, diaphoresis, pallor, fatigue, or weakness. Some clients have atypical or silent ischemia, so ask about associated symptoms, not only chest pain.
questions.strategy: Two wrong options borrow one feature of angina: the exertion and rest pattern, or the shoulder location. Check every report for both a site angina reaches and a pattern ischemia follows.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Jaw, back, and shoulder are sites angina reaches. The calf is not.
Fatigue, weakness, dyspnea, and diaphoresis can all accompany ischemia.
Shoulder pain that started with a lift and changes with arm movement points to a muscle or joint.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client with chronic angina for 3 years, whose chest pressure has always come only with exertion, arrives at the emergency department with chest pressure that began 30 minutes ago while sitting at a desk. Pain 6 of 10. Blood pressure 150/90 mm Hg, heart rate 102 beats per minute. Which process best explains the change in the client's chest pressure?

options.text: The plaque has slowly grown, so flow now falls short only when exertion raises the heart's demand
options.rationale: Slow growth of a fixed plaque explains angina with exertion. This pressure began at rest, so exertion is not the trigger.

options.text: A plaque has likely ruptured and a clot has formed, cutting flow to the heart muscle even at rest
options.rationale: Plaque rupture with thrombosis turns chronic narrowing into an acute coronary syndrome. Pressure that starts at rest in a client whose pressure came only with exertion fits that change.

options.text: New LDL entered the artery wall today and formed a fatty streak that is now blocking the artery
options.rationale: A fatty streak is an early lesion that develops over time. It does not form in a day or block an artery.

options.text: The blood pressure of 150/90 mm Hg raised demand above what the narrowed artery can supply
options.rationale: Higher pressure does raise demand, but the client is sitting at a desk. A sudden change to pressure at rest points to rupture and a clot, not this blood pressure.

questions.takeaway: Plaque rupture and thrombosis are what turn chronic coronary artery disease into an acute coronary syndrome or acute myocardial infarction. Angina that changes to occurring at rest is the cue.
questions.strategy: Ask what changed. Angina with exertion is a narrowing problem. Pressure at rest in a client whose angina came only with exertion means something new happened in the artery: rupture and a clot.

steps.detail: Pressure has always come with exertion. Now it began at rest.
Gradual growth and a new fatty streak do not cause sudden pressure at rest.
150/90 mm Hg at a desk does not explain the abrupt change.
Rupture and a clot cut flow at rest.

elimination.verdict: Plaque rupture with a clot.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.scenario: A client with coronary artery disease diagnosed 6 months ago arrives at the emergency department. Chest pressure began 40 minutes ago while lying on the sofa. Pain 7 of 10, radiating to the left arm, with diaphoresis and shortness of breath. Blood pressure 156/92 mm Hg, heart rate 106 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Lungs are clear in both bases, and there is no edema in either ankle.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Draw blood for a troponin level as prescribed
options.rationale: Troponin T and I are the preferred biomarkers for acute myocardial infarction.

options.text: Obtain a chest X ray to look for pulmonary congestion
options.rationale: A chest X ray is a CAD diagnostic, but the lungs are clear in both bases, so it does not answer the question this presentation raises.

options.text: Teach a low sodium diet before discharge
options.rationale: Diet teaching is part of risk reduction, but it does not address pressure at rest happening now.

options.text: Obtain a 12 lead ECG
options.rationale: The 12 lead ECG is a core diagnostic test for coronary artery disease and acute coronary syndrome.

options.text: Draw a B type natriuretic peptide level to assess for heart failure
options.rationale: BNP points to ventricular stretch and fluid overload. Clear lungs and no edema do not suggest heart failure; ischemia is the problem.

options.text: Left sided heart failure
options.rationale: Left sided failure causes pulmonary congestion with crackles. The lungs are clear in both bases.

options.text: Acute coronary syndrome
options.rationale: Pressure at rest, 7 of 10, with diaphoresis and dyspnea in a client with known coronary artery disease fits an acute coronary syndrome.

options.text: Chronic angina with a predictable pattern
options.rationale: Predictable angina comes with exertion and ends with rest. This pressure began while lying on the sofa.

options.text: Hypertensive crisis
options.rationale: Hypertensive crisis is a blood pressure of 180/120 mm Hg or higher. This reading is 156/92 mm Hg.

options.text: Orthostatic blood pressure
options.rationale: Orthostatic checks are a hypertension and medication assessment. Standing a client with active ischemia raises demand and is not the priority.

options.text: Capillary blood glucose
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario points to a glucose problem; pain and rhythm show whether ischemia continues.

options.text: Heart rhythm on the cardiac monitor
options.rationale: Ischemic muscle is irritable, and a heart rate of 106 beats per minute is already above range.

options.text: Daily weight
options.rationale: Daily weight tracks fluid in heart failure. Lungs are clear and there is no edema.

options.text: Chest pain intensity
options.rationale: Pain intensity shows whether ischemia is continuing or easing with treatment.

questions.takeaway: Chest pressure at rest with diaphoresis and dyspnea in a client with coronary artery disease is an acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise. Obtain a 12 lead ECG and a troponin, and watch pain intensity and heart rhythm.
questions.strategy: Rule out each condition with one stem fact: the pressure began at rest, the pressure is below 180/120 mm Hg, and the lungs are clear. Then choose the actions that diagnose the problem now and the parameters that show whether ischemia is continuing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pressure at rest with diaphoresis and dyspnea: acute coronary syndrome.
Not predictable angina, not 180/120 mm Hg or higher, lungs clear.
12 lead ECG and troponin.
Lungs clear, no edema.
Pain intensity and heart rhythm.

elimination.verdict: Actions: 12 lead ECG and troponin. Condition: acute coronary syndrome. Parameters: pain intensity and heart rhythm.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A nurse in the emergency department reviews the chest symptoms and test results of six clients with coronary artery disease. Which findings are consistent with an acute coronary syndrome rather than chronic angina with a predictable pattern? Select all that apply.

options.text: Chest heaviness when climbing two flights of stairs that ends after 3 minutes of rest, unchanged for 8 months
options.rationale: A predictable trigger and relief with rest, unchanged for months, is chronic angina.

options.text: Chest pressure that began while lying in bed reading
options.rationale: Angina at rest is unstable and needs urgent evaluation.

options.text: Jaw ache during yard work that ends with sitting down, in a pattern present for 1 year
options.rationale: Radiation to the jaw can occur with any angina. The trigger, relief, and 1 year pattern make this predictable.

options.text: A first episode of chest squeezing, which started yesterday
options.rationale: New angina is unstable. There is no established pattern to call predictable.

options.text: Chest pressure with a troponin I of 0.4 ng/mL
options.rationale: Troponin is the preferred biomarker for acute myocardial infarction. A value above range with chest pressure points to infarction.

options.text: Pressure with brisk walking that ends after a nitrate, in a pattern unchanged over the past year
options.rationale: Predictable angina is relieved by rest or nitrates.

questions.takeaway: Chronic angina is predictable with exertion or stress and relieved by rest or nitrates. Angina that is new, worsening, or at rest is unstable, and troponin above range points to myocardial infarction; both are acute coronary syndromes.
questions.strategy: Ignore how dramatic a symptom sounds. Jaw ache can be part of a predictable pattern. Sort each finding by trigger, relief, and whether the pattern is new or changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Look for rest or new onset
steps.detail: Pressure in bed and a first episode are unstable.
Troponin I above 0.03 ng/mL points to infarction.

steps.action: Look for the same trigger and relief over time
steps.detail: Stairs, yard work, and brisk walking with relief by rest or a nitrate are predictable.
Jaw ache does not by itself make angina unstable.

elimination.verdict: B, D, E.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client arrives at the emergency department with chest pressure that began 45 minutes ago while watching television. Pain 5 of 10. The 12 lead ECG shows no ST elevation. The first troponin I is 0.01 ng/mL. The provider prescribes continuous cardiac monitoring and repeat troponin levels. The client says, "My heart tracing and blood test are normal, so can I go home now?" Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "These results point to unstable angina rather than a heart attack, so the repeat levels are a routine precaution."
options.rationale: Unstable angina does not raise troponin, so this sounds reasonable. But the pressure began only 45 minutes ago, too early for troponin to separate unstable angina from an infarction without ST elevation. The repeat levels are not a formality.

options.text: "Troponin can take hours to rise after heart muscle is damaged, so the repeat levels come first."
options.rationale: In infarction without ST elevation, troponin may be normal at first and rise over 3 to 12 hours. The pressure began 45 minutes ago, so the first value is too early to rule out infarction.

options.text: "You will need a treadmill stress test first, and if it shows no changes, you can go home later today."
options.rationale: A stress test is part of the workup, but it is done after the acute stage. Exercise now would raise demand while pressure from 45 minutes ago may still be an acute event.

options.text: "Your tracing shows no ST elevation, so this is not a heart attack, and the repeat test checks for other causes."
options.rationale: Infarction can occur without ST elevation, and in that case troponin rises over 3 to 12 hours.

questions.takeaway: Troponin T and I are the preferred markers for acute myocardial infarction, but they are drawn as a series. In infarction without ST elevation the first value may be normal and rise over 3 to 12 hours, so an early normal result does not rule out infarction.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The stress test sounds like the logical next diagnostic step. The deciding cue is time: pressure began only 45 minutes ago, too early for troponin to have risen, and stress testing waits until after the acute stage.

steps.detail: The pressure began 45 minutes ago.
Troponin may rise over 3 to 12 hours, so one early normal value does not rule out infarction.
It comes after the acute stage, not during pressure at rest.
45 minutes is too early to call unstable angina or rule out infarction.

elimination.verdict: Explain that troponin can take hours to rise, so the repeat levels are needed.

questions.stem: A client in the emergency department with chest pressure 7 of 10 has a prescription for sublingual nitroglycerin. Blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg, heart rate 98 beats per minute, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Which finding requires the nurse to clarify the prescription before giving the dose?

options.text: A blood pressure of 138/84 mm Hg, which is above the normal range
options.rationale: Checking blood pressure before a nitrate is right, but a reading of 138/84 mm Hg is well above the level at which nitroglycerin is withheld.

options.text: The client chewed aspirin 325 mg at home 30 minutes before arrival
options.rationale: Chewed aspirin is part of emergency care for new chest pressure. It does not interact dangerously with nitroglycerin.

options.text: The client took tadalafil for erectile dysfunction 14 hours ago
options.rationale: Nitroglycerin within 24 to 48 hours of a phosphodiesterase inhibitor such as tadalafil can cause profound hypotension. 14 hours is inside that window.

options.text: The client reports a mild headache that began this morning
options.rationale: A mild headache is not a reason to withhold nitroglycerin. Headache is a common nitrate effect, so the nurse expects it may worsen after the dose, but it does not make the dose unsafe.

questions.takeaway: Before giving nitroglycerin, ask about sildenafil, tadalafil, avanafil, or vardenafil in the past 24 to 48 hours. Together they can cause profound hypotension. Recheck pain and vital signs 5 minutes after each dose.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Three findings are expected in chest pressure or its treatment. The one that makes the drug dangerous is an interaction, not a vital sign that is above range.

steps.detail: A reading of 138/84 mm Hg is well above the level at which nitroglycerin is withheld.
Chewed aspirin belongs in chest pain care.
A mild headache does not contraindicate nitroglycerin.
Tadalafil 14 hours ago is within 24 to 48 hours.

elimination.verdict: Tadalafil taken 14 hours ago.

questions.stem: A client with coronary artery disease is due for oral metoprolol at 0900. At 0845, heart rate is 64 beats per minute and blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg. The client reports no chest pain, and the lungs are clear in both bases. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the dose, because both values are within their reference ranges
options.rationale: Both values sit inside the stated ranges, but a beta blocker is held for a systolic pressure below 100 mm Hg. 88 mm Hg is below that hold point.

options.text: Give the dose and recheck the blood pressure in 1 hour
options.rationale: The dose would lower an already low systolic pressure before the recheck.

options.text: Give half of the dose to limit the drop in blood pressure
options.rationale: Changing a prescribed dose is outside the nurse's scope, and any dose would lower the pressure further.

options.text: Hold the dose and report the blood pressure to the provider
options.rationale: Beta blockers lower heart rate and cardiac output. A systolic pressure below 100 mm Hg is a hold point even when the heart rate is acceptable.

questions.takeaway: Assess heart rate and blood pressure before every beta blocker dose. Hold and contact the provider for a pulse below 50 beats per minute or a systolic pressure below 100 mm Hg; either one alone is enough, and a value inside a general reference range can still be below a drug hold point.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Both values sit inside their stated reference ranges, which makes giving the dose look acceptable. The drug has its own hold point: a systolic pressure of 88 mm Hg is below 100 mm Hg, and that alone is reason to hold.

steps.detail: Heart rate 64 beats per minute is above the hold point. Systolic 88 mm Hg is below 100 mm Hg.
Either value below its hold point means hold.
The dose would lower the pressure further before the recheck.
The nurse does not change a prescribed dose.

elimination.verdict: Hold the dose and report the blood pressure.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: The plan of care for a client with coronary artery disease includes several treatments. Blood pressure on admission was 152/94 mm Hg. Which treatments reduce myocardial oxygen demand? Select all that apply.

options.text: A beta blocker that slows the heart rate
options.rationale: A slower heart rate means less work for the heart muscle, so it needs less oxygen.

options.text: Percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent
options.rationale: PCI opens the narrowed artery. It improves coronary flow, the supply side, rather than lowering demand.

options.text: Rest periods between activities such as bathing and walking
options.rationale: Rest lowers the heart's workload and therefore its oxygen needs.

options.text: Lowering the blood pressure from 152/94 mm Hg toward the goal of below 130/80 mm Hg
options.rationale: The heart pumps against the blood pressure. Lowering it toward the goal of below 130/80 mm Hg reduces workload and oxygen demand.

options.text: Coronary artery bypass grafting
options.rationale: CABG routes blood around the blocked artery. It improves supply, not demand.

options.text: Antiplatelet therapy
options.rationale: Antiplatelet therapy helps keep a clot from forming on plaque. It protects flow, the supply side.

questions.takeaway: CAD treatment works on both sides of the balance: improve coronary flow (PCI or stent, CABG, antiplatelet therapy) and reduce myocardial oxygen demand (beta blockers, rest, blood pressure control), while preventing complications.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Sort each treatment by side: does it bring more blood to the muscle, or make the muscle need less? Revascularization and antiplatelet therapy all work on supply.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Slower heart rate, rest, and lower blood pressure all cut workload.
PCI, CABG, and antiplatelet therapy all protect or restore flow.
A, C, D.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client is admitted with coronary artery disease. Cardiac catheterization shows long, calcified narrowings in three coronary arteries. Which treatment does the nurse prepare the client for, and why?

options.text: Percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent, because it opens the vessel without surgery
options.rationale: PCI works best for single or double vessel disease with discrete, noncalcified lesions. These narrowings are long, calcified and in three vessels.

options.text: Coronary artery bypass grafting, because it improves cardiac output in heart failure
options.rationale: Bypass grafting is the right procedure, but improving cardiac output is a heart failure goal. CAD treatment aims to improve flow, reduce myocardial oxygen demand, and prevent complications.

options.text: Coronary artery bypass grafting, because grafts carry blood around the diseased arteries
options.rationale: CABG bypasses occluded arteries with grafts. It is indicated for multivessel disease that PCI does not suit, such as long, calcified narrowings in three vessels.

options.text: Fibrinolytic therapy, because it dissolves the material that is narrowing the arteries
options.rationale: Fibrinolytics dissolve a fresh clot. They do not treat fixed calcified narrowing.

questions.takeaway: CAD treatment aims to improve coronary flow, reduce myocardial oxygen demand, and prevent complications, using risk factor reduction, nitrates, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, antiplatelet therapy, and revascularization by PCI or CABG.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ask what each treatment does: opens a discrete lesion, bypasses disease a stent cannot treat, or dissolves a fresh clot. Then check that the reason matches a CAD goal, not a heart failure goal.

steps.action: Match the disease to the procedure
steps.detail: Long, calcified narrowings in three vessels do not suit PCI: CABG.
Fibrinolytics act on a fresh clot, not calcified plaque.
Only one gives the reason that fits CAD; improving cardiac output belongs to heart failure.

elimination.verdict: C. Coronary artery bypass grafting, because grafts carry blood around the diseased arteries.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A nurse evaluates discharge teaching on risk factor reduction with six clients who have coronary artery disease. Which client statements indicate a need for further teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: "My diabetes is a risk I can change, because keeping my glucose in my target range lowers it."
options.rationale: Diabetes and insulin resistance are modifiable risk factors, and glucose control lowers the risk.

options.text: "My LDL reached my target on the statin, so the fried food I eat most days no longer adds to my risk."
options.rationale: Reaching an LDL target is real progress, but an atherogenic diet is its own modifiable risk factor. The cue is fried food most days.

options.text: "Being 67 years old is a risk I cannot change, so I will put my effort into my weight and my walking."
options.rationale: The client correctly separates a nonmodifiable factor from modifiable ones and acts on the modifiable ones.

options.text: "My parent had a heart attack at 52, so my risk is already set and stopping smoking would not change much."
options.rationale: Family history is nonmodifiable, but it does not cancel the benefit of changing modifiable factors. Smoking is one of the most important to stop.

options.text: "My pressure is 126/78 mm Hg on my medicine, so I will keep taking it and keep my salt low."
options.rationale: Hypertension is controlled by both the drug and sodium reduction, and the client keeps both going.

options.text: "I lost 10 lb, so my weight is no longer a risk factor even though I stopped walking last month."
options.rationale: Weight loss lowers the obesity risk, but a sedentary lifestyle is a risk factor too. The cue is that the client stopped walking.

questions.takeaway: Modifiable CAD risk factors are dyslipidemia, hypertension, smoking, diabetes and insulin resistance, obesity and sedentary lifestyle, and atherogenic diet; age and family history are not modifiable. Progress on one factor never cancels another, and a nonmodifiable risk never makes the modifiable ones pointless.
questions.strategy: Each statement starts with something true. Read to the end for the cue that turns it wrong: fried food most days, would not change much, or stopped walking.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A statin target does not cancel diet; weight loss does not cancel inactivity.
Family history does not make quitting smoking pointless.
Glucose control, acting on modifiable factors at 67, and drug plus salt reduction are all correct.

elimination.verdict: B, D, F.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client had chest pressure that began at 0600 on day 1 and was diagnosed with an acute myocardial infarction. Percutaneous coronary intervention opened the blocked artery at 0900. Compared with a client whose artery stays blocked, this client's troponin I and creatine kinase MB levels peaked earlier, which reflects [[1]].

On day 6, troponin I is still elevated, while creatine kinase MB has returned to the client's baseline. This pattern is expected because [[2]].

The nurse explains that troponin T and I are the preferred markers for an acute myocardial infarction because [[3]].

options.text: A larger area of heart muscle damage than in a blocked artery
options.rationale: An earlier peak reflects the return of flow, not the size of the damage. Reperfusion is meant to limit damage.

options.text: A second infarction that occurred during the procedure
options.rationale: A second infarction would cause a new rise later. An early peak after flow returns is the expected pattern.

options.text: Washout of the markers from the heart muscle once blood flow returned
options.rationale: Restoring flow carries the markers out of the injured muscle into the blood quickly, so levels peak earlier after reperfusion.

options.text: Injury to the leg muscle where the catheter was inserted
options.rationale: Troponin T and I are specific to heart muscle, so a catheter site cannot explain an earlier troponin peak.

options.text: Troponin stays elevated for days longer than creatine kinase MB
options.rationale: Creatine kinase MB returns to baseline within a few days, while troponin remains elevated for more than a week after an infarction.

options.text: The infarction has healed by day 6, so creatine kinase MB is no longer released
options.rationale: Healing takes weeks. The difference reflects how long each marker stays in the blood, not completed healing.

options.text: Troponin rises again each day that ischemia continues
options.rationale: A persisting troponin after one infarction is expected. It does not mean new ischemia is happening each day.

options.text: They rise within minutes of reversible ischemia
options.rationale: Reversible ischemia, as in unstable angina, does not cause a detectable troponin rise. Troponin rises over hours after cell death.

options.text: They are released only from damaged heart muscle
options.rationale: Troponin T and I are specific to cardiac muscle, so an elevated level points to heart muscle injury.

options.text: They also rise with injury to skeletal muscle, which widens the time to detect damage
options.rationale: Troponin T and I are specific to cardiac muscle. Skeletal muscle injury does not raise them, which is why they are preferred over less specific markers.

questions.takeaway: Troponin T and I are the preferred markers for acute MI because they are specific to heart muscle, and they stay elevated for more than a week. Creatine kinase MB returns to baseline within a few days. Reperfusion makes both markers peak earlier.
questions.strategy: Read the graph in two parts: reperfusion changes when the markers peak, and each marker's lifespan in the blood explains the day 6 pattern.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Flow returned at 0900, so the markers wash out and peak early.
Creatine kinase MB clears in days; troponin lingers longer.
Troponin is specific to heart muscle.

elimination.verdict: Washout after flow returned; troponin stays elevated longer; troponin is released only from damaged heart muscle.
