questions.stem: A client, 64 years old, had a stent placed in a coronary artery 2 days ago and is going home on aspirin 81 mg and clopidogrel 75 mg, both once daily. Which statement by the client shows understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "I will call my provider if I have black stools, nosebleeds or bruises I cannot explain."
options.rationale: Bleeding is the major side effect of aspirin and clopidogrel taken together. Black stools, nosebleeds and unexplained bruising are signs to report.

options.text: "I can take an over the counter pain reliever with aspirin for my back, since aspirin protects my heart."
options.rationale: Products with added aspirin raise the dose and the bleeding risk. Over the counter pain relievers with aspirin are avoided.

options.text: "Once a month passes with no chest pain, I can stop the clopidogrel on my own."
options.rationale: Clopidogrel keeps platelets from clumping on the stent and is continued for up to 12 months. Stopping it without the provider raises the risk of a clot.

options.text: "I will take my aspirin on an empty stomach so that it starts working faster."
options.rationale: Aspirin is taken with food because it irritates the stomach. Taking it on an empty stomach raises that risk.

questions.takeaway: After a stent, dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor such as clopidogrel prevents clotting on the stent. Teach to report bleeding, avoid extra aspirin, take with food and never stop the drugs without the provider.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each wrong option sounds like a reasonable plan for the client. Ask which one matches the main risk of two antiplatelet drugs together: bleeding.

steps.detail: Two antiplatelet drugs together raise bleeding risk.
Extra aspirin adds to that risk.
Stopping clopidogrel early risks a clot in the new stent.
Aspirin is taken with food.

elimination.verdict: The client will report signs of bleeding.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client with coronary artery disease and a predictable pattern of angina calls the clinic from home. Chest pressure began 7 minutes ago while carrying laundry upstairs. The client sat down and placed 1 sublingual nitroglycerin tablet under the tongue 5 minutes ago. The pressure is 5 of 10, the same as before the tablet. The client adds, "The tablet did not tingle. That bottle was opened 8 months ago and I keep the pills in a plastic pill box. I have a new bottle in the cabinet." Which instruction does the nurse give?

options.text: "Your tablets have likely lost strength. Take one from the new bottle now, and call back if the pressure has not eased in 5 minutes."
options.rationale: The old tablets may well have lost potency, since they lose strength over 3 to 5 months and outside a glass container. But the rule is about time, not the tablet: no relief 5 minutes after 1 tablet means 911 now.

options.text: "Call 911 now. While you wait for the ambulance, take a tablet from the new bottle."
options.rationale: Chest pressure that has not eased 5 minutes after 1 tablet calls for 911 now, whatever the reason the tablet failed. The client may then take a fresh tablet while waiting.

options.text: "Lie down and rest 10 more minutes, because rest is what usually ends your pressure."
options.rationale: The client has already rested 7 minutes and taken a tablet with no relief. Pressure that does not respond is not the usual pattern.

options.text: "Have a neighbor drive you to the emergency department now, and bring the old bottle with you."
options.rationale: Emergency care is needed, but a private car cannot give care if the rhythm or pressure worsens on the way. Emergency services are called.

questions.takeaway: At home: stop, sit or lie down, take 1 nitroglycerin tablet, and wait 5 minutes. If there is no relief, call 911, then repeat the tablet every 5 minutes while waiting. Replace tablets every 3 to 5 months and keep them in a glass, light resistant container.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The old bottle is a real problem and makes A tempting. The deciding cue is the time: 5 minutes after 1 tablet with the pressure unchanged. The 911 call does not wait for a second try.

steps.detail: 5 minutes after 1 tablet, pressure unchanged at 5 of 10.
No relief at 5 minutes means call 911 now.
Lost potency explains the failure but does not change the rule; a fresh tablet is taken while waiting.
More rest delays care; a private car cannot give care on the way.

elimination.verdict: Call 911 now and take a fresh tablet while waiting.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a client with suspected coronary artery disease about the diagnostic tests the provider has prescribed. Which statements by the client indicate correct understanding? Select all that apply.

options.text: "The catheterization will show exactly where my heart arteries are narrowed and how much."
options.rationale: Cardiac catheterization shows the extent and exact location of coronary obstructions and helps decide between PCI and CABG.

options.text: "The treadmill stress test watches my heart tracing for signs of low oxygen while my heart works harder."
options.rationale: The exercise tolerance test looks for ECG changes of ischemia as exertion raises the heart's demand.

options.text: "The thallium scan shows cold spots where blood is not reaching my heart muscle."
options.rationale: Thallium imaging shows areas of reduced or absent perfusion, called cold spots, that mark ischemia or infarction.

options.text: "The echocardiogram measures how much troponin my heart muscle is releasing."
options.rationale: An echocardiogram is an ultrasound of heart structure and motion. Troponin is measured with a blood test.

options.text: "The chest x ray can show whether my heart is enlarged or fluid is building up in my lungs."
options.rationale: A chest x ray shows the size of the heart and congestion in the lungs. It does not show plaque inside the coronary arteries.

options.text: "The stress test is done while I have chest pressure so the tracing catches the problem."
options.rationale: A stress test is done after an acute episode has passed. Exercising during active chest pressure would worsen ischemia.

questions.takeaway: Catheterization maps the location and extent of narrowing; the stress test shows ischemia under exertion; thallium shows cold spots; echocardiography shows structure; troponin is a blood test; the chest x ray shows heart size and lung congestion, not plaque.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Match each test with what it actually measures. Wrong options pair a real test with a job that belongs to a different test.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Location and extent of narrowing: correct.
Ischemia under exertion and cold spots: correct.
Heart size and lung congestion: correct.
An echocardiogram does not measure troponin.
No stress test during active chest pressure.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E.

questions.stem: A client in a cardiac unit has chest pressure, 6 of 10, at 1400. Blood pressure is 136/82 mm Hg and heart rate is 88 beats per minute. The nurse has the client lie down and gives 1 sublingual nitroglycerin tablet, prescribed every 5 minutes for up to 3 tablets. At 1405, chest pressure is 4 of 10, blood pressure is 104/64 mm Hg, and heart rate is 94 beats per minute. The client is alert and denies dizziness. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the second tablet, because the pressure persists and the systolic pressure is above 100 mm Hg
options.rationale: The systolic is above 100 mm Hg, but it has fallen 32 mm Hg in 5 minutes. The textbook rule is to lower the head of the bed and notify the provider if the systolic is less than 100 mm Hg or 25 mm Hg lower than the previous reading.

options.text: Give the second tablet and recheck the pressure in 5 minutes, because the chest pressure is easing
options.rationale: Easing pain shows the drug is working, but it does not make another dose safe after a 32 mm Hg fall. A second tablet could drop the pressure further.

options.text: Sit the client upright and recheck the blood pressure in 5 minutes before deciding on the dose
options.rationale: Rechecking is reasonable, but sitting upright can lower the pressure further. The head of the bed is kept low after a nitrate causes a large drop.

options.text: Withhold the second tablet, keep the head of the bed low, and notify the provider
options.rationale: The systolic fell from 136 to 104 mm Hg, more than 25 mm Hg below the previous reading. The nurse holds the next dose, keeps the client low and reports for another plan.

questions.takeaway: Before repeating sublingual nitroglycerin, check the blood pressure 5 minutes after each dose. Hold the next dose, lower the head of the bed and notify the provider if the systolic is below 100 mm Hg or 25 mm Hg lower than the previous reading.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A tempts because the prescription allows up to 3 tablets and the systolic is still above 100 mm Hg. The deciding cue is the 32 mm Hg fall from 136 to 104 mm Hg in 5 minutes.

steps.detail: Systolic 104 mm Hg is above 100, but it fell 32 mm Hg.
A fall of more than 25 mm Hg means hold the next dose.
A and B both give the second tablet.
C raises the head when it should stay low.

elimination.verdict: Withhold the second tablet, keep the client low and notify the provider.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the history of a client, 58 years old, before teaching about atherosclerosis. Which findings are risk factors for atherosclerosis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Type 2 diabetes for 10 years
options.rationale: Diabetes is a listed risk factor for atherosclerosis and also injures the endothelium.

options.text: Rheumatoid arthritis treated for 6 years
options.rationale: Autoimmunity is a listed risk factor for atherosclerosis, even though the disease is best known for its joint effects.

options.text: Heartburn after large meals for 2 years
options.rationale: Heartburn can mimic chest discomfort, but a digestive problem is not a risk factor for plaque in the arteries.

options.text: Smokes half a pack of cigarettes a day
options.rationale: Smoking is a listed risk factor, and even a lower daily amount injures the endothelium.

options.text: Mitral valve prolapse found on an echocardiogram
options.rationale: This is a structural valve problem. It is a cardiac finding, but it does not cause plaque to form in the arterial wall.

options.text: Blood pressure averaging 148/92 mm Hg over 3 visits
options.rationale: Hypertension is a listed risk factor and a cause of endothelial injury.

questions.takeaway: Risk factors for atherosclerosis are diabetes, smoking, hyperlipidemia or dyslipidemia, hypertension, and autoimmunity. A cardiac or chest finding is not a risk factor unless it promotes plaque in the arterial wall.
questions.strategy: Check each finding against the five listed risk factors. Watch for the autoimmune disease that looks unrelated, and for cardiac sounding findings that do not build plaque.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Diabetes, smoking, and hypertension are listed.
Rheumatoid arthritis is autoimmune, and autoimmunity is listed.
Heartburn and a valve problem do not build plaque.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, F.

questions.objective: Explain how atherosclerosis contributes to the development of coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: A client, 62 years old, has had chest pressure only with brisk walking for 2 years, in a predictable pattern that ends with rest. The client was told the diagnosis is coronary artery disease and says, "My neighbor had a heart attack and was told it was coronary artery disease too. Do we have the same problem?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "Both are coronary artery disease. Your angina is the chronic form, and the acute coronary syndromes are unstable angina and heart attack."
options.rationale: Coronary artery disease is any disorder that narrows or occludes the coronary arteries, leading to ischemia or infarction. It includes chronic angina with a predictable pattern and the acute coronary syndromes, unstable angina and myocardial infarction.

options.text: "Both are coronary artery disease. Your angina is the chronic form, and the acute coronary syndromes are unstable angina and heart failure."
options.rationale: The chronic form is correct, but heart failure is not an acute coronary syndrome. The acute coronary syndromes are unstable angina and myocardial infarction.

options.text: "Both are acute coronary syndromes, because any chest pressure from a narrowed heart artery belongs in that group."
options.rationale: Angina in a predictable pattern that ends with rest is the chronic form. Acute coronary syndromes are new, worsening, or at rest pain from unstable angina, or a myocardial infarction.

options.text: "No. Coronary artery disease means a heart attack has damaged the muscle, so your angina is a separate condition."
options.rationale: Coronary artery disease covers ischemia as well as infarction. The client's angina is coronary artery disease without an infarction.

questions.takeaway: Coronary artery disease is any vascular disorder that narrows or occludes the coronary arteries, causing ischemia or infarction. The spectrum runs from chronic angina in a predictable pattern to the acute coronary syndromes: unstable angina (reversible ischemia) and myocardial infarction.
questions.strategy: Two options share the same frame. Check what each places under the acute coronary syndromes: unstable angina and myocardial infarction, not heart failure.

steps.detail: Narrowing or occlusion of coronary arteries causing ischemia or infarction.
Predictable pattern that ends with rest: the chronic form.
Acute coronary syndromes are unstable angina and infarction, not heart failure.
Not every angina is acute, and the disease is not limited to infarction.

elimination.verdict: Both are coronary artery disease, at different points on the spectrum.

questions.objective: Recognize common risk factors, manifestations, diagnostic tests, and treatment approaches for CAD.

questions.stem: A client with chronic angina in a predictable pattern started a calcium channel blocker 3 weeks ago. Episodes of angina are now 1 per week, were 4 per week before the drug. Today: blood pressure 116/72 mm Hg sitting, was 138/86 mm Hg before the drug, and heart rate 74 beats per minute; the client denies dizziness. There is new 2+ pitting edema in both ankles. Neck veins are flat with the head of the bed at 45 degrees, the lungs are clear in both bases, and weight is unchanged on the same scale for 3 weeks. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: New right sided heart failure, because the ankle edema shows blood backing up into the systemic veins
options.rationale: Dependent edema is a right sided finding, but flat neck veins, clear lungs, and an unchanged weight do not support venous congestion or fluid gain.

options.text: A desired effect of the drug, since the angina episodes have dropped and the edema shows better perfusion
options.rationale: Fewer episodes do show benefit, but edema is not a sign of better perfusion. It is an adverse effect that the nurse monitors.

options.text: Peripheral edema, a known adverse effect of the drug, to report to the provider
options.rationale: Calcium channel blockers cause vasodilation, and the nurse monitors for hypotension and peripheral edema. With flat neck veins, clear lungs, and no weight gain, the edema fits the drug rather than heart failure. The lower pressure without dizziness is the expected effect, not hypotension.

options.text: Fluid overload from sodium retention caused by the drug, so the client should restrict fluids
options.rationale: The weight is unchanged and the lungs are clear, so there is no evidence of fluid overload. Fluid restriction is not a nursing decision and does not address a drug effect.

questions.takeaway: Calcium channel blockers promote vasodilation and myocardial perfusion. Monitor for hypotension and peripheral edema, and review how often angina episodes occur to judge benefit.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Ankle edema makes heart failure tempting. Look for the findings that would go with venous congestion or fluid gain; when JVD, crackles, and weight gain are all absent, the edema points to the drug.

steps.detail: Angina down from 4 to 1 episode per week: the drug is helping.
Flat neck veins, clear lungs, unchanged weight: no congestion or fluid gain.
Peripheral edema is a known adverse effect of a calcium channel blocker, and a lower pressure without dizziness is an expected effect.
Edema is not a benefit, and fluid restriction is not indicated.

elimination.verdict: Peripheral edema from the drug, reported to the provider; the lower pressure is an expected effect.
